units.title: How a type is built
units.blurb: What every object has: System.Object, the header and the type pointer, the Equals/GetHashCode contract; casts, is, as and unboxing; primitives, checked and overflow, dynamic and its cost.

lessons.title: System.Object inside out
lessons.sub: Six methods, the object header and the Equals/GetHashCode contract

cards.title: What every type inherits
cards.body:
Every type in .NET — class, struct, record, array — ultimately derives from System.Object. That is why every value has the same set of methods:

Public: Equals, GetHashCode, ToString — virtual, you can override them; GetType — not virtual.
Protected: MemberwiseClone — a shallow copy; Finalize — called by the garbage collector.
Static: ReferenceEquals and Equals(a, b).

cards.title: An object on the heap: two hidden words
cards.body:
When you write new Order(), the heap gets more than room for the fields. Two bookkeeping words sit in front of them:

The object header — bits for lock, the default hash code and a link to a sync block if one was needed.
The type pointer (MethodTable) — the address of the structure where the CLR keeps everything about the type: size, parent, interfaces, the virtual method table.

A reference in a variable points exactly at the type pointer. GetType, casts and virtual calls all work through it.
cards.deep:
On a 64-bit platform the header and the type pointer take 8 bytes each. The header sits at a negative offset: the reference points at the MethodTable word, and the header is 8 bytes before it. Even an empty class has a minimum object size of 24 bytes: the collector needs room for at least one pointer-sized field.

A struct on the stack or inside another object has neither word — just its fields. They appear when the struct is boxed: the box is an ordinary heap object with its own header and type pointer.

cards.q: How many bytes does an instance of an empty class Empty { } take on the heap in a 64-bit process?
cards.explain: 8 bytes of header, 8 bytes of type pointer and the minimum room for one pointer-sized field. On x64 no object is smaller than 24 bytes.

wrong.1: There are no fields, but every object has the bookkeeping words.
wrong.3: 16 is just the header and the type pointer. The CLR still reserves room for one more word.

cards.title: Why GetType cannot be overridden
cards.body:
GetType computes nothing: it takes the type pointer from the object itself and returns the matching Type. If the method were virtual, a class could lie: "I am a string." And all of type safety rests on that pointer telling the truth: casts, is, calling the right method.

So GetType is not virtual. You can hide it with new, but code that looks through object still gets the real type.
cards.deep:
The difference from typeof(T): typeof is the type known to the compiler, GetType() is the type of a particular object at run time. With Animal a = new Cat() the static type is Animal, but a.GetType() returns Cat.

A Nullable twist: int? x = 5; x.GetType() returns System.Int32. The call goes through boxing, and a boxed int? is simply a boxed int. If x is null, you get a NullReferenceException.

cards.q: Which System.Object methods can you override with override? Select all.
cards.explain: GetType and MemberwiseClone are not virtual. Finalize is virtual too, but in C# you write it with finalizer syntax ~Name() rather than override.

cards.title: How a dictionary finds a key
cards.body:
Dictionary and HashSet search in two steps: GetHashCode picks a bucket, and Equals compares against the entries in that bucket. Hence the contract:

1. If a.Equals(b), their hashes must match. The reverse is not required: equal hashes for different objects are an ordinary collision.
2. While an object is a dictionary key, its hash must not change.
3. Equals is reflexive, symmetric, transitive and returns false for null.

By default a class compares references in Equals, and GetHashCode is different for every object. Override only Equals and you break rule 1. The compiler warns you: CS0659.

cards.q: Point overrides only Equals. What does this code print?
cards.code:
var set = new HashSet<Point> { new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 } };
Console.WriteLine(set.Contains(new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 }));
cards.explain: Two different objects have different default hashes. The lookup goes to the wrong bucket (or is filtered out by the hash mismatch) and never reaches Equals. True is only possible on an accidental hash match.

wrong.3: CS0659 is a warning, not an error. The code builds and quietly works wrong.

cards.q: Point now overrides both Equals and GetHashCode using X and Y. Which line prints False?
cards.explain: After p.X = 10 the hash changed, but the object sits in the bucket computed from the old hash. The set looks in the new bucket and finds nothing — even though it is the very same object. Dictionary keys should be immutable.

cards.q: Complete the pair of methods so the contract holds
cards.explain: The pattern is Point p checks the type and rules out null at the same time. HashCode.Combine mixes the field hashes. Even simpler is a record: the compiler writes Equals and GetHashCode over all fields for you.

cards.title: MemberwiseClone and Finalize: what they cost
cards.body:
MemberwiseClone creates a new object of the same type and copies the fields bit by bit. No constructor runs, and reference fields are copied as references: the original and the copy share the same list. The method is protected — outside code cannot copy an object this way, only the type itself can.

Finalize is written in C# as ~Name(). It is not a destructor in the C++ sense: the garbage collector decides when it runs. Such an object is more expensive to create (it is registered in the finalization queue), and it survives an extra garbage collection.
cards.deep:
The compiler turns a finalizer into protected override void Finalize() that calls base.Finalize() in a finally. In modern .NET finalizers do not run at process exit (in .NET Framework they did), so you cannot rely on them even "at the very end". For resources use IDisposable and SafeHandle.

The with expression on records does not use MemberwiseClone: the compiler generates a copy constructor and a hidden clone method. The copy is still shallow.

cards.q: Match the method to what it does
pairs: Is it the very same object?
A shallow copy without a constructor

cards.q: What does object.ReferenceEquals(42, 42) return?
cards.explain: ReferenceEquals takes object, so each 42 is boxed into its own box. Two different boxes are two different references. For value types ReferenceEquals is always false.

lessons.title: Casts: is, as and patterns
lessons.sub: How the CLR checks a type, why (long)(object)42 fails and where operators stay silent

cards.title: Up is free, down is checked
cards.body:
A cast to a base type or an interface is implicit: the compiler already knows a Manager is an Employee. Nothing happens at run time; the reference stays the same.

Going back down to a derived type takes an explicit cast in parentheses. The compiler does not know what really sits in the variable, so it inserts a check that runs at run time.

The same parentheses do different things: for numbers, (int)3.9 is a conversion of the value (you get 3); for references, it is only a check of the type, and the object does not change.

cards.title: How the CLR checks a cast
cards.body:
For (Manager)o the compiler emits the IL instruction castclass. At run time the CLR reads the type pointer from the object and compares it with Manager. No match — it walks up the parent chain, and for an interface, through the type's list of interfaces. Found — the cast succeeds. Not found — InvalidCastException.

An important detail: null passes any cast to a reference type. There is nothing to check, so there is no exception.
cards.deep: In modern .NET this logic lives in managed code (the CastHelpers class in the runtime) and uses a cache of cast results. A cast to a sealed class is often reduced by the JIT to a single pointer comparison: there are no subclasses, so the type must match exactly. A cast to an interface or to a class deep in a hierarchy costs more. These are nanoseconds, but in a hot loop over millions of objects the difference shows up in a profiler.

cards.q: Manager derives from Employee. Which line throws InvalidCastException?
cards.explain: o holds an Employee, not a Manager: a parent does not become a subclass. The null line passes: casting null to a reference type always succeeds.

cards.title: is, as and patterns
cards.body:
is and as compile to the IL instruction isinst: the same check, but without an exception. is returns a bool, as returns the reference or null.

Older code often checks the type twice: first with is, then with a cast. The pattern is Manager m does one check and hands you a variable of the right type straight away.

cards.q: Match the expression to what happens when o is not a Manager
Why does int n = o as int; not compile?
options: as returns null on failure, and an int cannot be null
An int cannot be taken out of an object
You have to write as Int32
cards.explain: For value types write o as int? or, better, o is int n: the check and the unboxing in one step.

cards.title: is null and is not null
cards.body: A class can overload == — and then x == null calls its code, which may be wrong or slow. The patterns is null and is not null never call overloaded operators: the compiler compares the reference itself with null.

cards.title: Unboxing: the exact type only
cards.body:
A boxed int is a heap object whose type pointer says "Int32". Unboxing (IL unbox) checks that the box holds exactly the requested type and copies the value. It does no numeric conversion at all.

That is why (long)(object)42 fails with InvalidCastException, even though (long)42 works. Unbox to the exact type first, then convert.
cards.code:
object o = 42;          // the box holds Int32
long a = (long)o;       // InvalidCastException
long b = (long)(int)o;  // unbox the int, then widen
int c = (int)(object)null!; // NullReferenceException
cards.deep: The "exactly the same type" rule has exceptions. An enum and its underlying integer type unbox into each other: (DayOfWeek)(object)1 works. A boxed int can be unboxed into int?, and a boxed int? does not exist at all: boxing turns a Nullable into either a box with an int or null. Unboxing null into int gives a NullReferenceException, into int? simply null.

cards.q: object o = 42; Which expression runs without an exception?
cards.explain: The box can only be unboxed into Int32. After that, (long) is an ordinary widening numeric conversion.

cards.title: Conversion operators are invisible through object
cards.body:
A user-defined explicit operator is a static method. The compiler picks it based on static types: from Celsius to Fahrenheit, it calls the operator. But if the value sits in an object, the compiler sees "object → Fahrenheit" and emits a plain unbox. At run time the box holds a Celsius, not a Fahrenheit — InvalidCastException.

The same scenario breaks code during a refactoring: a parameter changes from Celsius to object, everything compiles, and the cast starts failing.

cards.q: Which lines throw InvalidCastException? Select all.
options: object o = new Celsius(5); var f = (Fahrenheit)o;
cards.explain: A string is not an int; unboxing needs the exact type; a conversion operator is not called through object. null passes a cast to string, and an int unboxes fine from a box holding an int.

cards.q: Complete the pattern checks
cards.code:
if (o is ___ m) m.Approve();

if (input is not ___) Use(input);
cards.explain: is Manager m is a type check and a variable in one step. is not null checks the reference without any overloaded !=.

lessons.title: Primitives, checked and dynamic
lessons.sub: int is System.Int32, overflow is silent by default, and dynamic pays on every call

cards.title: int is just another name
cards.body:
C# keywords are aliases for library types: int is System.Int32, long is System.Int64, string is System.String, object is System.Object. A compiled assembly has no "int" in it — only Int32.

The size does not depend on the platform: an int is always 32 bits. The exception is nint and nuint: these are pointer-sized integers, 32 bits in a 32-bit process and 64 in a 64-bit one.
cards.code:
int a = 5;
System.Int32 b = a;        // the same type, not a conversion
Console.WriteLine(a.GetType());   // System.Int32

nint p = 0;                // System.IntPtr
Console.WriteLine(IntPtr.Size);   // 8 in a 64-bit process
cards.deep: nint and nuint arrived in C# 9 as separate keywords on top of IntPtr/UIntPtr, with arithmetic. Since C# 11 and .NET 7 they are full aliases: nint and IntPtr are the same thing, operators included. They are for interop and low-level code: indexes into native memory, buffer lengths, offsets.

cards.q: Match the C# keyword to the CLR type

cards.title: What "primitive" means to the CLR
cards.body:
To the CLR, a primitive is a type that has its own IL instructions. Adding two ints is the add instruction, and the JIT turns it into a single machine instruction.

decimal looks the same — it has literals like 1.5m and operators. But to the CLR it is an ordinary 16-byte struct. For decimal, a + b compiles to a call to the op_Addition method, and the arithmetic is done in software. That is why decimal is noticeably slower than double — you pay for an exact decimal fraction.
cards.code:
int x = a + b;       // IL: add
double y = c + d;    // IL: add
decimal z = m + n;   // IL: call Decimal.op_Addition
cards.deep: Type.IsPrimitive returns true for Boolean, Byte, SByte, Int16, UInt16, Int32, UInt32, Int64, UInt64, IntPtr, UIntPtr, Char, Single and Double. For decimal and string it returns false. A const decimal is allowed in C#, but the metadata does not store it as an ordinary literal constant — it uses the DecimalConstantAttribute attribute instead.

cards.q: What does typeof(decimal).IsPrimitive return?
cards.explain: decimal has no IL instructions of its own: its operators are ordinary static methods of the Decimal struct.

cards.title: Overflow is silent by default
cards.body:
For integers the compiler emits the add instruction by default. It does not check for overflow: the high bits are simply dropped. int.MaxValue + 1 gives int.MinValue — no exception.

In a checked context the compiler emits add.ovf, and overflow throws OverflowException. The same goes for an explicit narrowing: (int)someLong cuts off the high bits when unchecked and throws when checked.

The cost of the check is a compare and a conditional jump after the operation. Usually that is pennies, but in tight loops it can get in the way of JIT optimizations.

cards.q: A project with default settings. Which line throws OverflowException?
cards.explain: The default context is unchecked: a becomes int.MinValue, and b gets the low 32 bits (705032704). The exception only happens where checked is written explicitly.

cards.title: Constants, the project flag and where checked ends
cards.body:
Constants are evaluated by the compiler itself and are always checked: int x = int.MaxValue + 1; is error CS0220. When overflow is intended (in a hash function, say), write unchecked(...).

The project flag <CheckForOverflowUnderflow>true</CheckForOverflowUnderflow> makes checked the default context for the whole project. It is often turned on in Debug to catch overflows during tests.

Boundaries: checked only affects code written inside the block. Methods called from there are compiled by their own rules.

Other numbers: decimal always throws OverflowException, double and float never throw — they go to infinity.
cards.code:
int x = int.MaxValue + 1;             // error CS0220
int y = unchecked(int.MaxValue + 1);  // allowed: -2147483648

checked { Helper(); }  // inside Helper — its own context
cards.deep: Since C# 11 a numeric type of your own can declare two versions of an operator: the regular one and operator checked +. The compiler calls the checked version in a checked context. That is how the built-in types in generic math work, for example Int128.

cards.q: What throws OverflowException without any checked? Select all.
cards.explain: decimal always checks for overflow, and so do the Convert methods. An int silently wraps when unchecked, and a double becomes infinity.

cards.title: dynamic: the type is resolved at run time
cards.body:
To the CLR, dynamic is object with a marker. The compiler does not check whether the value has the method; instead, at every operation it creates a call site — an object that picks the method at run time.

On the first call, the runtime binder from the Microsoft.CSharp assembly looks at the actual types of the arguments and finds the method using C# rules. It compiles the result into a rule — "if the types are these, call that" — and puts it in the call site cache. Later calls with the same types go straight through the ready rule.

No method found — RuntimeBinderException at run time, not a compile error.
cards.code:
dynamic d = "text";
int n = d.Length;   // 4: Length is found at run time
d = 42;             // the int is boxed: dynamic is object
d.Foo();            // RuntimeBinderException
cards.deep:
A call site is a CallSite<T> with a Target delegate. The cache has several levels: the rule in the delegate itself, a set of recent rules for this call site and a shared binder cache. If one place receives a string one time and a List the next, the rules multiply, and with frequently changing types the cost of the check grows too.

What dynamic cannot do: extension methods (the binder does not look for them), and lambdas as arguments without an explicit delegate type. It also does not get along well with trimming and Native AOT: the binder relies on reflection and on generating code at run time.

cards.q: Put in order what happens on the first call to d.Foo(1)
items: The compiler has already created a call site for this operation
The call site cache is empty — the call goes to the runtime binder
The binder looks at the actual types of d and the argument
It picks the Foo method using C# rules
It compiles a rule and puts it in the cache
The next call with the same types uses the cached rule
cards.explain: Only the first pass is expensive: binding and compiling the rule. After that it is a type check and a call through a delegate.

cards.q: dynamic d = new List<int>(); d.Sum(); — what happens?
cards.explain: Sum is an extension method from System.Linq. The binder only looks at the type's own methods, so it does not find it. This works: Enumerable.Sum((List<int>)d).

wrong.2: With dynamic the compiler checks nothing — the error only shows up at run time.

cards.q: What is true about the cost of dynamic? Select all.
options: The first call at each call site is expensive
Value types in dynamic are boxed
Type errors only show up at run time
After the first call it is as fast as a regular call
cards.explain: Even from the cache, the call goes through a delegate with a type check — slower than a direct call. dynamic fits COM, schemaless JSON and scripting, not hot code.

lessons.title: Final: inside a type
lessons.sub: Objects on the heap, casts, primitives and dynamic

cards.q: An object on the heap of a 64-bit process. Which are true? Select all.
options: The reference in a variable points at the word holding the type pointer (MethodTable)
The object header sits 8 bytes before that word
A boxed int takes 24 bytes on the heap
A struct in a local variable also has a header and a type pointer
GetType reads the type from the object header
cards.explain: A boxed int is an ordinary object: an 8-byte header, an 8-byte type pointer and 4 bytes of value, padded up to the 24-byte minimum. A struct outside a box has no overhead words. GetType reads the type pointer; the header holds bits for lock and the hash code.

cards.q: Equals compares fields, and GetHashCode returns 0 for every object. What happens to a dictionary that uses these objects as keys?
options: Keys are found, but they all land in one bucket and lookups become linear
The contract is broken: the dictionary starts losing keys
Nothing changes: the hash only affects Equals
cards.explain: The contract demands one thing: equal objects produce equal hashes. Zero for everyone satisfies it. But there is a single bucket for all keys, and every lookup compares the key with each element via Equals — O(n) instead of O(1).

wrong.1: A key gets lost when equal objects produce different hashes. Here the hashes are always equal.
wrong.2: CS0659 warns that GetHashCode is not overridden at all. Here it is.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.code:
int? x = 5;
Console.WriteLine(x.GetType());
cards.explain: GetType is non-virtual and defined on object, so the int? is boxed first. A boxed int? that has a value is a box with a plain int. If x were null, boxing would produce null and the call would throw NullReferenceException.

cards.q: Which line throws InvalidCastException?
cards.explain: The box holds an Int16. (short)o unboxes the exact type, then short widens to int implicitly. (int)o tries to unbox an Int32 from a box holding an Int16 — exception. An enum and its underlying type unbox into each other, and as returns null on failure.

cards.q: Match the IL instruction to the C# expression it comes from
What does this code print?
cards.explain: Each 1 is boxed into its own box. == on two objects compares references, and the boxes are different. Equals is virtual: Int32.Equals runs and compares the values.

cards.q: A project with default settings. What does this code print?
cards.explain: checked only affects code written inside the block. The addition is in Add, and Add is compiled in the project context — unchecked, a plain add instruction with no check.

wrong.1: checked does not extend into called methods: Add contains a plain add instruction.
wrong.3: CS0220 is for constant expressions. A method call is not a constant.

cards.q: You want an exception instead of dropping the high bits, and then a type check plus unboxing in one step
cards.explain: checked turns the narrowing into conv.ovf, which throws OverflowException. The pattern is int i checks that the box holds exactly an Int32 and unboxes it. as does not work with int: on failure it has nothing to return.

cards.q: What is the compile-time type of n?
cards.code:
dynamic d = new List<int> { 1, 2 };
var n = d.Count;
options: It will not compile: dynamic has no Count
cards.explain: The result of an operation on dynamic is dynamic too: the compiler does not know what Count returns. So n.Foo() compiles and fails only at run time. To get compiler checks back, write the type explicitly: int n = d.Count.

units.title: Value types all the way
units.blurb: Boxing you cannot see in the code: interfaces, GetType and ValueType methods; a mutable struct in a collection and in foreach; ValueType.Equals via reflection, IEquatable<T>, record struct and field layout.

lessons.title: Boxing you cannot see
lessons.sub: Interfaces, GetType, ValueType methods and the constrained call

cards.title: Where the compiler emits box without asking
cards.body:
The rule from the ".NET inside out" course is simple: a value is boxed when you put it where a reference is expected — into object or an interface. There boxing is visible: object o = is right there on the left.

It gets harder when the one expecting a reference is not a variable but a method. A method declared in a class (Object, ValueType) receives this as a reference to a heap object. A struct has no such reference, so calling that method needs a box. You do not see it in C# — you see it in IL (box) and in the allocation counter.

This lesson covers four places where it happens: calls through an interface, GetType, non-overridden ToString/Equals/GetHashCode, and enumerators.

cards.title: An interface on a struct: three ways to call it
cards.body:
A struct can implement an interface, but a box does not always appear. What decides is what you call through:

  • through a variable of the struct itself — an ordinary call to its method, no box;
  • through a variable of the interface type — the value is boxed first, and the call goes to the box;
  • in a generic with a where T : IShape constraint — no box, more on that below.

If the method is implemented explicitly (double IShape.Area()), you cannot call it through the struct: you have to cast to the interface, and that is boxing.
cards.deep:
The JIT treats struct methods as sealed: a struct has no subclasses, so s.Area() is a direct call and easy to inline. A call through IShape is interface dispatch via the type pointer of the box.

Explicit implementation hides rarely needed members: that is how int hides the IConvertible methods (ToBoolean, ToChar…). You can still call them, but only through the interface — that is, with boxing, unless the JIT removes it.

cards.q: Temp is a struct that implements IComparable<Temp> and overrides GetHashCode but not ToString. Where is there boxing? Select all.
cards.explain: An interface variable needs a box. ToString is not overridden — the call goes to ValueType.ToString, which needs a this object. CompareTo and GetHashCode are the struct's own — direct calls. List<Temp>.Sort goes through Comparer<Temp>.Default and generic code with no boxes.

cards.title: Non-overridden ToString, Equals, GetHashCode
cards.body:
A struct always has these three methods: the base class System.ValueType provides them. But they are class methods, and they need a this object.

The compiler emits p.ToString() with a constrained. prefix. At run time the runtime checks: if the struct overrides the method, it calls it directly, no box. If not, it boxes the value and calls the ValueType version.

Equals(object) is worse: the argument is also object, so it is boxed no matter what. And ValueType.Equals itself, as you will see in lesson 3, may go through reflection.
cards.deep:
The IL for a.ToString():

ldloca.s a
constrained. P
callvirt instance string System.Object::ToString()

Per ECMA-335 the constrained. prefix works like this: if the type is a value type and implements the method itself — a direct call on the address; if not — box and a virtual call. The JIT decides when it compiles the method, so an overridden ToString on a struct costs nothing beyond the method itself.

cards.q: P is a struct of two ints that overrides nothing. How many boxes does a.Equals(b) create according to the IL?
cards.explain: The argument b is boxed because the Equals parameter is object. And a itself is boxed because Equals is not overridden and its this must be a ValueType object. Two boxes for one comparison.

wrong.1: That is only true for a struct that implements Equals(P) — then overload resolution picks it and there are no boxes.
wrong.2: The argument is not the only box: ValueType.Equals is called on an object, so a gets boxed too.

cards.title: GetType: always through a box
cards.body:
GetType is a non-virtual Object method: it reads the type pointer from the object (unit "How a type is built"). A struct on the stack has neither a header nor a type pointer. So for s.GetType() the compiler first emits box, then call Object::GetType.

The struct type is already known at compile time, so instead of s.GetType() it is more honest to write typeof(Square). In a generic where the type is not known yet — typeof(T): for value-type T the JIT compiles separate code, and typeof(T) there is just a constant.
cards.deep: The modern JIT recognizes the box + GetType pair for an exactly known type and often folds it into a constant with no allocation. This is an optimization, not a guarantee: in a debug build and on an older runtime the box will be there. The check value.GetType() == typeof(X) is especially common — the JIT can fold that too.

cards.title: A call through an interface changes the box, not the original
cards.body:
If an interface method modifies the struct, boxing turns from an extra allocation into a logic bug. The box is a copy. The method changes a field inside the box, and the original variable stays as it was.

An on-the-fly cast is especially sneaky: ((ICounter)c).Inc(). A box is created, the counter inside it changes, and the box immediately becomes garbage. The compiler will not warn you.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: i is its own box with a copy: after i.Inc() it holds 1. ((ICounter)c).Inc() creates another box and changes it — the result is lost. c.Inc() is a direct call on the variable itself: c.Value = 1.

wrong.1: That is what you would get if Counter were a class: then c, i and the cast would all point to the same object.
wrong.2: Casting to ICounter does not give you a reference to c — it boxes a copy. The change goes into a box nobody keeps.

cards.title: A constrained generic: an interface without a box
cards.body:
For a value-type T the JIT compiles a separate version of the method (unit "Generics"). With where T : ICounter the compiler emits x.Inc() as constrained. T callvirt ICounter::Inc. For T = Counter this becomes a direct call to Counter.Inc on the variable itself — no box.

Two traps nearby:

  • a parameter without ref — the method changes its own copy, not the caller's variable;
  • a non-generic interface: where T : IComparable does not help, the argument of CompareTo(object) is still boxed. You need IComparable<T>.
cards.code:
static void BumpRef<T>(ref T x) where T : ICounter => x.Inc(); // changes the original
static void Bump<T>(T x) where T : ICounter => x.Inc();         // changes a copy
static void BumpI(ICounter x) => x.Inc();                       // box at the call
cards.deep:
using and foreach use the same mechanism: the compiler calls Dispose on a struct resource and MoveNext on a struct enumerator without boxing, even though formally these are methods of the IDisposable and IEnumerator<T> interfaces.

For shared instantiations over reference T the same constrained. simply becomes an ordinary callvirt: one piece of IL works for both cases.

cards.q: Fill in the constraint so that Max<int> compares without boxing
cards.code:
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : ___
    => a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
cards.explain: With IComparable<T>, CompareTo(T) is called: a constrained call on a and an argument b of type T — not a single box. With the non-generic IComparable the code also compiles, but b goes into CompareTo(object) and is boxed on every comparison.

cards.q: Match each expression with what happens in it. list is a List<int>.
pairs: The enumerator is boxed on the heap
A constrained call with no box
p.ToString() on a struct without override
A box for the sake of ValueType.ToString

cards.title: Then and now: the JIT removes some boxes
cards.body:
A box in IL does not yet mean an object on the heap. Over time the JIT has learned to remove common cases:

  • Enum.HasFlag in .NET Framework boxed both the value and the argument. Since .NET Core 2.1 it is a JIT intrinsic — one bitwise operation;
  • the JIT shortens a box that is immediately followed by unboxing or a type check;
  • in .NET 9–10 the "object does not leave the method" analysis (escape analysis) was extended to boxes: in some cases the box lives on the stack or disappears.

Hence the rule: judge boxes in hot code by measurement, not by IL. And the other way round: no visible object in the code does not mean there are no boxes.
cards.deep: Measuring without a profiler: GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() before and after the loop. In BenchmarkDotNet — the [MemoryDiagnoser] attribute, the Allocated column. JIT optimizations work in Release and after tier-up (tiered compilation), so measure after warm-up and not in Debug.

cards.q: You need to find out whether a hot loop boxes values on .NET 9. What is more reliable?
options: Measure allocated memory in Release after warm-up
Find every box instruction in the IL
Search the C# code for casts to object
Run it in Debug under a debugger and inspect the heap
cards.explain: IL shows where a box may be, but the JIT removes some of them. Many boxes are not visible in C# code at all. Debug disables optimizations and will show boxes that do not exist in Release. Only measuring allocations in the real configuration settles it.

wrong.1: box in IL is an upper bound. After JIT optimizations there may be fewer real allocations.

lessons.title: The mutable struct
lessons.sub: Collections, foreach and changes that land in a copy

cards.title: Why list[0].X = 1 does not compile
cards.body:
An array element is a variable: it has an address inside the array. arr[0].X = 1 compiles to "take the address of the element" (ldelema) and write the field at that address.

The List<T> indexer is a method, get_Item. It returns a value, that is, a copy of the struct in a temporary slot. Writing a field into a temporary copy is possible but pointless: it vanishes right after the line. So the compiler forbids it with error CS1612: "cannot modify the return value because it is not a variable".

The same rule protects a dictionary (dict[key].X = 1) and a property that returns a struct (shape.Center.X = 1).

cards.q: Point is a mutable struct with fields X and Y. Which line does not compile?
cards.explain: The array indexer and Span<T> give you a variable: the Span indexer returns ref T. List<T> returns a copy — writing a field into it is forbidden (CS1612).

cards.title: A method on a copy compiles silently
cards.body:
CS1612 only catches assignment to a field or property. If you call a method that mutates the struct instead, the compiler will not object: it puts the copy into a temporary variable and calls the method on it.

The method honestly changes the fields — of the copy. The list element stays the same. No error, no warning.
cards.deep: Why does the compiler not forbid this too? It does not know whether the method changes this. The method might only read fields, and then calling it on a copy is perfectly fine. It can only know if the method is marked readonly or the struct is a readonly struct (the defensive copies lesson in the "Performance" unit): then mutation is forbidden inside the method itself.

cards.q: What does this code print, with the same Point struct?
cards.explain: get_Item returned a copy, Offset added 5 to the copy, the copy vanished. The second list[0] returned a fresh copy of the unchanged element: X = 1.

wrong.1: That is what you would get with a Point[] array or if Point were a class.
wrong.3: CS1612 is only about assignment. Calling a method on a temporary copy is allowed.

cards.title: foreach: the loop variable is read-only
cards.body:
The foreach variable is a copy of the current element, and it is read-only. You cannot assign to its field: error CS1654.

You can call a mutating method, and it is easy to get this wrong in both directions. The compiler makes no defensive copy for the loop variable: the method changes p itself, and the next line of the body sees the new value. But p is already a copy of the element, so the collection element does not change. On the next iteration p is filled again, and the change is gone.
cards.deep: For a readonly field, though, the defensive copy is real, and it produces a famous infinite loop: the List<T>.Enumerator enumerator is a mutable struct. Put it in a readonly field, and every _e.MoveNext() runs on a fresh defensive copy: it always starts at the beginning, always returns true, and _e.Current stays the default value.

cards.q: Point is a mutable struct, list is a List<Point>, arr is a Point[]. Which lines actually change the data in the collection? Select all.
cards.explain: An array element is a variable, the method changes it in place. with creates a modified copy, and the assignment puts it back into the list. AsSpan gives a Span over the list's internal array, and its indexer returns a ref. list[0].Offset changes a temporary copy, and foreach changes the loop variable, which is itself a copy of the element, even for an array.

cards.title: How to change an element in place
cards.body:
• Replace it whole. list[i] = list[i] with { X = 1 }; — with works with any struct since C# 10. Two copies, but honest code.
  • A ref local. ref var p = ref arr[i]; — an alias for the array element, all changes go into it.
  • ref in foreach. foreach (ref var p in span) — over a Span<T>, whose enumerator yields ref T.
  • A list and a dictionary. CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list) (.NET 5) and CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrNullRef(dict, key) (.NET 6) give a ref into the internal storage.
cards.deep: CollectionsMarshal is a "dangerous" API: you hold a ref into the internal array. Add an element to the list and it may move to a new array: the old span keeps looking at a stale copy. For a dictionary, any add or remove invalidates the ref. So do not change the collection between getting a ref and using it.

cards.q: Shift every point in the list in place, with no copies
cards.code:
foreach (___ var p in CollectionsMarshal.___(list))
    p.X += 1;
cards.explain: AsSpan gives a Span<Point> over the list's internal array, and foreach (ref var …) gives a reference to each element. ToArray would copy the data, and the changes would go into the copy.

cards.title: A boxed struct behaves like a class
cards.body:
There is a third mode. If structs are stored in a collection of interfaces (List<IMover>) or of object, the list holds boxes. A call through the interface changes the box — the very one in the list. The change is visible.

But unbox an element into a variable of the struct type, and you hold a copy again. The same type behaves sometimes like a value, sometimes like a reference — depending on how you reached it. This is the main argument against mutable structs.
cards.code:
var movers = new List<IMover> { new Point() };
movers[0].Move(5);               // the box in the list changes
var p = (Point)movers[0];        // unboxing — a copy, X = 5
p.Move(1);                       // only p changes
Console.WriteLine(((Point)movers[0]).X);  // 5

cards.q: Point is a mutable struct with a Move method. Match each call with what it actually changes.
pairs: A temporary copy of the element
The box stored in the list
p.Move() in foreach (var p in list)
The loop variable, a copy of the element
The memory element under the span

cards.title: The takeaway: do not make structs mutable
cards.body:
The .NET design guidelines say it plainly: do not define mutable value types. Every trap in this lesson follows from one fact: a struct is copied on every read, and the change lands in whichever copy the code happened to reach.

An immutable struct: readonly struct or readonly record struct (C# 10). Read-only fields, and instead of mutating methods — methods that return a new value, plus with. Then list[0] = list[0].Offset(5) is the only way, and it works.
cards.deep: The BCL itself has exceptions to the rule, all for speed: collection enumerators, ValueTuple (its Item1, Item2 fields are mutable), internal runtime builders like ValueStringBuilder. They are structs to avoid allocation, and are used only as local variables — never put into collections or readonly fields.

cards.q: Which line is a silent bug: it compiles but changes nothing in the list?
cards.explain: The compiler allows a method call on a temporary copy, and the change is lost. list[0].X = 1 does not compile (CS1612), and the other two lines honestly change the data.

wrong.1: This line is not silent at all: the compiler stops it with error CS1612.

lessons.title: Equality and layout
lessons.sub: ValueType.Equals, IEquatable<T>, record struct and the bytes of a struct

cards.title: How ValueType.Equals works
cards.body:
A struct without its own Equals is compared by value — ValueType.Equals(object) does it. It does not know your fields in advance and goes like this:

  • the argument is null or of another type (checked via GetType) — false;
  • if the struct can be compared byte by byte — it compares the memory of both values as byte arrays. That is fast;
  • otherwise — reflection: it gets the list of fields via GetFields and calls FieldInfo.GetValue on both values for each one. Every value-type field gets boxed along the way, then compared with Equals.

The slow path is several times, even an order of magnitude, slower than a hand-written comparison and allocates on every call.
cards.deep: Sources: ValueType.cs in dotnet/runtime (CoreLib) and the CanCompareBitsOrUseFastGetHashCode check in the runtime. The check result is cached in the type data (MethodTable), so the "fast or slow" decision is made once per type.

cards.title: When the comparison is bytewise
cards.body:
The fast path kicks in only if every condition holds:

  • the struct has no references: two different strings with the same text are different addresses, the bytes will not match;
  • the struct is tightly packed — no alignment gaps. Gaps can hold anything, their bytes are undefined;
  • no float or double fields: 0.0 and -0.0 are equal but have different bytes; NaN is the other way round;
  • neither the struct nor its field types override Equals or GetHashCode.

Break even one — reflection.
cards.code:
struct Fast { public int X, Y; }            // bytes
struct Slow1 { public int Id; public string Name; } // a reference
struct Slow2 { public byte Flag; public int Value; } // a 3-byte gap
struct Slow3 { public double X, Y; }        // double
cards.deep: The float/double check was not there from the start: in older runtime versions a struct with a double was compared bytewise, and new S(0.0).Equals(new S(-0.0)) returned false even though the fields are equal. Reflection compares fields via double.Equals, for which 0.0 and -0.0 are equal and NaN equals NaN.

cards.q: Which structs will ValueType.Equals compare bytewise in modern .NET? None of them overrides anything. Select all.
options: struct A { int X; int Y; }
struct B { int Id; string Name; }
struct C { float X; float Y; }
struct D { byte Flag; int Value; }
struct E { long Ticks; int Kind; int Extra; }
cards.explain: A is 8 bytes with no gaps. E is 8 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes, aligned with no holes. B has a reference, C has floats, and D has three alignment bytes after the byte before the int: all three go through reflection.

cards.title: ValueType.GetHashCode: a hash of one field
cards.body:
The default hash also has two paths. The fast one (same conditions) hashes all the bytes of the struct. The slow one hashes only one field: the first one that is not null. The other fields do not go into the hash at all.

Equals still compares every field, so the contract is formally kept. But if the first field is the same for many keys, they all land in one dictionary bucket. Lookup turns from O(1) into walking a chain.
cards.deep: The slow path picks the field at run time (GetHashCodeStrategy): a reference — its GetHashCode, double/float — their hash, a nested struct — recursively by the same rules. The struct type is always mixed into the hash. .NET Framework had the same "first field" rule, so the advice "override GetHashCode on a struct key" is not outdated.

cards.q: A dictionary holds a million Key { Region, Id } keys, Region is "EU" in all of them. Equals and GetHashCode are not overridden. What happens to lookups?
options: Every key is in one bucket: each lookup is a long walk with comparisons via reflection
Business as usual: the hash includes Id too
The dictionary throws when a duplicate hash is inserted
Lookups are fast but eat a lot of memory for boxes
cards.explain: The slow-path hash comes from the first non-null field — the string "EU". All keys got the same hash, one bucket. Each comparison along the chain is ValueType.Equals via reflection with boxed fields.

wrong.2: Equal hashes are an ordinary collision, and Dictionary is ready for it. It just becomes slow.

cards.title: IEquatable<T>: why collections need it
cards.body:
Dictionary, HashSet, List.Contains, Array.IndexOf, Distinct compare through EqualityComparer<T>.Default. It picks an implementation once per type:

  • if T : IEquatable<T> — it calls Equals(T): no boxes, an ordinary method that can be inlined;
  • if not — it calls Equals(object): the argument is boxed, and without an override it goes on to ValueType.Equals.

The full set for a struct: IEquatable<T>, an Equals(object) that calls it, GetHashCode over the same fields, and the ==/!= operators.
cards.deep: For a value-type T the JIT knows the exact type of EqualityComparer<T>.Default and since .NET Core 2.1 devirtualizes the call: Dictionary<int, …> compares keys almost like hand-written code. That is why Dictionary even has a separate code branch for value-type keys without a custom comparer.

cards.q: Complete equality with no boxes and no reflection
cards.explain: IEquatable<Point> gives collections Equals(Point) without boxing. Equals(object) just delegates to it so the two methods never diverge. ReferenceEquals is always false for a struct: two boxes are two objects.

cards.title: record struct writes it for you
cards.body:
Since C# 10 a record struct generates everything from the previous card: IEquatable<T>, Equals(T) over all fields via EqualityComparer<TField>.Default, Equals(object), GetHashCode, ==, != and a ToString that shows the contents. No reflection, no boxes.

The difference from a plain struct shows at once: a plain struct has no == operator, and a == b does not compile (CS0019). The compiler does not try to guess what value equality means.

Remember: the positional properties of a record struct are mutable (get; set;). The immutable flavor is readonly record struct.
cards.deep: The generated equality compares double fields via double.Equals, not via ==. So two records with a double.NaN field are equal (a == b is True), even though NaN == NaN is false. This is by design: otherwise such a record could never be found in a dictionary.

cards.q: P is a plain struct with fields X and Y and no operators. What happens?
cards.explain: A struct has no == operator until you write one (or declare a record struct). Equals is always there — ValueType provides it — but the operator is not.

wrong.2: False for two different objects is what == on a class would give — it compares references. A struct simply has no ==.

cards.title: Layout: fields get aligned
cards.body:
For structs the C# compiler emits [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential)]: fields go in declaration order. But each field is aligned to its size: a long to an address that is a multiple of 8, an int to 4. And the size of the whole struct is rounded up to the strictest alignment, so that every element in an array is aligned too.

Field order changes the size. To find it out without unsafe — Unsafe.SizeOf<T>().
cards.code:
struct Loose { byte A; long B; byte C; }   // 1 + 7 gap + 8 + 1 + 7 gap
struct Tight { long B; byte A; byte C; }   // 8 + 1 + 1 + 6 gap

Unsafe.SizeOf<Loose>();   // 24
Unsafe.SizeOf<Tight>();   // 16
cards.deep: The numbers are for x64. An empty struct takes 1 byte: every value must have its own address. sizeof(T) for your own structs requires an unsafe context in C#, Unsafe.SizeOf<T> does not — it is a JIT intrinsic.

cards.q: Arrange the struct fields so that Sequential layout leaves no gaps between them: from largest to smallest
cards.explain: 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 bytes of data, each field already at an aligned address. The size rounds up to 16 — one gap at the end. Largest to smallest is a simple way not to lose bytes.

cards.title: StructLayout, references and marshaling
cards.body:
• LayoutKind.Auto — the runtime reorders fields itself, usually more tightly. But such a struct cannot be passed to unmanaged code.
  • Pack = 1 — no alignment: Loose becomes 10 bytes, but reading an unaligned long may cost more.
  • LayoutKind.Explicit + [FieldOffset] — a field at an exact offset, fields may overlap.

An important caveat from the docs: if a struct has references, Sequential does not control its layout in managed memory — the runtime lays such fields out as Auto. Sequential then only affects marshaling.

And the link back to the start of the lesson: alignment gaps disable the bytewise ValueType.Equals.
cards.deep:
Marshal.SizeOf<T>() is the size when marshaled, not in .NET memory. For struct { bool A; bool B; } Unsafe.SizeOf is 2, while Marshal.SizeOf is 8: by default bool is marshaled as a 4-byte Win32 BOOL.

The "version 2" scenario: reorder the fields of a Sequential struct that goes to P/Invoke or is written to a file as bytes, and native code and old files now read the wrong fields. For such structs the field order is part of the contract.

cards.q: Match each tool with what it gives you
pairs: The size when passed to unmanaged code
The runtime picks the field order
Fields back to back with no alignment
A field at an exact offset

lessons.title: Final: value types
lessons.sub: Hidden boxes, copies and equality

cards.q: Counter is a mutable struct implementing ICounter with an Inc method. What does this code print?
cards.explain: The first cast boxes a copy of the element — the change is lost. arr[0].Inc() changes the array element itself: 1. ICounter i = arr[0] boxes a copy holding 1, i.Inc() takes the box to 2, and the element stays at 1.

wrong.2: i is a box with a copy of the element. Changing it never reaches the array.

cards.q: S is a struct with no overrides that implements IDisposable and IComparable<S>. Where is there boxing, unless the JIT removes it? Select all.
cards.explain: GetType is an Object method, it needs an object. Equals and GetHashCode are not overridden — they go to ValueType with a box (Equals also boxes its argument). Dispose in using and CompareTo in a constrained generic are called via constrained with no box.

cards.q: Point is a mutable struct with an Offset method. Which line compiles but changes nothing in the data?
cards.explain: The List<T> indexer returns a copy: Offset changes a temporary. The array yields the element itself, with plus assignment writes a new value, and ref via AsSpan gives a reference straight into the list's internal array.

cards.q: struct Key { string City; int Id; } is a dictionary key, nothing overridden. Why is this bad when many keys share a city?
options: The default hash comes from City only: those keys land in one bucket, and Equals goes through reflection
Equals compares only City, so different Ids overwrite each other
A dictionary does not accept a struct with a reference as a key
It is fine: ValueType.GetHashCode mixes all the fields
cards.explain: The reference closes the fast path. The slow GetHashCode hashes the first non-null field — City. Equals still compares every field, so data does not get mixed up, but lookup becomes a walk with reflection.

wrong.1: Equals via reflection compares every field. Keys do not get mixed up — everything is just slow.

cards.q: A struct key: equality with no boxes or reflection, in one line
cards.code: public ___ record ___ Key(string City, int Id);
cards.explain: readonly record struct generates IEquatable<Key>, Equals, GetHashCode over all fields and ==, and readonly makes the properties init — the key cannot be spoiled after insertion. A record class would give equality too, but that is a reference type with an allocation per key.

cards.q: Match each struct with how ValueType.Equals compares it
pairs: Its own Equals, ValueType is not involved

cards.q: What does Unsafe.SizeOf<R>() return on x64?
cards.explain: Sequential: Kind at 0, then a 7-byte gap up to the aligned double at 8, Id at 16, 20 in total — rounded up to a multiple of 8: 24. Put the double first and the byte last, and it is 16.

wrong.1: 13 is the sum of field sizes without alignment. You would only get that with Pack = 1.
wrong.2: You get 16 if you reorder the fields: double, int, byte.

cards.q:
A HashSet

, where P is a struct without IEquatable

but with overridden Equals(object) and GetHashCode. What happens in Contains?
options: No reflection, but the argument is boxed on every Equals(object) call
No boxes and no reflection — the override is enough
It does not compile: HashSet requires IEquatable<T>
cards.explain:
Without IEquatable

, EqualityComparer

.Default calls Equals(object): your own override, so no reflection, but the argument is object, which means a box per comparison. IEquatable

removes that too.

wrong.3: HashSet works with any T: without IEquatable<T> it just falls back to Equals(object).

units.title: Type members and versioning
units.blurb: What breaks for a library consumer without a recompile: const versus static readonly, initialization order and beforefieldinit, virtual/new/override and call/callvirt, operators, conversions and extension methods up to C# 14 extension blocks.

lessons.title: const and static readonly
lessons.sub: A constant is baked into the calling assembly, and version 2 makes it visible

cards.title: Two "constants" of different nature
cards.body:
const is a value the compiler knows. It is stored in metadata as a literal, and such a field has no storage in memory. A const is always static: you cannot write static const.

static readonly is an ordinary static field. An initializer or the static constructor fills it at run time, and code reads it at run time. You can assign it only during type initialization.

That gives the first difference: const accepts only numbers, bool, char, string, decimal, enums and null. DateTime, arrays, TimeSpan need static readonly.

cards.title: What the compiler writes at the call site
cards.body:
Look at the IL of code that reads both values. For the constant the compiler substitutes the number right into the calling method: the instruction ldc.i4.s 100. There is no reference to the MaxItems field in that code at all.

For static readonly the IL has ldsfld, "load static field". The value comes from the owning assembly on every run.

Substitution is both a plus and a minus. The plus: you can use a constant wherever a compile-time value is required. The minus is on the next card.
cards.deep:
A string constant becomes ldstr "..." and lands in the string heap of the calling assembly. const decimal works differently: the CLR cannot store a decimal as a literal, so the field is marked with DecimalConstantAttribute, and at the call site the compiler builds the value through a decimal constructor. The substitution still happens.

Since there is no field reference, the source assembly is not needed at run time for that line. If code takes only constants from a library, the runtime may never load it at all.

cards.q: Which IL instruction does the compiler emit at the call site to read public static readonly string Name?
cards.explain: static readonly is an ordinary field, read with ldsfld at run time. An ldstr with the ready value would be emitted for a const string.

wrong.1: That is what the compiler does for a const string: the value is baked in. It leaves static readonly alone.
wrong.2: get_Name is a property accessor. This is a field, not a property.

cards.title: Version 2: the library is updated, the app is not
cards.body:
The scenario this whole lesson is about. Library Shop.Core.dll version 1 declares MaxItems = 100 and MaxUsers = 100. The app is compiled against it.

Version 2 ships: both values become 200. The new dll is dropped next to the app, and the app itself is not recompiled. That happens with plugins, shared packages, hotfixes.

  • MaxUsers is 200: the app reads the field from the new assembly.
  • MaxItems is still 100: the number was baked into the app IL at build time.

Inside the library itself it is already 200. Two parts of one program see different values, with no error at compile time or at run time.

cards.q: A plugin was built against Shop.Core v1, where DefaultPageSize = 20. In v2 both values became 50, the plugin was not rebuilt. Which plugin line still works with 20?
cards.explain: DefaultPageSize is a const: when the plugin was built, 20 was written into its IL, and the new dll will not change that. MaxPageSize is read from the field, so it is already 50. The last line divides by max, also 50.

cards.title: Where a constant is required
cards.body:
Some places in the language demand a compile-time value, and static readonly will not pass there:

  • case labels in a switch and constant patterns (x is Limits.MaxItems);
  • attribute arguments: [MaxLength(Limits.MaxItems)];
  • default values of optional parameters: int size = Limits.MaxItems.

In all of these places the value is baked into the calling code too. A default parameter value lives at the call site on the same principle; more on that in the unit about parameters.

cards.q: Where does static readonly int Max fail to compile? Select all.
cards.explain: case, an attribute argument and a default parameter value require a constant. An array size and a comparison are ordinary expressions; any value works there.

cards.title: Enums are constants too
cards.body:
Every enum member is a const of the underlying numeric type. Status.Paid in calling code turns into a number.

Version 2 with an enum breaks most quietly. In v1 it was New, Paid, Shipped, that is 0, 1, 2. In v2 someone inserted Pending second, and Paid became 2. The old app writes 1 to the database, meaning Paid, and the new library reads 1 as Pending.

The rule for public enums: give the numbers explicitly and add new values only at the end.

cards.q: The app was built against v1, where enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }. In v2 it is enum Color { Red, Yellow, Green, Blue }. The app was not rebuilt. What does library v2 receive if the app passes Color.Green?
cards.explain: The app IL has the number 1 baked in, which is what Green was in v1. In v2, 1 is Yellow. Neither the compiler nor the runtime knows: to them it is just an int.

wrong.1: The name Green never reaches the library, only the number from the app IL.
wrong.3: The Green field is not looked up at the call: the value is already substituted as a number.

cards.title: What to choose
cards.body:
public const only for what will never change: int.MaxValue, days in a week, codes from an external standard.

static readonly for everything that may change in a future version: limits, timeouts, addresses, protocol versions.

private and internal const are fine: only your own assembly sees them, and it is compiled as a whole, so the values have nowhere to diverge (unless there is InternalsVisibleTo).

Do not worry about speed: on a hot path the difference usually disappears, see "Deeper".
cards.deep:
With tiered compilation a hot method is recompiled at tier 1 after the type static constructor has already run. The JIT sees that the value of a primitive static readonly field can no longer change and substitutes it as a constant, with constant folding and dead branch removal after that. That makes static readonly bool flags a cheap way to switch code off on hot paths.

.NET Framework had no such optimization: static readonly was honestly read from memory. Hence the old advice "const is faster", which has mostly lost its meaning in modern .NET.

cards.q: Match the value with how to declare it in a public library
pairs: A cache key visible only inside the assembly

cards.q: Declare the limit so consumers see the new value after the dll is replaced without a rebuild
cards.explain: static readonly is a field, read with ldsfld from the current assembly. A const would be baked into every consumer.

lessons.title: Initialization order
lessons.sub: Field initializers, base(), the constructor body, the static constructor and beforefieldinit

cards.title: Field initializers do not exist
cards.body:
The CLR has no notion of a "field initializer". The C# compiler moves every = ... on a field into the constructor, at the very start, before the base class constructor is called.

A constructor in IL looks like this:

  • the field initializers of its own class, in declaration order;
  • the base(...) call;
  • the constructor body you wrote.

If there are several constructors, the initializers are copied into each one that calls base. A constructor with : this(...) does not get them, or the fields would be filled twice.
cards.deep:
Fields without an initializer get nothing assigned: the CLR hands out object memory already zeroed. So int count = 0; is a redundant store: it adds an instruction to every constructor and the result is the same. Analyzer CA1805 suggests removing it.

The order "initializers before base" differs from Java, where field initializers run after the super() call.

cards.q: class D : B. Both have field initializers and constructor bodies. Put in order what runs on new D()
cards.explain: The D constructor first fills its own fields, then calls the B constructor. That one fills the B fields and calls object. The bodies run on the way back: B first, then D.

cards.title: A virtual call from a constructor
cards.body:
An object type in the CLR does not change while it is being built: from the first instruction it is already Derived. So a virtual method called from the Base constructor lands in the Derived override, while the Derived constructor body has not run yet.

What the override sees:

  • Derived fields with initializers are already filled (they run before base);
  • fields assigned in the Derived constructor body are still default: 0, null, false.

Hence a NullReferenceException "out of nowhere". The rule: do not call virtual methods from a constructor. Analyzer CA2214 warns about it.
cards.deep:
C++ works differently: inside the base class constructor the object still counts as the base type, and a virtual call goes to the base version. In .NET the type pointer (MethodTable) is written into the object at allocation, before any constructor, and never changes after that.

Nullable analysis does not help here: the compiler considers text assigned after the constructor, and the call happens earlier, inside it.

cards.q: new Label() from the example above. Which line throws NullReferenceException?
cards.explain: Render is called from the Widget constructor. By then font is already "Arial": its initializer ran before base(). But text is assigned by the Label constructor body, which has not started, so text is null.

cards.title: The static constructor
cards.body:
Static fields are filled by the static constructor, the .cctor method in IL. The compiler puts static field initializers at its start, followed by the body of static Name() { } if you wrote one.

CLR guarantees:

  • it runs once per type for the lifetime of the process;
  • it is thread-safe: if two threads touch the type at once, one runs .cctor and the other waits;
  • you cannot call it yourself; it has no parameters and no access modifiers.

If it throws, the type is broken for good: every later access gets a TypeInitializationException.
cards.deep: Cycles between static constructors are dangerous. On a single thread a cycle does not hang: if the .cctor of A touches B and the .cctor of B touches A, then B sees A half-initialized, with default field values. Across threads (thread 1 initializes A, thread 2 initializes B) the same cycle risks a deadlock or the same read of a half-initialized type. That is why static constructors are kept short and free of cross dependencies.

cards.title: When it runs: beforefieldinit
cards.body:
It all depends on one flag in the type metadata: beforefieldinit.

No explicit static constructor (only initializers): the compiler sets the flag. It means "initialize whenever you like, but before the first access to a static field". The runtime may do it earlier or later, and calling a static method that does not touch fields does not trigger initialization.

An explicit static Name() { }, even an empty one: no flag. Then the moment is precise: right before the first access to any static member or before the first instance is created.

The price of precision: code the JIT compiled before the type was initialized gets "is the type ready?" checks before those accesses.
cards.deep:
With tiered compilation a hot method reaches tier 1 when the types it needs are usually already initialized, and the JIT drops the checks. So the real speed difference shows mostly in cold code.

When a beforefieldinit type gets initialized depends on the runtime version: in older .NET Framework versions the JIT often ran it ahead of time, while compiling a method that uses the type. Modern .NET is usually lazier. Do not rely on a specific moment, only on "no later than the first field read".

cards.q: Settings has no explicit static constructor. The code only calls Settings.Describe(), which returns a constant string and touches no fields. Will Load() run?
options: Not necessarily: the type is beforefieldinit and nobody read the field
Yes, always: any static method call triggers initialization
No, never: static field initializers are lazy only for properties
cards.explain: Without an explicit static constructor the type is marked beforefieldinit. The runtime must initialize it only before the first read of a static field. Describe reads no fields, so Load may not run at all, or may run earlier, at the runtime discretion.

wrong.1: That would be true if Settings had an explicit static constructor: then a call to any static member triggers it.

cards.title: Statics, inheritance and new D()
cards.body:
A static constructor belongs to its own type and is not inherited: B and D each have their own .cctor, and each runs once.

The order for new D() when both D and B have explicit static constructors:

  • the D static constructor, before the D instance is created;
  • the D field initializers;
  • the B static constructor: it is triggered by the call to the B constructor from the D constructor, the first access to type B;
  • the B field initializers, the B body, the D body.

Note that the derived statics run before the base statics, while for the instance the base goes before the derived one, but only the bodies, not the initializers. The D field initializers even run before the B static constructor.

cards.q: Class Cache has an explicit static constructor. Which of these triggers it if the type is not initialized yet? Select all.
options: Declaring a variable Cache c = null;
cards.explain: Without beforefieldinit the static constructor is triggered by the first access to any static member or by creating an instance. typeof only gets a Type object, and declaring a variable set to null does not touch the type at run time at all.

cards.title: Version 2: initialization is part of the contract
cards.body:
Initialization order is something a library consumer relies on without noticing. A real-life example: in v1 the Registry type registered handlers in a static field initializer, and it had an empty explicit static Registry() { }. The app called Registry.Ping() to "wake up" the type.

In v2 the author removed the "useless" empty constructor. The type became beforefieldinit, Ping does not touch fields, and the registration no longer happens at the expected moment. The app was not recompiled, the compiler said nothing.

The takeaway: side effects in static initialization are fragile. If you need explicit initialization, write an explicit Init() method or use Lazy<T>.
cards.deep:
The same flag explains the old singleton trick: an empty static constructor is written so that the instance is created exactly on the first access to Instance and not earlier. Today Lazy<T> or a nested holder class is simpler and clearer.

There is also [ModuleInitializer] (C# 9), a method the runtime runs when the module loads, before any access to its types. It is an honest way to "run the registration" without betting on the .cctor moment.

cards.q: Match what runs with when it runs
pairs: At the start of the constructor, before base()
Before the first access to a static member or the first instance
A static field initializer in a beforefieldinit type
At any moment before the first static field read

cards.q: Make the initialization moment precise: before the first access to any static member
cards.explain: An explicit static constructor, even an empty one, removes the beforefieldinit flag. Access modifiers are not allowed on it, and it has no return type.

lessons.title: virtual, new and override
lessons.sub: The method table, call and callvirt, and what breaks for a consumer when new becomes override

cards.title: The virtual method table
cards.body:
Every type has a MethodTable, the structure an object points to (see the unit "How a type is built"). It holds a table of slots: one slot per virtual method, and each slot holds a code address.

A derived type gets a copy of the parent table, and then:

  • override replaces the address in the parent slot: same slot, new code;
  • new leaves the parent slot alone: a method with the same name becomes a separate method (and new virtual becomes a new slot at the end of the table).

A virtual call means "take the object MethodTable, take slot number N, jump to the address". The object decides which code runs, not the variable type.

cards.q: The classes from the example above. What does the code print?
cards.explain: The call goes through the Shape.Name slot. Circle has its override in the slot; Square still has the Shape method: new created a separate method that is visible only through a variable of type Square.

wrong.1: Square.Name with new would be called only through a variable of type Square. Through Shape the slot leads to Shape.Name.

cards.title: Modifiers in IL
cards.body:
C# keywords turn into method flags in metadata:

  • virtual → newslot virtual: a new slot;
  • override → virtual without newslot: take the parent slot with the same signature;
  • sealed override → final virtual: the slot is taken, no further overriding;
  • new on a non-virtual method → a plain method with no flags;
  • abstract → newslot abstract virtual, with no code.

The word new itself never reaches IL. It is just an answer to the compiler: "I know I am hiding the parent method".
cards.code:
.method public hidebysig newslot virtual instance string Name()   // virtual
.method public hidebysig virtual instance string Name()           // override
.method public final hidebysig virtual instance string Name()     // sealed override
.method public hidebysig instance string Name()                   // new
cards.deep:
The hidebysig flag says the method hides the parent one only when the signature matches, not by name alone. C# always sets it.

An implicit interface method implementation without virtual looks like virtual final newslot in IL: the CLR needs it virtual to call it through the interface, but for C# it stays non-virtual and sealed.

cards.title: call and callvirt
cards.body:
IL has two instructions for calling an instance method:

  • call: call exactly this method, the address is known up front. No null check.
  • callvirt: check the reference for null, and if the method is virtual, find the code through the object slot.

C# emits callvirt for almost every instance method call on a reference type, even a non-virtual one: that way a call on null immediately throws NullReferenceException. For a non-virtual method the JIT still makes a direct call, adding a cheap null check.

C# uses call for static methods, struct methods and base.Method(): there it needs exactly the parent method, not the slot.
cards.code:
order.Total();      // callvirt  Order::Total   (even if Total is not virtual)
Math.Max(a, b);     // call      Math::Max
point.Length();     // call      Point::Length  (Point is a struct)
base.ToString();    // call      Object::ToString — bypasses the slot

cards.q: Match the call with the IL instruction C# emits

cards.title: The cost of a virtual call, and sealed
cards.body:
A virtual call is two memory reads (the MethodTable, then the slot) and an indirect jump. By itself that is nanoseconds. What costs more: the JIT cannot inline a method whose code is unknown until run time.

If the JIT is sure of the exact type, it devirtualizes: a direct call, and then inlining. What helps:

  • sealed on a class or a method: no derived types, the slot will not be replaced;
  • the exact type is visible in the code: new Circle().Name();
  • dynamic PGO (on by default since .NET 8): the JIT notices that Circle almost always arrives and emits a check "if Circle, call directly, else go through the slot".
cards.deep:
That is why modern codebases often make classes sealed by default, and analyzer CA1852 suggests sealing internal classes that have no derived types. A bonus: is and casts to a sealed type boil down to comparing the MethodTable pointer.

A call through an interface is more involved than through a class slot: the CLR uses stubs (virtual stub dispatch) with a cache keyed by the object type. In .NET 8–10 guarded devirtualization through PGO works for it too.

cards.q: When can the JIT call Name() directly, without going through the slot? Select all.
options: Class Circle is sealed, the call is through a Circle variable
Circle declares the method as sealed override, the call is through a Circle variable
The call is through a Shape variable, and Shape is an abstract class
Name is declared virtual, but nobody has overridden it
cards.explain: A sealed class and a sealed override guarantee the slot will not be replaced further down. For new Circle() the exact type is visible right in the code. Shape being abstract says nothing about the derived type, and the JIT cannot know that "nobody overrode it": an assembly with a derived type may be loaded later. Dynamic PGO puts a type check with a fallback through the slot in such places, which is no longer an unconditional direct call.

cards.title: Version 2: new is changed to override
cards.body:
Library Shapes.dll v1: Square.Name() is declared with new. The app keeps squares in a List<Shape> and prints s.Name(), getting "shape". Tests and reports are written around this behavior.

In v2 the author fixed the "bug": replaced new with override. The app was not recompiled. What happens:

  • the app IL still has callvirt Shape::Name: the reference is valid, no load errors;
  • but the Name slot of Square is now taken by the override, and the same call prints "square".

Binary compatibility survived, the behavior changed. The reverse change override → new just as quietly breaks calls through the base type: they stop reaching the derived class.

cards.q: The app was built against Shapes v1, where Square.Name is declared with new. It runs with v2, where it is override. Which line changes its output?
cards.explain: sq.Name() lands in Square.Name in both v1 and v2: the variable type is Square. sh.Name() goes through the Shape.Name slot: in v1 it holds the Shape method, in v2 the Square override. GetType().Name is always "Square".

cards.title: Version 2: a method appears in the base class
cards.body:
The opposite case. The app has class MyButton : Button with its own void Refresh(). In v2 of the UI library, Button gets a virtual void Refresh() and calls it internally on redraw.

Without a recompile, the app method is a plain non-virtual method in IL; it does not take the Button.Refresh slot. The library calls its own version, and MyButton.Refresh stays silent.

On recompile the compiler gives warning CS0114: "the member hides an inherited member; add override or new". By default C# treats it as new, a deliberate language decision: a new method in a base class must not silently take over someone else's code.
cards.deep:
Other library changes that break consumers without a recompile:

  • the class became sealed while a consumer derives from it: TypeLoadException when the consumer type loads;
  • an abstract method was added to the base class: the consumer derived class has no implementation, also TypeLoadException;
  • a method stopped being virtual: the consumer override has nothing to override anymore, so it becomes a separate method and is no longer called through the base.

Making a non-virtual method virtual is safe for C# callers: they already call it through callvirt.

cards.q: Which changes break a derived consumer built against v1 when only the library dll is replaced? Select all.
options: An abstract method was added to the base class
A public base class method became virtual
A new private method was added to the base class
cards.explain: You cannot derive from a sealed class, and an unimplemented abstract method makes the type unloadable: both give TypeLoadException. Adding virtual is safe: calls already go through callvirt. The consumer cannot see a private method.

cards.q: Forbid further overriding while keeping your own override
cards.explain: sealed override takes the parent slot and sets the final flag: classes derived from Circle cannot override it, and the JIT can devirtualize a call through a Circle variable.

lessons.title: Operators and extensions
lessons.sub: op_Addition, implicit and explicit, extension methods and C# 14 extension blocks

cards.title: An operator is a static method
cards.body:
The CLR has no "operator overloading". When you write operator +, the compiler creates an ordinary static method with the special name op_Addition and the specialname flag. The expression a + b becomes call Money::op_Addition(a, b).

C# rules:

  • an operator is public static, and at least one parameter is your type;
  • paired operators are declared together: == with !=, < with >, <= with >=;
  • if you declare ==, override Equals and GetHashCode, or get warnings CS0660/CS0661;
  • += is built from + and an assignment by default.
cards.deep:
Names like op_Addition, op_Equality, op_Implicit are reserved by the ECMA-335 standard, and other .NET languages recognize operators by them. A language without operator overloading can call the same method by name.

C# 11 added checked operators (op_CheckedAddition), and C# 14 added user-defined compound assignment: an instance public void operator +=(Money m) named op_AdditionAssignment changes the object in place, without creating a new one. Useful for large buffers and tensors.

cards.q: Money is the struct from the example above. What does the compiler turn total += price into?
cards.explain: Money has no += operator, so the compiler takes op_Addition and assigns the result. It is a static method: the call instruction, no callvirt. The IL add instruction works only with primitives.

wrong.1: Operators are static and called with call: there is no receiver object and no slot.
wrong.2: add is for int, double and other CLR primitives. The Money struct is not one of them.

cards.title: The operator is chosen at compile time
cards.body:
Since an operator is a static method, the compiler chooses it by static types, just like method overloads. No virtual dispatch.

The classic trap is == through object. string has its own op_Equality that compares characters. But if both variables are declared as object, the compiler sees only object == object: a reference comparison.

Same in generics: in a method with where T : class the expression a == b is always a reference comparison, even if T turns out to be string. To compare values use Equals or EqualityComparer<T>.Default.

cards.q: What does Same("ab", string.Concat("a", "b")) return?
cards.code: static bool Same<T>(T a, T b) where T : class => a == b;
options: Does not compile: == is not allowed for T
cards.explain: With the class constraint the compiler allows == and binds it to reference comparison: it does not see string op_Equality when compiling the generic. Concat creates a new string, so the references differ.

wrong.2: That would be true without the class constraint. With where T : class, == is allowed but compares references.
wrong.3: The string from Concat is created at run time and is not interned, so the references differ.

cards.title: implicit and explicit
cards.body:
