User-defined conversions are static methods too: op_Implicit and op_Explicit. The CLR itself allows overloading by return type for any method, but in C# this is the only place where it shows up: one class can have several op_Implicit methods with the same parameter and different results.

  • implicit: the compiler inserts the call itself. Only for conversions that lose no data and never throw.
  • explicit: you have to write (Type)x. For anything that may truncate or fail.

You cannot declare a conversion to or from an interface, to object, to a base class or a derived class: the CLR already has those casts. And remember from the unit "How a type is built": user-defined conversions are not called through object.

cards.q: Which declarations inside public class Money compile? Select all.
options: public static implicit operator Money(decimal d)
public static explicit operator decimal(Money m)
public static implicit operator object(Money m)
public static implicit operator IComparable(Money m)
cards.explain: A conversion to object is forbidden: it is a base class (CS0553). To an interface is not allowed either (CS0552). And without static the operator cannot be declared at all.

cards.title: Version 2: operators are baked into the calling IL
cards.body:
The operator is chosen at compile time and written into the consumer IL as a specific method. Hence two "version 2" scenarios:

  • v2 adds a more precise overload, say Money + decimal. The old consumer keeps calling what the compiler chose earlier: op_Implicit(decimal), then op_Addition(Money, Money). The new overload kicks in only after a recompile.
  • v2 removes an implicit conversion or turns it into explicit. For source code that is a compile error, and for an old consumer it is a MissingMethodException on the first call of a method that used op_Implicit.

An operator signature is as much a part of the public API as a method name.

cards.title: An extension method is a static call
cards.body:
An extension method is a static method of a static class whose first parameter is marked with this. The compiler puts ExtensionAttribute on it.

The call title.Truncate(10) is syntactic sugar. In IL it is call StringExt::Truncate(title, 10): no callvirt, no null check on the receiver. That is why an extension method can be called on null: an exception happens only if the method itself touches the parameter.

To make the method visible you need a using for the namespace of its class. Remove the using and the method "disappears".

cards.q: StringExt from the example above. What happens?
options: Prints True, then NullReferenceException inside Truncate
NullReferenceException on the very first call
Prints True and an empty string
Does not compile: null has no methods
cards.explain: An extension call is a static call; null is simply passed as an argument. IsBlank handles null. Truncate reads s.Length and fails inside the method.

wrong.1: That is what an instance method would do: callvirt checks the receiver for null. An extension is called with call.

cards.title: An instance method always wins
cards.body:
The compiler looks for a method in two stages. First among the instance methods of the type. Only if none is applicable does it look at extensions in visible namespaces.

Note: "applicable" does not mean "a better match". If the type has Log(object), the call x.Log(5) goes there with boxing, even if an extension Log(this X x, int n) with the exact type is right next to it.

Version 2. You wrote a Shuffle extension for someone else's type. In v2 of the library the type gets its own Shuffle(). Your old assembly keeps calling your extension: its IL has a static call. But after a recompile every call silently moves to the library method, without a single warning.

cards.q: Which line prints inst?
cards.explain: item.Show(5): the instance Show(object) is applicable, the int gets boxed to object. Once an applicable instance method is found, extensions are not considered, even though Show(int) is more precise. item.Show() with no arguments does not fit the instance method, so the extension runs. Ext.Show(item, 5) is an explicit static call.

cards.title: C# 14: extension blocks
cards.body:
C# 14 (.NET 10) introduced extension members. Inside a static class you write an extension(receiver) block, and it can declare more than methods:

  • extension properties: name.IsBlank without parentheses;
  • static members of the type: a block without a receiver name, called as string.Dash;
  • operators for someone else's type.

Old this methods are still here. An instance method in a block compiles to the same IL as a this method, so a library can move to the new syntax without breaking consumers, neither binary nor source.
cards.deep:
Blocks have the same restrictions as classic extensions: a top-level, static, non-generic class. Type parameters go on the block itself: extension<T>(IEnumerable<T> source).

The priority has not changed: an instance member of the type still beats an extension. The compiler turns an extension property into a static accessor method with the receiver as the first parameter and adds auxiliary metadata that lets the consumer compiler recognize the block. Extension indexers arrive in the next version, C# 15.

cards.q: Declare an extension property in C# 14 style
cards.explain: The block extension<T>(List<T> list) declares the receiver for all members inside. this before a parameter is the syntax of classic extension methods; a property cannot be declared that way.

lessons.title: Final: type members and versioning
lessons.sub: Constants, initialization, slots and extensions: what breaks without a recompile

cards.q: The app was built against Api v1, where Version = "1" and Url = "https://v1". In v2 they became "2" and "https://v2". The dll was replaced, the app was not rebuilt. What does it print?
cards.explain: The string constant is baked into the app IL as ldstr "1". static readonly is read with ldsfld from the new dll, which already says https://v2.

wrong.1: That happens only after the app is recompiled: a const value comes from the caller IL.
wrong.3: The other way round: the const is what is baked in, and the field is read from the new assembly.

cards.q: class D : B. D has an explicit static constructor; both have field initializers and constructor bodies. Type D has not been touched yet. Put in order what runs on new D()
cards.explain: Before the first instance is created, the D static constructor runs. Then the D constructor: its own initializers, the base call (B initializers and the B body), and only then the D body.

cards.q: new SqlRepo("Server=db"). Which line throws NullReferenceException?
cards.explain: Warmup is called from the Repo constructor and reaches SqlRepo through the slot. The table initializer has already run: it comes before the base call. But conn is assigned by the SqlRepo constructor body, which has not been reached yet.

cards.q: The library was updated to v2, the consumer was not rebuilt. Which changes quietly alter its behavior, with no exceptions? Select all.
options: A new member was inserted in the middle of an enum
A derived class replaced new with override
A base class the consumer derives from became sealed
An implicit conversion the consumer used was removed
cards.explain: Constants and enum members are baked in as numbers, and override takes the slot the old callvirt goes through. sealed gives TypeLoadException, a removed op_Implicit gives MissingMethodException: loud, not quiet.

cards.q: Area is a non-virtual method of class Shape and touches no fields. What happens?
cards.code:
Shape s = null;
Console.WriteLine(s.Area());
options: The method runs: it does not need this
NullReferenceException only if Area reads a field
cards.explain: C# calls instance methods of reference types with callvirt, and it checks the receiver for null before entering the method. Only an extension method would pass without an exception: it is called with call.

wrong.1: That would be the case with the call instruction. But C# emits callvirt even for non-virtual methods precisely for this check.

cards.q: Match what you see in IL with the C# construct
Consumers must see the new value after the dll is replaced, and initialization must happen at a precise moment, without beforefieldinit
cards.explain: static readonly is read with ldsfld from the current assembly. An explicit static constructor, even an empty one, removes the beforefieldinit flag.

cards.q: You have an extension ToJson(this Order o). In v2 of the library Order gets its own public string ToJson(). What happens to the order.ToJson() calls in your code?
options: Before a recompile, your extension; after it, the library method, with no warnings
The library method right away: the CLR picks the instance method at load time
After a recompile, an ambiguous call error
Always your extension: it is declared closer to the call
cards.explain: Your IL has a static call to the extension, and replacing the dll does not touch it. On recompile the compiler first looks for instance methods, finds ToJson on Order and never gets to extensions. There is no warning.

wrong.1: The CLR does not re-choose methods: the IL already names a specific static method.
wrong.2: There is no ambiguity: the instance method simply wins, extensions are not considered.

lessons.title: ref inside out
lessons.sub: Managed pointers, ref readonly and ref returns

cards.title: One pointer, four keywords
cards.body:
You saw the basics — a copy, ref, out, in — in the lesson "Passing to a method" of the ".NET inside out" course. Now let us look underneath.

To the CLR, all four by-reference forms are one and the same type: a managed pointer, written int32& in IL. The differences are just flags and attributes in the parameter metadata. The C# compiler reads them, the runtime does not.

Hence the rule: you cannot overload a method on ref/out/in alone — in IL such methods have the same signature. That is error CS0663. A by-value plus by-reference pair is fine: int and int& are different types.
cards.code:
// C#                  →  IL parameter signature
void A(ref int x)       // int32& x
void B(out int x)       // [out] int32& x
void C(in int x)        // [in] int32& x + IsReadOnlyAttribute
void D(ref readonly int x) // [in] int32& x + RequiresLocationAttribute
cards.deep:
Only the C# compiler checks that an out parameter is assigned (the definite assignment rules). The CLR does not: a method written in another language or in IL can return without writing anything. The [out] flag matters mostly to the marshaler when calling native code.

A managed pointer can point inside an object — at a field or an array element. The garbage collector knows about such interior pointers: while a reference to arr[5] is alive, the whole array stays alive, and when the heap is compacted the pointer moves along with it.

cards.q: Which set of overloads will not compile?
options: void M(ref int x) and void M(out int x)
void M(int x) and void M(ref int x)
void M(int x) and void M(in int x)
void M(ref int x) and void M(ref long x)
cards.explain: ref and out are the same int32& in IL; only a flag differs. The signatures collide and the compiler reports CS0663. A by-value plus by-reference pair is legal: int and int& are different types.

wrong.2: It compiles. A call M(x) with no modifier picks the by-value version, M(in x) picks the in one.

cards.title: in accepts anything
cards.body:
in was designed for speed: pass a big struct by address instead of copying it. That is why it is so accommodating:

  • you may omit the modifier at the call site: Print(p);
  • you may pass a value instead of a variable — Print(new Point(1, 2)). The compiler silently creates a hidden local and passes a reference to it.

For "just read it" this is convenient. But if the method wants to remember the address (build a span over it, compare addresses), a reference to a temporary copy is a quiet bug: each call gets its own copy, and it lives for one expression.

Defensive copies when calling methods on an in struct are covered in the "Performance" unit.

cards.title: ref readonly (C# 12): I need an address, I will not write
cards.body:
A ref readonly parameter is read-only like in, but it requires a real location in memory:

  • the call site writes ref or in;
  • no modifier — a warning;
  • a value instead of a variable — a warning (a temporary is still created);
  • out — an error.

Why: libraries had methods that need an address but never write to it. Some took ref — and rejected readonly fields. Others took in — and quietly accepted temporaries. The single-element constructor of ReadOnlySpan<T> was one of them.
cards.deep:
In metadata a ref readonly parameter is [in] T& with RequiresLocationAttribute; virtual methods also get modreq(InAttribute). It has no IsReadOnlyAttribute, so an older compiler sees a plain ref.

The "version 2" scenario: changing ref to ref readonly in a library is source-safe for callers: ref x at the call site is still allowed. And in C# 12 passing a ref argument to an in parameter became a warning instead of an error — also to ease this kind of migration.

cards.q: Match the parameter modifier to what it allows at the call site
pairs: Only a writable variable, ref at the call site is required
The variable may be unassigned, the method must write it
Any value, a temporary copy is made for it
A variable, even readonly; a value gives a warning
The method gets its own copy

cards.q: Peek takes a ref readonly int. Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: You cannot pass out to a ref readonly parameter: the method does not promise to write a value. Peek(v) with no modifier compiles, with a warning; ref and in are allowed.

cards.title: A ref return: the method hands out a location, not a value
cards.body:
A method can return not a value but a reference to a variable: an array element, a field of an object, a parameter that came in by reference. The caller then has a choice:

  • ref int m = ref FindMax(a); — a ref local, an alias of the element. Writing to m changes the array;
  • int m = FindMax(a); — without ref at the call site the value is simply copied.

Since C# 7.3 a ref local can be re-pointed: m = ref other;. A plain m = 5 writes to wherever it points.

cards.q: FindMax returns ref int, as above. What ends up in the array?
options: Does not compile: ref is required
cards.explain: Without ref at the call site and on the variable, the returned reference is dereferenced right away: m is an ordinary copy of the number 9. The array does not change.

wrong.3: It compiles: a ref return can be read as an ordinary value. You need ref only if you want an alias.

cards.title: Where ref returns already work for you
cards.body:
Arrays: arr[i] is the variable itself, so arr[i].X = 5 changes the struct right inside the array.
Span<T>: the indexer returns ref T — the same behavior.
List<T>: the indexer is an ordinary property and returns a copy. list[i].X = 5 on a struct does not compile (CS1612): you would change a copy and throw it away.

For hot code there is CollectionsMarshal: AsSpan(list) gives a span over the list's internal array, and GetValueRefOrAddDefault(dict, key, out exists) gives a ref to the value in a dictionary in one hash lookup instead of the two of a TryGetValue + write pair.
cards.deep: The price is guarantees. The span from AsSpan looks at the current internal array: add elements, the list moves to a new array, and the span stays on the old one. The reference from GetValueRefOrAddDefault is valid only while the dictionary is not modified: an insert can rebuild its storage. That is why both methods live in System.Runtime.InteropServices — "I know what I am doing".

cards.q: Point is a mutable struct with a field X. Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: The List<T> indexer returns a copy of the struct, so changing its field is pointless — CS1612. An array element and a span element are variables (ref), so the write goes in place.

cards.title: What a ref return cannot do
cards.body:
You can return a reference only to something that outlives the method: an array element, a field of a heap object, a parameter that came in by ref. A reference to your own local is forbidden (CS8168): the stack frame will be gone and the reference would dangle.

More limits: a ref local lives only on the stack. A lambda cannot capture it, a class field cannot hold it. Async methods and iterators allow ref locals since C# 13, but not across await and yield.
cards.deep: The compiler tracks this with the ref safety rules: every reference has a "how far it may escape" — to the caller, or only inside the method. The scoped keyword (C# 11) narrows a parameter to "inside only", and then it cannot be returned. Only a ref struct may store a ref in a field (ref fields, C# 11) — that is how Span<T> itself is built.

cards.q: A word counter with a single dictionary lookup
cards.explain: The method returns a ref int to the value in the dictionary (a new key gets 0). ref on the left and ref at the call make c an alias of that value, and c++ writes straight into the dictionary. The last parameter is out bool exists, which we discard.

cards.q: Why does return ref x not compile when x is a local variable of the method?
options: The method frame disappears on return, so the reference would point at dead memory
You can return ref only to class fields
Locals always live in registers and have no address
The variable has to be marked scoped
cards.explain: A local lives in the stack frame, and the frame is released on return. You can return a ref to something that outlives the method: an array element, an object field, a ref parameter.

wrong.1: An array element and a ref parameter work too.
wrong.3: scoped does the opposite: it forbids returning the reference.

lessons.title: Arguments: defaults and params
lessons.sub: Where a default value lives and which overload wins

cards.title: A default value lives in the caller
cards.body:
An optional parameter looks like part of the method. In fact the method knows almost nothing about it. In metadata the parameter carries an [opt] flag and a constant — the default value.

When you write Retry(), the compiler of your project reads that constant from the library metadata and puts it into the call. Your assembly's IL holds an ordinary call with the argument 3. The method itself always receives the argument explicitly.
cards.deep:
In the library IL this is .method ... Retry([opt] int32 times) plus the line .param [1] = int32(3). [CallerMemberName], [CallerLineNumber] and [CallerArgumentExpression] work the same way: the compiler inserts the string or the number at the call site, at compile time.

The value must be a compile-time constant, default, or new S() for a struct. DateTime.Now is not allowed — there is no way to write it into metadata. For decimal the compiler records the value with a DecimalConstantAttribute.

cards.q: Library v1: Retry(int times = 3). In v2 the author changed the default to 5. The app was not rebuilt, only the DLL was replaced. What does Retry receive for the call Retry()?
cards.explain: The 3 was baked into the app's IL at compile time. The new DLL never sees it: the method receives the argument 3. The 5 appears only after the app is rebuilt.

wrong.2: The signature did not change — Retry(int32) is still there, the method is found.

cards.title: Version 2: adding an optional parameter breaks binaries
cards.body:
Another trap from the same mechanism. In v2 you added a parameter: Retry(int times = 3, bool log = false). Callers' source compiles as before. But an old compiled assembly references Retry(int32), and that method no longer exists — the call throws MissingMethodException.

Hence the rules for public libraries:

  • do not change a default value after release — treat it as part of the contract, like a const;
  • add a new parameter as a new overload, keep the old one and let it call the new one.
cards.deep: A twist with interfaces and inheritance: the default is taken from the static type the call goes through, not from the actual object. If the interface declares level = 1 and the class declares level = 2, a call through the interface inserts 1 and a call through the class inserts 2. The virtual call lands in the same method, but with different arguments.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: The compiler takes the default from the type of the expression at the call: log is a Log, so it inserts 2; ilog is an ILog, so it inserts 1. The very same method runs, with different arguments.

cards.title: Named arguments
cards.body:
Named arguments are also compile-time only. The compiler matches a name to a parameter and puts the arguments in their places. IL has no names at all.

Consequences:

  • Evaluation order follows the call site, left to right, not the parameter order. If the orders differ, the compiler stores values in temporaries and then lays them out.
  • Renaming a parameter in a public API breaks the source of everyone who called it by name. Binaries are fine: names play no part in IL.
  • Since C# 7.2 a named argument may appear before positional ones if it is in its own position.
cards.code:
Send(to: "ann@x.io", subject: "Hi", urgent: true);
Send("ann@x.io", subject: "Hi", true);   // C# 7.2+: the name is in its own position

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: Arguments are evaluated in the order they are written at the call: b gets 1 first, then a gets 2. M prints a, then b — "21".

cards.title: params T[]: an array per call
cards.body:
params int[] values is syntactic sugar at the call site. The compiler turns Sum(1, 2, 3) into Sum(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }): a new heap array on every call.

  • With no arguments: Sum() → Sum(Array.Empty<int>()), a shared empty array, no allocation.
  • Pass an existing array and it goes as is, with no copy. The method can change it, and you will see that.
  • Sum(null) passes null, not an array with one null.
cards.code:
static int Sum(params int[] values) { /* ... */ }

Sum(1, 2, 3);     // new int[] { 1, 2, 3 } — an allocation
Sum();            // Array.Empty<int>() — no allocation
Sum(myArray);     // the same array, no copy

cards.title: params collections (C# 13)
cards.body:
Since C# 13 params accepts not only an array but any type a collection expression can build: Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>, IEnumerable<T>, IReadOnlyList<T>, List<T> and others.

The key one is params ReadOnlySpan<T>: the compiler can lay the arguments out in a buffer on the stack and pass a span over it. No heap array.

In .NET 9 the libraries gained such overloads for common methods: string.Join, string.Concat, Path.Combine, Task.WhenAll and others. Rebuild your project for .NET 9 and the same lines of code start calling the new overloads and allocate less.
cards.deep:
Exactly how the compiler builds the span is an implementation detail: on .NET 8+ it uses a synthesized struct with the [InlineArray] attribute in the caller's frame, and for constants of primitive types the span can come straight from the assembly's static data. A params parameter of a ref struct type is implicitly scoped: the method cannot store it or return it — otherwise it would outlive the buffer.

params List<T> or params IEnumerable<T> save nothing: the collection is still created on the heap on every call.

cards.q: A class has two overloads: Sum(params int[]) and Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int>). Which one does Sum(1, 2, 3) pick?
cards.explain: Both apply only in their expanded form, and then the C# 13 rule prefers the span. No heap array is created.

wrong.2: There is no ambiguity: C# 13 added an explicit rule for this case — a span beats an array.

cards.title: How overload resolution picks among params
cards.body:
Roughly in this order; the first rule that tells candidates apart decides:

  • an exact type match beats a conversion: Sum(arr) with int[] arr picks params int[], not the span. This rule is stronger than expansion: with M(long x) and M(params int[] xs) the call M(5) goes to the params one;
  • non-generic beats generic;
  • applicable without expansion wins: with M(int x) and M(params int[] xs) the call M(5) goes to M(int);
  • if both apply only in expanded form, ReadOnlySpan<T> and Span<T> beat an array and other collections.

The "version 2" scenario: a library adds a span overload next to the array one. Old assemblies keep working — the array method is still there. Rebuilt clients quietly move to the span. If the two overloads behave differently, the client gets the surprise.
cards.deep: C# 14 had a similar effect with implicit array-to-span conversions: array.Contains(x) may bind to MemoryExtensions.Contains instead of Enumerable.Contains. In ordinary code that is faster, but expression trees (for example, in ORM queries) cannot use spans, so such spots are worth checking after a language upgrade.

cards.q: Match the call to what it costs
pairs: A new heap array on every call
A buffer in the caller's frame
A new List on the heap on every call
A constant baked into the caller's code

cards.q: A logging method without an array per call
cards.explain: params ReadOnlySpan<object?> (C# 13) puts the arguments in a buffer on the stack. List and IEnumerable still create a collection on the heap. The argument objects themselves, if they are boxed numbers, stay on the heap — only the array is saved.

lessons.title: Properties and tuples inside out
lessons.sub: get_/set_, field, init, anonymous types and ValueTuple

cards.title: A property is two methods
cards.body:
To the CLR there is no property "variable". There are methods get_Age() and set_Age(int) plus a metadata record tying them together under the name Age — the compiler, the debugger and reflection read it.

For an auto-property the compiler also creates a private field <Age>k__BackingField. The angle brackets keep that name out of C#, so you cannot reach the field directly.

The access p.Age = 5 is a call set_Age. In Release the JIT inlines a trivial getter, and it costs as much as a field read. But you cannot declare your own method named get_Age next to a property Age — the name is taken (CS0082).
cards.deep: The "version 2" scenario: the field public int Count; became the property public int Count { get; set; }. Callers' source compiles almost unchanged, but in binary terms it is a different member: old IL does ldfld Count, the field is gone — MissingFieldException. Source breaks too wherever the field was passed as ref/out: a property is not a variable. That is why public types do not expose fields, even "simple for now" ones.

cards.q: In library v2 the public field Count became a property. The app was built against v1, the DLL was just replaced. What happens when reading lib.Count?
options: It works: the read syntax is the same
cards.explain: The app's IL reads the field with an ldfld by name and type. In v2 there are get_Count/set_Count methods in its place, and no field. The C# syntax is the same, the compiled code is not.

wrong.3: The app is already compiled, the error comes at run time. After a rebuild everything compiles.

cards.title: field (C# 14): your logic without your own field
cards.body:
It used to be that adding one check to a setter meant giving up the auto-property and declaring a field by hand. In C# 14 there is a contextual keyword field inside an accessor — the hidden field the compiler creates.

  • You can mix: one accessor automatic, the other with a body.
  • It works in init too.
  • A property initializer writes straight to the field, bypassing the setter.

A breaking change: if the type already has a member named field, inside accessors the word now means the hidden field. Reach your member with this.field or @field.

cards.q: What is new User().Name?
options: Does not compile: a property with a setter body has no initializer
cards.explain: The property initializer writes the value straight into the hidden field, the setter is not called. Trim runs only on an assignment through Name = ....

wrong.3: In C# 14 an initializer is allowed on any property for which the compiler creates a field — including with field.

cards.title: init and required: what goes into metadata
cards.body:
You saw what init and required are in the "Modern C#" unit. Now — how they are built.

init is an ordinary set_Name method, but its return type carries modreq(IsExternalInit). A modreq is a required modifier: a compiler that does not understand it refuses to call the method. That is why old C# cannot "get around" init. The runtime checks nothing: through reflection an init property can be changed after construction.

required is a RequiredMemberAttribute on the member and on the type. The type's constructors get an [Obsolete] with the error flag and CompilerFeatureRequired("RequiredMembers"): a new compiler understands them and checks the initializer, an old one simply will not let you call the constructor.
cards.deep:
required is checked only by the compiler at a new call. Deserializers, reflection and Activator.CreateInstance bypass it. Since .NET 7 System.Text.Json honors required itself and throws if the JSON lacks the property — but that is the serializer's decision, not the CLR's.

The "version 2" scenario: adding a required member to an already released type breaks the source of everyone who creates it with new without that member.

cards.q: What does the compiler do for an Order class with the member public required string Customer { get; init; }? Select all.
options: Puts RequiredMemberAttribute on the Order type itself
Marks the Order constructors with Obsolete for older compilers
Adds a check to the constructor that Customer is not null
cards.explain: All of this is metadata for the compiler. There is no run-time check: if you bypass new (via reflection or a deserializer), Customer stays null.

cards.title: An indexer is a property named Item
cards.body:
this[int i] compiles to a property with a parameter, named Item: methods get_Item(int) and set_Item(int, T). The type gets [DefaultMember("Item")] — that is how VB and reflection know it is the default indexer. [IndexerName("Cell")] sets a different name.

Indexers overload on parameter types, like methods. An indexer can return ref T — that is what Span<T> does.

A free bonus: if a type has Length or Count and an int indexer, ^1 works — the compiler rewrites it to [Count - 1] itself. Add a Slice(int, int) method and ranges [1..3] work too.

cards.title: An anonymous type is a class the compiler writes
cards.body:
For new { Name = "Ann", Age = 30 } the compiler creates an internal sealed class with a name like <>f__AnonymousType0`2, generic over the property types. It has:

  • read-only properties;
  • Equals and GetHashCode over the values of all properties;
  • a ToString like { Name = Ann, Age = 30 }.

The same names, types and order of properties within one assembly mean the same type. A different order is a different type. Since C# 10 with works. An anonymous type can leave a method only as object or dynamic — it has no name in C#.
cards.deep: It is a reference type: every new { } is a heap object. The == operator is not overloaded on an anonymous type and compares references, while Equals compares values. In LINQ to Objects an anonymous type works as a composite key in GroupBy and Distinct precisely because of this Equals/GetHashCode.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: a and b are the same anonymous type, Equals compares values: True. == is not overloaded and compares references: False. c is a different type (a different property order), so Equals with it is False.

cards.title: ValueTuple: a mutable struct without names
cards.body:
(string Name, int Age) is System.ValueTuple<string, int>: a mutable struct with public fields Item1, Item2. After the seventh element comes a Rest field holding a nested tuple. Do not confuse it with the old System.Tuple — that one is a class, on the heap and immutable.

The names Name and Age exist only for the compiler. IL uses Item1/Item2 everywhere. To carry the names across an assembly boundary, the compiler writes a [TupleElementNames] attribute on the method, field or property signature.

The == comparison (C# 7.3) is element-wise and ignores the names.
cards.deep:
Anything that looks through reflection does not see the names. System.Text.Json does not serialize fields by default, so a tuple turns into {}, and with IncludeFields into {"Item1":...,"Item2":...}. For DTOs and public contracts, use a record.

The "version 2" scenario: renaming tuple elements in a return type is binary-safe (only the attribute changed), but it breaks the source of everyone who used the old names.

cards.q: What does this code print?
options: Nothing: a tuple has properties, not fields
cards.explain: The names Name and Age exist only in the compiler. The run-time type is ValueTuple<string, int>, and it has public fields Item1 and Item2.

cards.title: Deconstruction and Deconstruct
cards.body:
The compiler turns var (name, age) = person; into a call to a Deconstruct method with out parameters. The method is found by name and parameter count — an instance method or an extension method. There is no interface, it is a convention (like GetEnumerator for foreach).

Tuples deconstruct without a method — the compiler takes the fields directly. Positional records generate Deconstruct themselves, and KeyValuePair has one too. The positional pattern p is (0, var y) uses the same Deconstruct.

For the swap (a, b) = (b, a) the compiler usually lays out temporaries, and no tuple is created.

cards.q: Teach the Size class to deconstruct: var (w, h) = size;
cards.explain: The compiler looks for a method with the exact name Deconstruct and out parameters matching the number of variables on the left. ref or in will not do.

lessons.title: Final: parameters and tuples
lessons.sub: ref, defaults, params, properties and ValueTuple

cards.q: Why can you not declare void M(ref int x) next to void M(in int x)?
options: In IL both parameters are int32&, so the signatures collide
in and ref cannot be used in the same class
The compiler could not choose: the modifier is optional at the call site
The CLR forbids two methods with the same name
cards.explain: ref, out, in and ref readonly are one managed pointer; only flags and attributes differ. You cannot overload on them, while the pair M(int) and M(in int) is legal.

wrong.3: Overloading on different parameter types is normal for the CLR. The problem is that the types here are the same.

cards.q: Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: ref readonly is a read-only reference: you cannot assign through it. r is an ordinary ref local, r = 10 changes arr[0]. Reading ro into a copy is fine.

cards.q: Library v1: Connect(int timeout = 30). In v2: Connect(int timeout = 30, bool tls = true). The app was built against v1, the DLL was replaced. What happens on the call Connect()?
options: A call with timeout = 30 and tls = true
A call with timeout = 30 and tls = false
A compile error in the app
cards.explain: An added optional parameter changes the signature. The old IL looks for Connect(int32) and does not find it. Default values are inserted by the caller at compile time, and the app was not rebuilt. The fix is an overload with the old signature.

cards.q: Match the C# construct to what it leaves in metadata
What is true about (int X, int Y)? Select all.
options: It is the mutable struct ValueTuple<int, int>
At run time it has fields Item1 and Item2
It is the System.Tuple class on the heap
Reflection sees fields X and Y
cards.explain: The names live only in the compiler and the TupleElementNames attribute. The == comparison is element-wise and ignores names. System.Tuple is a different, older class type.

cards.q: There are Join(params string[]) and Join(params ReadOnlySpan<string>). Which overloads do Join("a", "b") and Join(arr), where arr is a string[], pick?
options: The first — span, the second — array
The first — array, the second — span
cards.explain: Join("a", "b") fits both only in expanded form — then the span wins (C# 13). Join(arr) fits both in normal form, and the exact string[] match beats converting the array to a span.

cards.q: The method hands out a reference to the first element, and the caller writes through it
cards.explain: ref in the return type, ref in the return, and a ref local in the caller. Without ref on the left, f would be a copy and arr would not change.

cards.q: A C# 10 project calls new Order() from a library where Order has a required member. What happens?
options: A compile error: the constructor is marked Obsolete as an error
It compiles and throws at run time
cards.explain: The compiler marks the constructors of a type with required members with Obsolete (as an error) and CompilerFeatureRequired. An old compiler does not understand required, but it does understand Obsolete — and will not let you create the object around the check.

cards.q: What is new Temp().C?
cards.explain: A property initializer writes straight into the hidden field (field), the setter is not called. The check runs only on an assignment C = ....

units.blurb: Why they exist, how the JIT compiles them for value and reference types, where constraints, covariance and contravariance, and generic math with INumber<T>.

lessons.title: Why generics
lessons.sub: One piece of code for many types — no object, no casts

cards.title: Life before generics
cards.body: In .NET 1.0, collections stored object. You could put anything in, but getting it out took a cast. Make a mistake and you found out at run time.
cards.code:
var list = new ArrayList();
list.Add(42);           // int is boxed into object
list.Add("forty-two");  // a string is fine too
int x = (int)list[1];   // InvalidCastException at run time

cards.q: Which line fails at run time?
cards.explain: The second element is a string, and the cast to int is only checked at run time.

cards.title: List<T>: the type is a parameter
cards.body: A generic is code with a type parameter T. The compiler plugs in a concrete type and checks everything up front. Value types are not boxed: List<int> stores real ints.

cards.task: Max must compare a and b and work with both int and string. Add the constraint it needs.

cards.q: Why can't you call a.CompareTo(b) without a constraint?
options: Nothing is known about T — an arbitrary type may not have CompareTo
You have to cast to object first
cards.explain: A constraint is a promise to the compiler: "T has this."

cards.title: How the JIT compiles generics
cards.body: For all reference types the JIT emits one shared piece of machine code: a reference is always 8 bytes. Each value type gets its own: List<int> and List<double> each get separate, fast code with no boxing.

cards.q: How many machine-code versions of Add do List<string>, List<object> and List<int> get?
options: Two: one shared by string and object, one for int
cards.explain: Reference types share code; value types get their own.

cards.q: Match them up
What do generics give you? Select all.
options: Code that runs without the JIT
cards.explain: The JIT still compiles the code — just for specific types.

lessons.title: where constraints
lessons.sub: class, struct, new(), unmanaged and interfaces

cards.title: What you can require of T
cards.body:
class — a reference type (can be null).
struct — a value type.
unmanaged — a value type with no references inside (works with stackalloc and pointers).
new() — has a public parameterless constructor.
An interface — T has its methods.

cards.task: A factory creates a new object of type T. It must work with List<int> and Point.

cards.q: Why doesn't string satisfy new()?
options: string has no public parameterless constructor
cards.explain: new string() does not compile — so string does not satisfy new() either.

cards.task: A cache holds a T value and can reset it to null. It must work with string and List<int>, but not with int.
A fast stack buffer via stackalloc. It must work with int and Point.

cards.title: What doesn't mix
cards.body: class and struct can't be combined. unmanaged already means "value type", so you don't write it with struct, class or new(). Order: class/struct/unmanaged first, then interfaces, new() last.

cards.q: Order of constraints
cards.code: T Make<T>() where T : ___, IDisposable, ___
cards.explain: new() always goes at the end of the list.

cards.q: What does default(T) return for T = int and T = string?
cards.explain: default means "zeros": the zero value for value types, null for reference types.

cards.q: Match the constraint to what it allows
Which types satisfy where T : struct? Select all.
cards.explain: string is a reference type. int? is Nullable<int>: it is a value type, but the struct constraint deliberately rejects it.

lessons.title: Variance and generic math
lessons.sub: out T, in T and INumber<T>

cards.title: Why List<string> is not a List<object>
cards.body: If that assignment were allowed, you could put a number into a list of strings through the "list of objects" — and break it.
cards.code:
List<object> objs = new List<string>();   // compile error
objs.Add(42);                              // and this is why

cards.title: Covariance: out T
cards.body: IEnumerable<T>, on the other hand, only hands out T and never takes one in. So a sequence of strings can safely be treated as a sequence of objects. That is marked with out: IEnumerable<out T>.
cards.code: IEnumerable<object> objs = new List<string> { "a", "b" };   // allowed

cards.title: Contravariance: in T
cards.body: Action<in T> only takes in T. An action that can print any object also works where an action for string is expected.
cards.code:
Action<object> print = o => Console.WriteLine(o);
Action<string> printText = print;   // allowed

cards.q: Which assignment compiles?
cards.explain: IList takes elements in (Add), so it is invariant.

cards.q: Match them up

cards.title: The array trap
cards.body: Arrays have been covariant since .NET 1.0 — before generics existed. The compiler lets this through, and it fails at run time:
cards.code:
object[] arr = new string[2];
arr[0] = 42;   // ArrayTypeMismatchException

cards.title: Generic math (C# 11, .NET 7)
cards.body: You used to be unable to write Sum<T> for any number type: T has no + operator. Now interfaces can require static members, and INumber<T> gives you +, −, Zero and the rest.

cards.q: A sum for any number type
cards.explain: Zero is a static property from the interface, so you write T.Zero.

cards.q: Why does the compiler accept object[] arr = new string[2], even though it is risky?
options: Array covariance stayed from .NET 1.0 for compatibility; the check happens at run time
cards.explain: Generic interfaces made variance safe, but arrays stayed as they were.

lessons.title: Final: generics
lessons.sub: Constraints, the JIT and variance

cards.task: The method creates a T and compares values. It must work with int, and must reject string.

cards.q: where T : struct, new() — what does the compiler say?
options: Error: a struct always has a parameterless constructor, so new() is not allowed with it
cards.explain: With struct, new T() is already allowed.

cards.q: You pass an IEnumerable<Cat> where an IEnumerable<Animal> is expected. Does it work?
cards.explain: Covariance works for reference types in interfaces and delegates.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: For reference-type T the JIT emits shared code
object[] arr = new string[1]; arr[0] = 1; fails at run time
cards.explain: string is a reference type, so it is not unmanaged.

cards.q: Match the task to the constraint
Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: An unconstrained T cannot be null — T might be int. default always works.

cards.q: The constraint that allows T x = null
cards.code: class Box<T> where T : ___
cards.explain: Only reference types (and Nullable<T>) can be null.

cards.q: Why did C# 11 add static abstract interface members?
options: So a generic can require operators and static properties — like + and Zero on numbers
cards.explain: INumber<T> and all of generic math are built on this.
