lessons.title: Explicit implementation and boxing
lessons.sub: Interface-only methods, a struct in a box and calls through a stub

cards.title: Implicit and explicit implementation
cards.body:
A class implements an interface method in one of two ways.

Implicitly — an ordinary public method with the same name and signature. It is visible both through the class and through the interface.

Explicitly — the name is prefixed with the interface and there is no access modifier. You cannot call such a method through a class variable, only through an interface reference.
cards.deep:
In IL an implicit implementation is a public method flagged virtual final newslot. The compiler makes it virtual so it gets a slot in the method table, and seals it unless you wrote virtual yourself.

An explicit implementation is a private method named System.IDisposable.Dispose with an .override directive (a MethodImpl record) that binds it to the interface method. You cannot write a dotted name in C#, so it never clashes with ordinary methods.

An explicit implementation cannot be virtual or abstract. If a derived class needs to change the behavior, the explicit method simply calls a protected virtual one — that is how the classic Dispose pattern works.

cards.q: Report implements IExportable.Export() explicitly. Which line does not compile?
cards.explain: An explicitly implemented method is not among the public members of the class. Through a variable of type Report it is invisible — error CS1061. Through the interface (a variable or a cast) it is fine.

cards.title: Why hide a method
cards.body:
Three typical reasons:

  • A name clash. Two interfaces require a method with the same signature but different meaning. Explicit implementation gives each its own code.
  • An old untyped method. IEnumerable<T> inherits the non-generic IEnumerable. The generic GetEnumerator is made public, and the one returning plain IEnumerator is made explicit so it stays out of the way.
  • A member nobody needs day to day. List<T> implements ICollection<T>.IsReadOnly explicitly: for a list it is always false and would only be noise in IntelliSense.

cards.q: A class implements IPrinter and IPlotter, and both require void Print(). Through IPrinter it must print text, through IPlotter it must draw a chart. How?
options: Implement at least one of the methods explicitly
Write two public Print() methods in one class
You cannot: these interfaces are incompatible in one class
Mark one of the methods with new
cards.explain: A single public Print() would satisfy both interfaces at once, but with one behavior. An explicit void IPlotter.Print() gives the second interface its own code, while the public Print() stays for IPrinter and for calls through the class.

wrong.1: Two methods with the same signature in one class is error CS0111.
wrong.2: They are compatible: identical signatures in different interfaces are common, and explicit implementation exists for exactly that.

cards.title: Explicit implementation on a struct: only through a box
cards.body:
As in the "Value types all the way" unit: an interface is a reference type, and a struct converted to it is boxed. A method called through the interface changes the box, not the original variable.

Explicit implementation makes this trap mandatory. On a class the explicit method is merely hidden, but on a struct there is no ordinary call path left at all: c.Inc() does not compile, and ((ICounter)c).Inc() creates a box, increments it and throws it away at once. The change is lost silently.
cards.deep:
In IL a call through the interface is box followed by callvirt on the interface method. The box is a full object with a header and a type pointer: for Counter on x64 that is 24 bytes.

That is why explicit implementation is avoided on mutable structs. In the libraries it shows up on struct enumerators: List<T>.Enumerator explicitly implements IEnumerator.Current (returning object) and IEnumerator.Reset. Nobody uses them through the public API, and foreach over a List<T> itself calls the public MoveNext and Current directly, without a box.

cards.q: Counter from the previous card: Inc is implemented explicitly. What does this print?
cards.explain: The first cast creates a box, increments it and throws it away: c.Value stays 0. ICounter a = c boxes c again, still with zero, and a.Inc() brings that box to 1.

wrong.1: That would be true if ((ICounter)c).Inc() changed the variable c itself. But the cast works on a copy.
wrong.3: Box a was created from c, and c still holds 0: the first box is already gone.

cards.title: The box-free path: a constrained generic
cards.body:
There is a way to call a struct's explicit method without boxing: a generic constrained with where T : ICounter. For a value-type T the JIT compiles a separate copy of the method, knows the exact type and calls the implementation directly — an explicit one too, since an explicit implementation is an ordinary method, just private.

For the change to reach the caller, pass the parameter by ref. Without it the method works on its own copy of the struct: no box, but nothing changes outside either.
cards.deep:
For x.Inc() inside a generic the compiler emits the constrained. prefix:

ldarg.0
constrained. !!T
callvirt instance void ICounter::Inc()

For a value-type T that implements the interface method itself — implicitly or explicitly — the runtime finds the implementation in the struct type and calls it through the managed pointer, without a box. The explicit method being private does not get in the way: access is checked against the interface method, not the implementation. The compiler uses the same trick in using and foreach with a struct: Dispose on a struct enumerator is called without boxing, even if it is implemented explicitly.

cards.q: Complete the method: it must increment any struct counter without boxing, and the change must be visible outside
cards.explain: ref gives the method access to the caller's variable itself. The ICounter constraint allows calling Inc and lets the JIT make a direct call without a box. With in, Inc would run on a defensive copy and the changes would be lost; with class you could not pass a struct at all.

cards.title: How the CLR finds an interface method
cards.body:
For a class's virtual method the slot number in the method table is known in advance: in a derived class the overridden ToString sits where the base one does. The call is a couple of memory reads and an indirect jump.

That does not work for interfaces. A class implements any number of interfaces, and the same method ICounter.Inc ends up in different slots in different classes. So CoreCLR calls an interface method through a stub with a cache: the call site remembers the type it has seen, and while objects of that type keep arriving, the call is almost as fast as a virtual one.

It gets more expensive where many different types pass through one call site: then the implementation is looked up in a shared hash table.
cards.deep:
The mechanism is called virtual stub dispatch (VSD). The call site goes through an indirection cell, and the runtime rewrites it as it learns more:

  • lookup stub — the first call: passes the method token and the object type to a shared resolver;
  • dispatch stub — afterwards: compares the object's MethodTable with the remembered one and jumps straight to the implementation, falling through to the resolve stub on a mismatch;
  • resolve stub — if misses pile up, the call site is treated as polymorphic and switched here: a lookup of the "token + type" pair in a global cache.

On top of that, the JIT with dynamic PGO (on by default since .NET 8) does guarded devirtualization: if the profile shows one class almost always arrives, the JIT inserts a type check and a direct — and therefore inlinable — call, keeping the stub as the fallback. Native AOT uses its own caching scheme without VSD. The details change between versions, so measure the cost of a specific call site.

cards.q: Why can an interface method not be called like a virtual one — by a slot number known in advance?
options: The same interface method sits in different slots in different classes
Interface methods do not go into the class's method table
Structs implement interfaces too, and they have no method table
Interface slots are reassigned on every garbage collection
cards.explain: Virtual method slots are inherited down the class chain, so an override keeps the same number. Each class has its own set of interfaces, and there is no common number for ICounter.Inc — it is looked up by the object's type and the result is cached in the stub.

wrong.1: They do: an implicit implementation is a virtual final method with its own slot. The point is that the slot number differs between classes.

cards.q: Counter is a struct implementing ICounter; c is a Counter variable; list is a List<int>. Where does boxing happen by the rules of the language and IL? Select all.
options: IEnumerable<int> e = list; foreach (var x in e) { }
Bump(ref c), where Bump<T>(ref T x) where T : ICounter
cards.explain: Assigning to an interface boxes the struct. Iterating through IEnumerable<int> gets List<int>.Enumerator through the interface — boxed as well. The constrained generic, reading a property of the struct and foreach over the List<int> itself manage without one.

cards.q: Match the construct to what it means
pairs: Explicit implementation: call only through the interface
A call without a box for a value-type T
IL prefix before callvirt in a generic
Checks the object type against the remembered one

lessons.title: Default methods and version 2
lessons.sub: How to change an interface without breaking other people's code, and what static abstract is

cards.title: Version 2: adding a method to an interface
cards.body:
You shipped a library with an IExporter interface, and dozens of teams implemented it. In version 2 you want to add ExportAsync.

Without extra measures this is a breaking change. The implementers' code stops compiling: CS0535, interface member not implemented. And an already built plugin assembly, loaded next to the new library version, fails when its type is loaded: TypeLoadException — "method does not have an implementation".

With an abstract base class it is easier: derived classes simply inherit a new virtual method with a body, changing nothing.

cards.q: A plugin was built against version 1 and never rebuilt. The app updated the library to version 2, where a method without a body was added to the interface. What happens?
options: TypeLoadException when the CLR loads the plugin class
Compile error CS0535 when the app starts
Everything works, and calling ExportAsync returns null
NotImplementedException only when ExportAsync is called
cards.explain: There is nothing left to compile — the assembly is built. When loading the class, the CLR builds its method table and sees an interface method with no implementation. The whole type is rejected: you cannot even call its old Export.

wrong.1: The compiler does not run at startup. The plugin authors will see CS0535 when they rebuild.
wrong.3: That would happen if the CLR filled in stubs. It does not: a type without an implementation simply does not load.

cards.title: A default method
cards.body:
Since C# 8 an interface method can have a body — a default implementation (default interface method, DIM). Classes that did not implement it get the body from the interface. Version 2 is no longer breaking.

This is a runtime feature, not just a compiler one: the CLR has to find the body in the interface when the class has no implementation. That is why DIM works from .NET Core 3.0 on and is unavailable on .NET Framework — even with a new compiler.
cards.deep:
The compiler checks for support via the RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces field in the target library. .NET Framework and .NET Standard 2.0 lack it — error CS8701: the target runtime does not support default interface implementation. .NET Standard 2.1 supports it, which is one reason .NET Framework does not implement it.

In IL a default method is an ordinary virtual interface method with a body (no abstract). A class can override it implicitly — with a public method — or explicitly. A derived interface can replace the base body with its own explicit implementation: void IBase.M() { … }.

cards.q: IExporter is from the previous card; ExportAsync has a default body. Which line does not compile?
cards.explain: A default member belongs to the interface; the class does not inherit it. CsvExporter has no ExportAsync method — error CS1061. Through an IExporter variable the call works.

cards.title: What DIM cannot do
cards.body:
• No state. Interfaces still have no instance fields. A default method works only through other interface members; it cannot see the object's data.
  • Not visible through the class. The class does not inherit a default member: you can call it only through the interface.
  • The diamond. If two derived interfaces give their own bodies to one base method, and a class implements both without writing its own method — a compile error: there is no most specific implementation.
  • Structs. Inside a default body this is the interface. A struct that did not override the method is boxed when such a method is called — even from a constrained generic.
cards.deep:
Along with DIM, C# 8 allowed interfaces to have access modifiers on members, private and static methods, static fields and a static constructor. There are still no instance fields or instance constructors: an interface does not hold object state.

Syntax for calling a base interface implementation (base(IShape).Name()) was discussed for C# 8 but did not make it into the language. If a class overrides the method, it cannot call the default body — shared code goes into a static interface method that both places call.

The diamond is fixed with one line: the class writes its own Name() — implicitly or explicitly — and that becomes the most specific implementation.

cards.q: What is true about default interface methods? Select all.
options: They let you add a method to an interface without breaking old implementations
They work on .NET Framework 4.8 if you build with a new compiler
You cannot call a default member through a variable of the implementing class
They give an interface instance fields
A struct that did not override a default method is boxed when it is called
cards.explain: DIM needs runtime support, and .NET Framework does not have it (CS8701). Interfaces did not get instance fields: only static fields are allowed.

cards.title: Static abstract members
cards.body:
An ordinary interface describes what an object can do. Since C# 11 (.NET 7) an interface can also require static members of the type: a factory, string parsing, a constant, an operator. They are called through the type parameter: T.Parse(...).

Before, this needed reflection or a separate factory object. Now the JIT finds the implementation: for a value-type T — when compiling the specialized copy of the method, for reference types — through the generic dictionary in shared code.

Generic math from the "Generics" unit is built on exactly this.
cards.deep:
In IL the call is constrained. !!T call on the static interface method: the same prefix as for instance calls in generics. There is no object at all, so there is no boxing either.

Restrictions. You cannot call through the interface itself: ICommand<Move>.Parse("1") is error CS8926. An interface with static abstract members cannot be a type argument: List<ICommand<Move>> does not compile (CS8920), since such a "type" has no body for T.Parse. There is also static virtual — with a default body. In the libraries, IParsable<TSelf> and ISpanParsable<TSelf> require static abstract methods, while a static virtual with a body exists, for example, in IBinaryInteger<TSelf>.DivRem.

cards.q: Complete loading a command from text
cards.code:
static T Load<T>(string text) where T : ___<T> =>
    ___.Parse(text);
cards.explain: A static member is called through the type parameter: T.Parse. There is no this in a static method, and the object does not exist yet — Parse is what creates it.

cards.title: Interface or base class
cards.body:
A base class gives you state, constructors, protected members and safe evolution: a new virtual method with a body breaks nothing. The price — you can inherit only one class, and a struct cannot inherit classes at all.

An interface gives multiple implementation, works with structs and imposes no hierarchy. The price is evolution: a new member either has a default body or breaks people. DIM softens the blow but gives no state.

A real example is Stream. In .NET Core 2.1 it gained Read(Span<byte>) as a virtual method whose body rents an array and calls the old Read(byte[], int, int). Every stream written before that kept working. Had Stream been an interface, this would have been impossible before DIM.
cards.deep:
The call cost is almost the same: a virtual call uses a fixed slot, an interface call uses a cached stub, and PGO often devirtualizes both. The difference shows only at polymorphic hot spots, and it is not a reason to pick a class over an interface.

A common library pattern is a narrow interface as the contract plus an abstract base class with shared code for those who like to inherit. Interfaces are also chosen for generics over structs: where T : IComparable<T> gives a call without boxing, while a base class cannot constrain a struct.

cards.q: Which version 2 change does not break already built derived classes or implementers?
options: Adding a virtual method with a body to an abstract class
Adding a method without a body to an interface
Adding an abstract method to an abstract class
Making a virtual method of the base class abstract
cards.explain: Derived classes get a new virtual method with a body as is. Every other option requires a new implementation from each derived type: without it, CS0534 or CS0535 on rebuild and TypeLoadException for old assemblies.

cards.q: Match the task to the tool
pairs: A capability that a struct implements too
A new interface member without breakage
A T.Create() factory in a generic

cards.q: A struct implements IShape but does not override Name() — it uses the default body. What happens when calling Describe(ref s), where Describe<T>(ref T x) where T : IShape => x.Name()?
options: Boxing: the default body needs a this of the interface type
A direct call without boxing, as with the struct's own method
A compile error: the struct has no Name()
A runtime exception: the method is missing from the struct's table
cards.explain: constrained. avoids the box only when the value type implements the method itself. The default body lives in the interface and treats this as an interface reference — so the runtime boxes the struct, and field changes inside such a method never reach s.

wrong.1: That would be the case if the struct wrote its own Name(). Then there is no box.

lessons.title: Final: interfaces
lessons.sub: Boxing, default methods and version 2

cards.q: Counter is a struct with a public Inc() method that increments Value. What does this print?
cards.explain: The box was created while c was 0. After that two independent copies live on: c grew to 1, the box to 2. The sum is 3.

wrong.1: That would be true if i referred to the variable c itself. But the interface holds a box with a copy.

cards.q: Which line does not compile?
cards.explain: Dispose is implemented explicitly and is not visible through a Cache variable. using works because it calls Dispose through IDisposable. DisposeAsync is an ordinary public method.

cards.q: S is a struct implementing IComparable<S>; s and t are variables of type S. What boxes s? Select all.
options: Max(s, t), where Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>
cards.explain: Converting to an interface or to object is always a box. In a constrained generic the JIT makes a separate copy for S and calls CompareTo directly. s.CompareTo(t) is a direct call to the struct's method.

cards.q: You added a method without a body to a public interface. What will a team see when it rebuilds its implementation against the new version?
options: Error CS0535: interface member not implemented
A warning, and the method will be empty
Nothing: the method gets a default body
cards.explain: A rebuild means the compiler, and it demands an implementation. TypeLoadException is for those who did not rebuild and just dropped in the new library. A default body appears only if you write it in the interface.

cards.q: Add a method to the interface that does not break old implementations
cards.explain: A body in braces makes it a default method. Inside it can use only other interface members — here Export. There is no base.Export in an interface.

cards.q: Match
pairs: No boxing for a value-type T

cards.q: ICommand<TSelf> contains static abstract TSelf Parse(string). Why does List<ICommand<Move>> not compile?
options: The interface has no body for static abstract members, and a type argument could reach a T.Parse call
Interfaces can never be type arguments
A record cannot appear in type arguments
cards.explain: The rule is general (CS8920): if an interface has a static abstract member without a most specific implementation, the interface itself cannot be a type argument — otherwise T.Parse would have to be called on a "type" with no body. Ordinary interfaces, as in List<IDisposable>, are fine.

cards.q: What happens to an interface call site in CoreCLR as the program runs? Put it in order
items: The call cell points to the lookup stub
The resolver finds the implementation for the incoming type
The cell is switched to a dispatch stub for that type
Different types start arriving, misses pile up
The cell is switched to the resolve stub with a shared cache
cards.explain: First a lookup through the shared resolver, then a fast check against one remembered type, and only if the site turns out polymorphic — a lookup in the global cache by the "method + type" pair.

units.title: Delegates, events and closures
units.blurb: Func and Action, multicast delegates, events and subscription leaks, lambdas and what exactly they capture; what a delegate is inside: a MulticastDelegate class, chains and exceptions in them, explicit add/remove.

lessons.title: Delegates and lambdas
lessons.sub: A method as a value

cards.title: A variable that holds a method
cards.body: A delegate is an object that holds a reference to a method. You can pass it to another method, put it in a list, or call it later.

cards.title: Func, Action, Predicate
cards.body:
Func<…, TResult> — takes arguments and returns a result (the last type parameter is the result type).
Action<…> — returns nothing.
Predicate<T> — returns bool.

cards.q: Match the signature to the delegate

cards.title: A lambda is a method without a name
cards.body: You can write a method right where you need it: x => x * 2. The compiler infers the types from where the lambda is passed.
cards.code:
var evens = numbers.Where(x => x % 2 == 0);
Func<int, int> twice = x => x * 2;

cards.q: A delegate that takes a string and returns bool
cards.code: ___<string, ___> isEmpty = s => s.Length == 0;
cards.explain: Predicate<string> would work too, but there are two gaps here — Func<string, bool>.

cards.title: One delegate, several methods
cards.body: Delegates are multicast: += adds a method to the invocation list. Calling the delegate runs them all in order. If it returns a value, you get the result of the last one.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: Both run, but you get the result of the last one in the list.

cards.q: How is Action different from Func?
options: Action returns nothing, Func returns a result
cards.explain: Func<int> returns an int; Action<int> takes an int and returns nothing.

cards.q: Which are true about delegates? Select all.
options: A delegate is an object on the heap
You can pass a delegate to a method
+= adds a method to the invocation list
A lambda cannot be a delegate
cards.explain: A lambda is exactly what turns into a delegate (or an expression tree).

lessons.title: Events
lessons.sub: A delegate outsiders can only subscribe to

cards.title: Why the event keyword
cards.body:
A public delegate field is dangerous: anyone can invoke it or wipe out every subscriber with =.

event leaves outsiders only += and -=. Only the owning class can raise the event.

cards.q: Which line will not compile outside the Button class?
cards.explain: From the outside an event only has += and -=. You cannot assign or invoke it.

cards.q: Why the ?. in Clicked?.Invoke(...)?
options: With no subscribers the event is null — without ?. you get a NullReferenceException
cards.explain: An event with no subscribers is null.

cards.title: The standard shape
cards.body: By convention a handler receives the sender and the arguments: EventHandler<TArgs>.
cards.code:
public event EventHandler<OrderEventArgs>? OrderPlaced;

shop.OrderPlaced += (sender, e) => Console.WriteLine(e.OrderId);

cards.title: A subscription holds on to the subscriber
cards.body: The publisher stores the delegate, and the delegate stores a reference to the subscriber object. As long as the publisher is alive and you have not unsubscribed, the garbage collector will not collect the subscriber. The classic leak: a window subscribes to a global event and never unsubscribes.

cards.q: A window subscribed to the static event App.ThemeChanged and closed without unsubscribing. What happens?
options: The window stays in memory: the event holds a reference to it
The garbage collector collects the window
The event unsubscribes the closed window by itself
cards.explain: More on this in ".NET under the hood", in the "Garbage collection and resources" unit.

cards.q: Raise the event only if there are subscribers
cards.code: Clicked___Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
cards.explain: A null-conditional call.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Raise only if there are subscribers
Unsubscribe and let the object go

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: Only the owning class can raise an event
An event with no subscribers is null
A subscription keeps the subscriber in memory
Outsiders can clear an event with =
cards.explain: Blocking = from the outside is exactly what event is for.

lessons.title: Closures
lessons.sub: A lambda captures the variable, not the value

cards.title: A lambda sees outer variables
cards.body: A lambda can use the variables of the method it was created in. So the variable can outlive the method, the compiler moves it into a hidden object on the heap, and the lambda holds a reference to that object.

cards.task: Three lambdas are created in a for loop. Step through: what will they print?

cards.q: Why did all three lambdas print 3?
options: They captured the same variable i, and by the time they ran it was 3
cards.explain: The variable is captured, not its value at the moment the lambda was created.

cards.task: Fix it: make it print 0 1 2, but keep the for loop.
And how does foreach behave?

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: The lambda changes the very same count variable — it now lives in the hidden object.

cards.title: foreach was fixed in C# 5
cards.body: Before C# 5, foreach had the same trap. It was fixed: the foreach variable is now fresh on every iteration. Not so with for: there really is one variable for the whole loop.

cards.title: The cost of capturing
cards.body: Capturing means a heap object plus a delegate. In hot code that runs millions of times, that is extra work for the GC. The static keyword in front of a lambda (C# 9) forbids capturing — the compiler checks that the lambda pulls nothing from outside.
cards.code: var r = items.Where(static x => x > 0);   // captures nothing

cards.q: What does static do in front of x => x > limit, where limit is a local variable?
options: Compile error: a static lambda cannot capture limit
cards.explain: static guarantees there is no capture.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: int j = i inside the loop

lessons.title: Delegates inside out
lessons.sub: The delegate class, chains, exceptions and explicit add/remove

cards.title: One delegate line is a whole class
cards.body:
The declaration delegate int Op(int a, int b); is not a "function type" but a class. The compiler generates a sealed class Op deriving from System.MulticastDelegate, with four methods:

  • a constructor (object, IntPtr) — an object and a method address;
  • Invoke(int a, int b) — with the same signature as the delegate;
  • BeginInvoke and EndInvoke — old-style asynchronous invocation.

These methods have no bodies: they are marked runtime managed, and the CLR supplies their code. Func and Action are the same kind of class, just already declared in the library.
cards.deep:
The compiler turns op(2, 3) into callvirt Op::Invoke. The JIT does not call Invoke like an ordinary method: it reads the object and the code address from the delegate and makes an indirect call — close to a virtual call in cost. The JIT usually cannot inline a delegate's target; with dynamic PGO (.NET 8+) it sometimes inserts a "is it that same method" check and a direct call — guarded devirtualization for delegates.

On .NET Framework, BeginInvoke ran the delegate on the thread pool through the remoting infrastructure. On .NET Core and later the method is still in the metadata but throws PlatformNotSupportedException. The replacement is Task.Run(() => op(2, 3)).

cards.q: What does the compiler turn op(2, 3) into, where op is a variable of type Op?
options: A direct call to the target method
cards.explain: Invoking a delegate is always a call to its Invoke method. The compiler does not know what will be inside the delegate: that is decided at run time.

wrong.1: DynamicInvoke is a slow reflection-based call with an argument array. The compiler never uses it on its own.
wrong.2: Which method the delegate holds is known only at run time.

cards.title: Inside: an object and a code address
cards.body:
A delegate instance is a heap object. It inherits two key fields from System.Delegate:

  • _target — the object to call an instance method on;
  • _methodPtr — the address of the method's machine code.

From outside you see them as the Target and Method properties. For a static method Target returns null. Creating a delegate in IL is ldftn (take the method address) plus newobj on the constructor: one allocation.
cards.deep:
A delegate to a static method is trickier inside: the real address sits in _methodPtrAux, while _methodPtr holds a small shuffle thunk that shifts the arguments, since there is no receiver object. The Target property still returns null. Because of the thunk, a delegate to a static method is slightly more expensive to call than one to an instance method.

That is why the C# compiler turns capture-free lambdas into instance methods of a hidden singleton class <>c and caches the delegate itself in a static field: creating it again does not allocate. Since C# 11 a static method group conversion is cached the same way (Func<int, int> f = Math.Abs;).

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.code:
Func<int, int> twice = x => x * 2;
Console.WriteLine(twice.Target is null);
options: False: Target is an instance of the hidden <>c class
True: a capture-free lambda compiles to a static method
False: Target is the delegate twice itself
Does not compile: a lambda has no Target
cards.explain: The C# compiler places capture-free lambdas in instance methods of the <>c singleton: a delegate to an instance method needs no argument-shuffling thunk. Target is that singleton.

wrong.1: It sounds logical, but the compiler avoids it on purpose: a delegate to a static method goes through a thunk and is slightly slower.

cards.title: A chain is a new object
cards.body:
a += b means a = (Action)Delegate.Combine(a, b). Combine changes neither a nor b: delegates are immutable. It creates a new delegate that holds an array inside — the invocation list of all methods in order.

-= is Delegate.Remove: also a new object, without the last occurrence of the method. Remove the last method and you get null.

Two consequences. Every += is an allocation, and a chain also has an array. And a copy of the delegate in another variable does not see new subscriptions: it points to the old object.
cards.deep:
In MulticastDelegate the chain lives in the _invocationList field (an object[] of delegates) and _invocationCount. Combine with null returns the other argument without allocating. When appending, the runtime can reuse an array with spare room if the next slot in it is still free — so a series of += does not copy the whole list every time.

Immutability makes invocation thread-safe: handler?.Invoke() works on one snapshot of the chain even if another thread is unsubscribing right now. That is why the old advice "copy the event to a local before the null check" boils down to ?. today.

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.explain: copy = log copies a reference to a single-method delegate. Each += creates a new chain and stores it only in its own variable: log is 1 and 2, copy is 1 and 3.

wrong.1: That would be true if += appended the method to a shared object. But delegates are immutable.

cards.title: Exceptions and results in a chain
cards.body:
Invoke on a chain is a loop over the invocation list. Hence behavior that is easy to forget:

  • An exception in the second method breaks the loop. The third and later ones are not called, and the exception flies to whoever invoked the delegate.
  • The return value comes from the last method; the other results are discarded. Each next method sees ref and out parameters already changed by the previous one.

If you need to call everyone independently or collect all results, walk GetInvocationList() yourself.

cards.q: On which line does Console.WriteLine never run?
cards.explain: The chain calls the methods in turn: "step 1", then the exception. The third method is never called — the exception has left Invoke. catch prints "error", then "done".

cards.q: Collect the results of all checks, not just the last one
cards.explain: GetInvocationList returns an array of delegates, one method each. Their Invoke returns its own bool. DynamicInvoke would return object — it does not go into a List<bool> without a cast, and a reflection call is slow anyway.

cards.title: An event with explicit add and remove
cards.body:
An ordinary event public event EventHandler? Changed; is expanded by the compiler into a private delegate field and two accessor methods: add_Changed and remove_Changed. Those are what += and -= call from outside.

You can write the accessors yourself — like get and set on a property. Then the compiler creates no field, and you decide where subscribers live: in one dictionary for all events, in another object, in weak references.
cards.deep:
Since C# 4 the generated add of an ordinary event takes no lock: in a loop it reads the field, calls Delegate.Combine and tries to store the result with Interlocked.CompareExchange until nobody interferes. Subscribing from different threads is safe. In your own accessors thread safety is on you — the dictionary in the example does not provide it.

Why bother: a class with a hundred events that usually nobody subscribes to would spend a field per event in every object. Windows Forms controls therefore keep subscribers in a single EventHandlerList. In metadata an event is an .event record linking the name to the add_ and remove_ methods.

cards.q: Which line inside the Panel class does not compile?
cards.explain: An event with explicit accessors has no field behind the name Resized. Even inside the class it can only appear on the left of += and -= (error CS0079). You invoke the delegate you store yourself — _resized.

cards.q: Match
pairs: The object to call the method on
A new delegate with an invocation list
The chain's delegates one by one

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: += on a delegate creates a new object; the old one does not change
If the second method in a chain throws, the third still runs
A delegate class derives from MulticastDelegate and is sealed
In .NET 8 BeginInvoke runs the delegate on the thread pool
An event with explicit add and remove cannot be invoked by name
cards.explain: An exception breaks the chain: the remaining methods are not called. On .NET Core and later BeginInvoke throws PlatformNotSupportedException — use Task.Run instead.

lessons.title: Final: delegates and closures

cards.task: Get the output 0 1 2 any way you like.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: The lambda reads the variable at the moment it is called.

cards.q: Where is the memory leak?
cards.explain: Subscribing to a static event without unsubscribing keeps the window in memory forever.

cards.q: Match them up
What does a lambda that captures a local variable create? Select all.
options: A hidden object for the variable
A copy of the variable on the stack
cards.explain: The variable moves into an object on the heap, and the lambda becomes a delegate.

cards.q: What does a multicast Func<int> made of two methods return?
options: The result of the last one
cards.explain: To get them all, loop over GetInvocationList().

cards.q: Unsubscribe when the window closes
cards.code: App.ThemeChanged ___ OnThemeChanged;
cards.explain: Once you unsubscribe, the event stops holding on to the window.

cards.q: Why does for have the closure trap while foreach does not?
options: Since C# 5 the foreach variable is fresh on each iteration, while for has one for the whole loop
cards.explain: The C# 5 change was technically breaking, but everyone saw it as a fix.

units.title: Strings, enums, arrays
units.blurb: A string in memory and the literal pool, ordinal versus culture and the Turkish i, Concat, StringBuilder, the interpolation handler, string.Create and u8 literals; enums as a struct over an integer, baked-in values and [Flags]; the cost of array covariance, jagged versus multidimensional, InlineArray, boxing int?.

lessons.title: Strings inside and comparison
lessons.sub: Heap layout, the literal pool, ordinal versus culture and the Turkish i

cards.title: What sits on the heap
cards.body:
You already know strings are immutable. Now let us look at how one is built. A string object is a header, a type pointer, a length field (int) and, right after it, the characters in UTF-16, 2 bytes per char. The CLR puts a null character at the end, so the string can be handed to native code without copying.

The length lives in the object and so do the characters — apart from arrays, it is the only variable-size type. That is why a string cannot "grow in place": any operation that changes the text allocates a new object and copies characters.

Immutability pays off later: a string can be shared between threads without locks, used as a dictionary key, and identical text can be stored once.
cards.deep:
In the runtime sources this is the String class with fields _stringLength and _firstChar: the address of the first character is just the address of that field. That is how fixed (char* p = s) and MemoryMarshal.GetReference(s.AsSpan()) work.

Starting with .NET 8, string literals are usually allocated in a separate heap the collector does not walk (the NonGC heap). Such an object never moves, so the JIT embeds its address straight into machine code instead of loading it through a table.

cards.q: How many bytes does the string "abc" take on the heap in a 64-bit process?
cards.explain: 16 bytes of bookkeeping, 4 bytes of length, 3 × 2 bytes of characters and 2 bytes of the null character — 28. Objects are aligned to 8 bytes, which gives 32.

wrong.1: 6 bytes is just the characters. A string is an object with a header, a type pointer and a length.
wrong.3: 28 is the sum of the fields, but on x64 the object size is rounded up to a multiple of 8.

cards.title: Interning: what goes into the pool
cards.body:
The IL instruction ldstr loads a literal. The CLR guarantees that identical literals across the whole process are one object, even when they live in different assemblies. For that the runtime keeps an intern pool — a hash table from text to string.

The compiler folds constants itself: "hel" + "lo" becomes a single literal "hello" at build time (constant folding).

Strings built at run time do not go into the pool. You can put them there with string.Intern(s): it returns the pooled string, adding it if it is not there yet.
cards.code:
string a = "hello";
string b = "hel" + "lo";           // one literal
string c = "hel" + Console.ReadLine(); // a heap string
string d = string.Intern(c);       // from the pool
cards.deep:
The cost of Intern: a hash over the whole text and a lookup in a shared runtime table. Pooled strings live until the process ends — the collector never frees them. Interning arbitrary input (names from requests, lines from a file) is a way to build a memory leak.

If you need to deduplicate repeated strings, say while parsing a large CSV, use your own dictionary or HashSet<string> that you can drop later. string.IsInterned(s) checks whether the text is pooled without adding it.

cards.q: The user typed "lo". Which expressions return true? Select all.
cards.explain: b is the same literal after constant folding. c is built at run time — a new object. Intern found the literal "hello" in the pool and returned it, so d is a, not c.

cards.title: Two ways to compare strings
cards.body:
Ordinal comparison goes by UTF-16 code units, one character at a time. It is fast and predictable: the result does not depend on the machine.

Linguistic (culture-sensitive) comparison applies language rules: "ß" and "ss" may compare equal, accented letters sort next to plain ones, invisible characters are ignored. The rules come from the ICU library (on Linux, macOS and recent Windows) or from NLS (on older Windows).

The catch is in the defaults:

  • ==, Equals, Contains, Replace, IndexOf(char) — ordinal;
  • CompareTo, string.Compare, StartsWith(string), EndsWith(string), IndexOf(string), ToUpper(), ToLower() — by the thread's current culture.
cards.deep: Sorting is linguistic too: List<string>.Sort() and OrderBy(s => s) go through Comparer<string>.Default, that is, through CompareTo. The analyzers CA1307 and CA1310 flag calls where the comparison mode is not explicit, and CA1309 suggests ordinal.

cards.q: Match the StringComparison value with what it does
pairs: Compares UTF-16 code units one to one
Code units, case folded without language rules
Language rules of the current thread
Language rules that are the same on every machine
Thread language, case does not matter

cards.title: The Turkish i
cards.body:
Turkish has two letters i: dotted (i → İ) and dotless (ı → I). So in the tr-TR culture "i".ToUpper() gives "İ" (U+0130), not the Latin "I".

Code that compares commands, keys or header names through ToUpper() breaks on a Turkish machine. There is no error — the comparison just quietly returns false.

The rule: compare identifiers (keys, protocols, paths, config names) ordinally — StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase or ToUpperInvariant(). Compare text for humans (sorting names in the UI) by culture.
cards.code:
CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = new CultureInfo("tr-TR");

"file".ToUpper();           // "FİLE"
"file".ToUpperInvariant();  // "FILE"
"file".Equals("FILE",
    StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase); // true

cards.q: The server runs with the tr-TR culture. A client sends the command "quit". What happens?
cards.code:
if (cmd.ToUpper() == "QUIT")
    Stop();
options: Stop is not called: ToUpper returns "QUİT"
Stop is called: ToUpper always uses Latin letters
cards.explain: ToUpper() with no arguments uses the current culture, and i turns into İ. Then == honestly compares code units — and they differ. The reliable way: cmd.Equals("quit", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase).

wrong.1: == on strings is ordinal and case-sensitive.

cards.title: ICU surprises since .NET 5
cards.body:
Before .NET 5, linguistic comparison on Windows went through NLS — the Windows library. Since .NET 5, ICU is used wherever it is available. Its Unicode rules are stricter, and old code started behaving differently.

The best-known example is .NET 5: for ICU the pair was one indivisible text element, and a culture-sensitive " ".IndexOf(" ") returned -1. .NET 6 fixed that behavior, but the lesson stays: the result of a linguistic search depends on the runtime and library version.

What still holds: linguistic comparison skips zero-width characters and \0, so s.IndexOf("\0") returns 0 for any string. Meanwhile IndexOf('\0') with a char is ordinal and honestly returns -1.
cards.deep: If the app does not need language rules, build it with <InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>: ICU is not loaded, and linguistic operations become ordinal. By default no culture other than the invariant one can be created in this mode: since .NET 8 new CultureInfo("de-DE") throws CultureNotFoundException. This is the usual choice for containers and Native AOT — smaller size and no libicu dependency. You can bring NLS back on Windows with the System.Globalization.UseNls setting, but that is a migration aid, not a path for new code.

cards.q: .NET 9 on Linux (ICU), culture en-US. The string has no \0 character. Which line still returns 0?
cards.explain: IndexOf(string) without a StringComparison is linguistic, and ICU skips \0: nothing is left of the pattern, so it is "found" at the very start. IndexOf(char), Contains and explicit Ordinal compare code units: they give -1 and false.

cards.title: Dictionaries, hashes and sorting
cards.body:
Dictionary keys are compared through an IEqualityComparer<string>. By default that is ordinal and case-sensitive. Need another mode — pass a comparer to the constructor: StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase. That is faster than upper-casing every key: no new strings are created.

To sort a list of names for the UI use StringComparer.CurrentCulture; for a stable order in a file or protocol use StringComparer.Ordinal.
cards.deep: string.GetHashCode() in .NET Core and .NET 5+ is randomized: the same string gets a different hash in different runs of the process (the Marvin algorithm with a random seed). This protects hash tables from collision-flooding attacks. In .NET Framework the default hash was stable, and old code sometimes saved it to a file or a database — after migration such code breaks. Never store a string hash outside the process.

cards.q: Make the header dictionary case-insensitive and the key culture-independent
cards.explain: StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase compares without case and without language rules. ToUpperInvariant changes case the same way on every machine — the Turkish i will not get in the way.

lessons.title: Building strings cheaply
lessons.sub: Concat, StringBuilder inside, the interpolation handler, string.Create and UTF-8 literals

cards.title: What the compiler does with plus
cards.body:
The compiler does not turn a + b + c into two additions. It gathers all operands into one call to string.Concat(a, b, c). Concat first sums the lengths, allocates the result once and copies the pieces into it. No intermediate a + b string ever appears.

Concat has overloads for 2, 3 and 4 strings. With more operands the compiler passes them as an array — one more allocation, but still a single result string.

So joining a fixed number of parts in one expression is already optimal. The problem is only a loop: there every += is a separate call and a separate string.
cards.deep: If an operand is not a string, for example "id=" + n with int n, older compilers picked Concat(object, object) and boxed the number. Modern Roslyn calls n.ToString() for value types and uses the string overload: no boxing, but a temporary string for the number remains. The interpolation from the next cards avoids even that.

cards.q: first and last are strings. How many new strings does this line create?
cards.code: string s = first + " " + last + "!";
cards.explain: One Concat call with four arguments: the lengths are known up front, so the result is allocated once. The literals " " and "!" already live in the pool.

wrong.1: That would happen if each + ran separately. The compiler folds the chain into one Concat.

cards.title: StringBuilder inside
cards.body:
StringBuilder keeps text in mutable pieces — chunks, which are char[] arrays. The default initial capacity is 16 characters. When it runs out of room, it does not copy the old text into a bigger array; it adds a new chunk and links it to the previous one. So a long build never rewrites what it has already collected.

ToString() allocates the result string and copies all chunks into it.

The cost: the StringBuilder object, its chunks and the final copy. For two or three parts that is more than one Concat. A builder pays off when there are many parts or their number is unknown in advance — loops, conditions, recursive walks.
cards.deep: In .NET Framework 4.0 StringBuilder was reworked from "a string you append to" into a linked list of chunks; a new chunk is at most 8000 characters, so the arrays stay out of the large object heap. The chain is stored from the last chunk back to the first, so sb[i] near the start of a long builder walks the list backwards — its indexer is not O(1). If you need to read and change text by index many times, work with a char[] or a Span<char>.

cards.q: Where is StringBuilder really needed? Select all.
options: Building a report line by line in a loop over a collection of unknown length
Joining a list with commas when string.Join is available
cards.explain: A fixed concatenation is one Concat. string.Join computes the length itself and allocates the string once. A builder is needed where there are many parts and they show up as the work goes on.

cards.title: Interpolation: a handler instead of Format
cards.body:
Before C# 10, $"Order {id}: {total}" became string.Format: arguments went into an object[], numbers were boxed, and the format string was parsed on every call.

Since C# 10 and .NET 6 the compiler expands interpolation into calls on a handler, DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler. It is a ref struct on the stack. It rents a buffer from ArrayPool<char>, writes literals and values into it, creates one string at the end and returns the buffer to the pool.

AppendFormatted<T> is generic, so an int is not boxed. If the type implements ISpanFormattable (numbers, dates, Guid), it formats itself straight into the buffer, with no temporary string.
cards.deep:
The first two constructor arguments are the total length of the literals (here 6 + 2 = 8) and the number of holes; the handler uses them to size its initial buffer. If every hole is a string, the compiler just uses string.Concat.

Other methods accept the same mechanism: StringBuilder.Append($"...") writes straight into the builder through its own handler, and Debug.Assert(cond, $"...") does not format the message at all when the condition is true. A custom handler is marked with the [InterpolatedStringHandler] attribute.

cards.q: Put in order the calls the compiler generates for $"Hi {name}, you are {age}" (age is an int)
cards.explain: First the handler with the literal length (3 + 10 = 13) and the number of holes, then literals and values left to right, and finally one result string. The buffer goes back to ArrayPool.

cards.title: string.Create: write straight into a new string
cards.body:
A string is immutable for everyone who can see it. Until anyone has seen it, writing is fine. That is the idea behind string.Create(length, state, action): the runtime allocates a string of the right length and hands you a Span<char> over its characters. You fill it in, and the string goes out already finished.

No intermediate buffers or copies: one allocation. Pass data through state and make the lambda static so no closure is created.

There is a second form — string.Create(IFormatProvider, $"..."): interpolation with a given culture and no extra strings.
cards.deep: For hexadecimal in particular there is already Convert.ToHexString (.NET 5) and ToHexStringLower (.NET 9); inside they work the same way. Another option for short strings is to build the text in a stackalloc char[] and call new string(span): also one allocation, but with a copy from the stack.

cards.q: Mask a card number, keeping the last four digits, with one allocation
cards.explain: string.Create allocates the string and gives a Span over its characters. CopyTo moves the number in, Fill paints over everything except the last four. What comes out is an already finished string.

cards.title: UTF-8 literals
cards.body:
.NET strings are UTF-16, while the network, HTTP, JSON and files are almost always UTF-8. You used to get the bytes like this: Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("...") — a new array per call — or by keeping a static readonly byte[].

Since C# 11 there is the u8 suffix. The compiler encodes the literal as UTF-8 at build time and puts the bytes into the assembly's data section. The expression "HTTP/1.1"u8 has type ReadOnlySpan<byte> and points straight at those bytes: no allocation at all.

Limits: it is not a constant (not allowed in const or as a parameter default), there is no interpolation, and .ToArray() creates a heap array. Two u8 literals can be joined with + — that is done at build time too.

cards.q: What is the type of the expression "ok"u8?
cards.explain: A read-only span over bytes in the assembly data. A byte[] would have to be allocated on the heap, and a Span<byte> would let you corrupt shared data.

wrong.3: A Span<byte> would let you write into the literal bytes shared by the whole program. That is why it is read-only.

cards.title: Interpolation remembers the culture
cards.body:
The interpolation handler formats values using the current culture, just like ToString(). On a German machine $"{1.5}" gives "1,5", and a date comes out in the local format. For text on screen that is right. For JSON, logs, SQL and file names it is a bug that shows up only for some users.

For machine text set the culture explicitly:

  • value.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
  • string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, $"...") — interpolation with a culture and no extra allocations;
  • there is also the older FormattableString.Invariant($"..."), but it creates a FormattableString object and boxes the arguments.
cards.deep: The analyzer CA1305 flags formatting calls without an IFormatProvider. In projects where all text is machine text, the simplest fix is to turn on InvariantGlobalization — then the current culture is always invariant, and by default no other culture can be created.

cards.q: The program runs with the de-DE culture. Which line gives "1,5" instead of "1.5"?
cards.explain: Interpolation without a provider uses the current culture, and German separates the fraction with a comma. The lines with InvariantCulture give a dot on any machine.

lessons.title: Enums and flags
lessons.sub: A struct over an integer, baked-in values, undefined values, [Flags] and HasFlag

cards.title: To the CLR an enum is a struct over an integer
cards.body:
An enumeration (enum) is a value type derived from System.Enum. It has exactly one instance field — value__ of the underlying integer type (int by default). The member names are constants: static literal fields holding a number.

So a Color variable takes as much space as its underlying type, and in machine code it is just a number. You can pick the underlying type: byte, short, long and their unsigned pairs.
cards.deep:
Since it is a plain integer inside, a boxed enum unboxes into its underlying type and back: (int)(object)DayOfWeek.Monday works — we saw this in the unit "How a type is built". Methods like ToString are declared in System.Enum, which is a reference type, so calling them on an enum value usually requires boxing.

The constraint where T : struct, Enum is available since C# 7.3; the generic APIs are built on it: Enum.Parse<T>, Enum.GetValues<T>() (.NET 5).

cards.q: enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }. What does Color c = (Color)42; do?
options: Compiles and runs: c holds the number 42
Runs, and c ends up as Blue
cards.explain: Casting an integer to an enum just changes the type of the number. The CLR does not check whether such a member exists. c.ToString() returns "42".

wrong.1: There is no check on the cast: an enum is the same integer.
wrong.3: The value is not clamped to the nearest member; it stays 42.

cards.title: Values are baked into the calling code
cards.body:
An enum member is a constant. When the app writes Status.Blocked, the compiler puts a number into its IL, not a reference to the field. After the build the app does not know the name, only 1.

The "version 2" scenario: the library inserted a new member at the start, and all implicit numbers shifted. An app built against the old version keeps comparing with the old numbers — which now mean something else. No load error, just a silently wrong result.

Rules for public enums: set values explicitly, add new members at the end, never renumber or remove old ones.

cards.q: The library was updated to v2 from the card above, and the app was not rebuilt. What does its check if (user.Status == Status.Blocked) do?
options: Compares with 1 and treats active users as blocked
Compares with Blocked by name and works correctly
cards.explain: The app's IL holds the number 1 — the value of Blocked at build time. In v2 one means Active. Nobody looks the field up by name, so there is no exception either.

wrong.2: MissingFieldException can happen when code accesses a field. The compiler has already substituted the constant as a number.

cards.title: Undefined values
cards.body:
An enum variable can hold any number: from a cast, a database, JSON, or default. Details that matter:

  • default(Color) and uninitialized fields are always 0, even if there is no member with value 0. That is why the first member is usually None or Unknown = 0.
  • Enum.TryParse<Color>("42", out c) returns true: a numeric string parses into the number whether or not such a member exists.
  • Enum.IsDefined(c) checks whether there is a member with exactly that value.
  • A switch statement without default simply skips an unknown value. A switch expression that lists every name produces warning CS8524 and throws SwitchExpressionException on an unknown value.
cards.deep:
Why the compiler wants a _ arm even though every name is listed: to it, Light is the whole int range, and the names are just a few points in it. The separate warning CS8524 (rather than the usual CS8509) is specifically about unnamed values — so you can suppress it if the input is definitely validated.

Enum.IsDefined in .NET 5+ has a generic form IsDefined<T>(T) without boxing; the runtime caches member values, but it is still a lookup, not a single comparison. On a hot path the range check is written by hand: (uint)l <= (uint)Light.Green, if the values are contiguous.

cards.q: enum Color { Red = 1, Green = 2 }. What is true? Select all.
options: Enum.TryParse<Color>("42", out var c) returns true
default(Color) is 0 even though there is no such member
A switch expression with arms for Red and Green and no _ gives a warning
cards.explain: Casting to an enum checks nothing — that is exactly why IsDefined and the _ arm exist. TryParse accepts any numeric string that fits the underlying type.

cards.title: Flags and what [Flags] does
cards.body:
A flags enum is one where every member is a separate bit: values 1, 2, 4, 8… Combinations are built with |, tested with &, cleared with & ~.

The [Flags] attribute does not assign powers of two — you write them yourself; otherwise for None, Read, Write, Exec implicit numbering gives 0, 1, 2, 3, and Read | Write collides with Exec. The attribute changes only the text form: ToString prints the combination by names, and Enum.Parse understands "Read, Write".
cards.deep: If a number cannot be fully decomposed into defined flags, ToString prints it as digits: for (Perm)9 — "9". Handy combinations can be declared as members: ReadWrite = Read | Write; ToString will prefer that name. Up to 64 flags fit into long/ulong; beyond that you need a BitArray or your own struct.

cards.q: The [Flags] attribute was removed from Perm, the values stayed. What does Console.WriteLine(Perm.Read | Perm.Write) print?
cards.explain: Without [Flags], ToString looks for a member with exactly the value 3, finds none and prints the number. The bitwise operations themselves work the same with or without the attribute.

cards.title: HasFlag: then and now
cards.body:
The signature is bool HasFlag(Enum flag). The parameter type is System.Enum, a reference type, so the argument is boxed. The method itself is declared in System.Enum, so the value it is called on is boxed too. Inside there is also a check that the types match, otherwise ArgumentException.

In .NET Framework each call cost two allocations, and hot code replaced it with (p & f) == f. Since .NET Core 2.1 the JIT recognizes HasFlag as an intrinsic and emits the same bitwise comparison — no boxing.

The logical trap remains: p.HasFlag(Perm.None) is always true — every number "contains" zero bits.
cards.deep: The optimization kicks in when the JIT sees both types exactly. In code where the value already sits in an Enum or object, the boxing has already happened earlier, and there is no miracle. One more subtlety: Enum.IsDefined returns false for a flag combination unless that combination is declared as its own member — you cannot validate flags with IsDefined.

cards.q: Which of the variables b–e gets true?
cards.explain: HasFlag(None) checks (p & 0) == 0 — always true. p has neither Write nor Exec, and the value 3 is not declared as a member, so IsDefined returns false.

cards.title: Cost: where an enum costs money
cards.body:
Comparisons, switch, bitwise operations — free: it is integer work. The JIT often turns a switch over dense values into a jump table.

You pay where a name or reflection is involved:

  • ToString() and interpolation — a name lookup by value (the runtime caches the names and returns the ready string for a declared member, but the call through System.Enum usually costs a boxing, and for flag combinations and unknown values a new string is built);
  • Enum.Parse, GetNames, GetValues — string parsing and new arrays on every call;
  • non-generic APIs (Enum.IsDefined(typeof(T), value), HasFlag before .NET Core 2.1) — boxing.

If names are needed on a hot path (logs, JSON), people write their own switch with string literals or a cached array of names.
cards.deep: Serializers solve it the same way: System.Text.Json with JsonStringEnumConverter caches the names, and its source generator emits code without reflection. For Native AOT the generic Enum.GetValues<T>() is preferable to the Type-based versions: the non-generic GetValues(Type) creates an array of a type the AOT compiler may not have prepared, and it is annotated with a warning.

cards.q: Complete a generic check that a value is a declared enum member
cards.code:
static bool IsKnown<T>(T value) where T : struct, ___
    => Enum.___(value);
cards.explain: The struct, Enum constraint (C# 7.3) admits only enums. Enum.IsDefined<T>(T) from .NET 5 works without boxing and without typeof.

lessons.title: Arrays and Nullable<T>
lessons.sub: The cost of covariance, jagged versus multidimensional, InlineArray, collection expressions and boxing int?

cards.title: Array covariance costs a check
cards.body:
You saw the trap object[] arr = new string[2]; arr[0] = 42; in the unit "Generics". Now let us see what it costs. Since an object[] may hide a string[], the CLR has to check every reference store into an array of a reference type. The IL instruction stelem.ref calls a runtime helper: it compares the value's type with the element type of the actual array and throws ArrayTypeMismatchException on a mismatch.

The JIT drops the check when it can prove it is not needed: the value is null, the element type is sealed (string[] has no derived element types), or the exact array type is known. Otherwise it is an extra call on every assignment.
cards.deep: Arrays of value types are not covariant in C#: object[] o = new int[3] does not compile. But the CLR treats integer arrays of the same size as compatible: (uint[])(object)new int[1] succeeds at run time, as does an enum array to an array of its underlying type. In hot loops the store check is avoided with a wrapper struct (struct Ref { public Animal Value; } and a Ref[] array) — a value type has no covariance, so there is nothing to check.

cards.q: What happens on the second line?
options: ArrayTypeMismatchException when the Span is created
Nothing: the exception comes on the third line
The Span copies the elements into a new object[]
cards.explain: Span<T> does not check every store — for speed. So it checks once, in the constructor: if an array of a reference type is not actually a T[], it throws ArrayTypeMismatchException right away.

wrong.1: A store through a Span is a plain memory write without stelem.ref. To keep it safe, the check was moved to the moment the Span is created.

cards.title: Jagged and multidimensional
cards.body:
A jagged array int[][] is an array of references to separate arrays. Each row is its own heap object with its own length. 1000 rows means 1001 allocations, and a[i][j] means two pointer hops and two bounds checks.

A multidimensional int[,] is one object with the data laid out as a rectangle. But for the CLR it is built differently from int[]. A single-dimension zero-based array (an SZ array) has its own IL instructions: newarr, ldelem, stelem. A multidimensional one does not: creation is newobj, access is calls to Get/Set/Address methods the runtime provides for the array type.

Historically that made int[,] slower than jagged. Since .NET 7 the JIT expands these calls into direct access, and the gap has shrunk a lot. But multidimensional arrays still get fewer of the SZ-array optimizations (bounds-check removal in loops, vectorization, Span).
cards.code:
int[][] jag = new int[3][];   // three nulls, rows come later
jag[0] = new int[5];

int[,] grid = new int[3, 5];  // one object for 15 elements
grid[1, 2] = 7;               // IL: call int32[,]::Set(...)
cards.deep: A common fast option is a one-dimensional array with a manual index: data[row * width + col]. One object, contiguous data, every SZ-array optimization and a Span over the whole table. The CLR also has single-dimension arrays with a non-zero lower bound (via Array.CreateInstance); their type is written int[*], and such an array cannot be cast to int[].

cards.q: Match the declaration with how it is built
pairs: Single dimension from zero: its own newarr and ldelem
One object, accessed through Get and Set methods
An array of references to separate rows
Eight elements right inside the struct
A view over assembly data, no allocation

cards.title: InlineArray (C# 12, .NET 8)
cards.body:
Sometimes you need a fixed-size buffer inside a struct — without a separate heap array. Before, the only tool was fixed int buf[8]: it needs unsafe, works only with primitives and does not check bounds.

The [InlineArray(N)] attribute tells the runtime: repeat the struct's single field N times in a row. Since C# 12 the language lets you index such a struct, iterate it with foreach and convert it to a Span<T>. The code is safe, the element type can be anything including references, and bounds are checked.
cards.deep: The struct size is N × the field size, so a large InlineArray in a local variable eats stack. The C# compiler uses the feature itself: for params Span<T> (C# 13) and collection expressions targeting Span it may generate a hidden inline struct on the stack instead of an array. Inside the runtime, InlineArray has replaced many places that used to have fixed buffers or hand-written fields _e0, _e1…

cards.q: Why is [InlineArray(8)] better than fixed int buf[8]?
options: No unsafe needed, elements can be of any type, bounds are checked
It lives on the heap and takes no stack
It is faster because it skips bounds checks
It can be resized at run time
cards.explain: Both live inside the struct. But a fixed buffer is an unchecked pointer and only for primitives, while an InlineArray is an ordinary safe type that converts to a Span.

wrong.3: The size is set in the attribute and fixed: it is part of the struct layout.

cards.title: Collection expressions: what the compiler generates
cards.body:
You saw the [1, 2, 3] syntax (C# 12) in the unit "Modern C#". What is more interesting is underneath: the compiler picks the code by the target type.

  • int[] a = [1, 2, 3] — a new array, like new[] { … };
  • int[] e = [] — Array.Empty<int>(), a shared empty array with no new allocation;
  • ReadOnlySpan<int> s = [1, 2, 3] from constants — a view over assembly data, zero allocations;
  • List<int> l = [1, 2, 3] — a list with the right capacity up front;
  • IEnumerable<int> x = [1, 2] — the compiler chooses the type, often a hidden read-only class.

.. (spread) inserts the elements of another collection; if the lengths are known, the compiler computes the final size in advance.
cards.deep: Your own type plugs into collection expressions through the [CollectionBuilder] attribute — that is how ImmutableArray<T> and other immutable collections work. For interfaces the compiler does not promise a concrete type: do not rely on IEnumerable<int> x = [..] being an array or a list, and do not cast it back.

cards.q: Which lines do not allocate a new heap object? Select all.
cards.explain: The empty array is the shared Array.Empty<int>(). A ReadOnlySpan of constants points at assembly data. The List and the non-empty array are new heap objects.

cards.title: Nullable<T> is an ordinary struct
cards.body:
int? is Nullable<int>: a struct with two fields, bool hasValue and T value. No reference and no heap: an int? takes 8 bytes (1 byte of flag, padding and 4 bytes of number), a long? takes 16.

The where T : struct constraint excludes Nullable itself, so there is no int??.

Operators are "lifted": if any operand is null, arithmetic gives null, and the comparisons <, >, <=, >= give false. The compiler turns x == null into !x.HasValue.
cards.code:
int? a = null;
int? sum = a + 1;        // null
bool gt = a > 0;         // false
bool le = a <= 0;        // false too!
int v = a.GetValueOrDefault(); // 0, no check
int w = a.Value;         // InvalidOperationException
cards.deep: GetValueOrDefault() just reads the value field, while .Value checks the flag first. bool? with the & and | operators follows three-valued logic: null & false is false, null | true is true, and null & true is null. In an int?[] array every element is 8 bytes versus 4 in int[]: the flag doubles the size.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.code:
int? a = null;
Console.WriteLine(a > 0 || a <= 0);
cards.explain: With null every ordering comparison is false, so "greater than zero or not greater" is false too. The familiar "one of the two" law does not hold for Nullable.

cards.title: How int? is boxed
cards.body:
For Nullable<T> the CLR makes an exception in the box instruction:

  • if there is no value, the result is null, not a box;
  • if there is one, T itself is boxed. A box holding a Nullable<int> does not exist — there is only a box holding an int.

Consequences: object o = (int?)null is truly null. A box with an int can be unboxed into both int and int?. And x.GetType() on an int? is called through boxing and returns System.Int32 — or throws NullReferenceException when there is no value.
cards.deep: This rule arrived shortly before .NET 2.0 shipped: in the beta versions a boxed empty int? was a non-null object, and o == null gave false. The runtime was changed, not just C#, so that null stays null in every language. Interfaces also go through boxing T: IComparable c = (int?)5 is a box with an int. To find out that a type is Nullable, use Nullable.GetUnderlyingType(typeof(int?)): the object itself loses that information.

cards.q: Which line throws an exception?
cards.explain: GetType is a non-virtual method of object, and calling it boxes b. An empty int? boxes to null — hence NullReferenceException. oa.GetType() prints System.Int32, and ob == null prints True.
