lessons.sub: String comparison, allocation-free building, flags, covariance and int?

cards.q: Which calls compare using the current culture by default? Select all.
cards.explain: == and Contains are ordinal. StartsWith(string), Compare and sorting through Comparer<string>.Default use the thread culture, and with ICU or tr-TR the result can surprise you.

cards.q: A cache key is built as url.ToLower(). On servers with the tr-TR culture some requests miss the cache. Which fix is right?
options: url.ToLowerInvariant() or a dictionary with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase
Compare keys with string.Compare(a, b, true)
cards.explain: In tr-TR "I" turns into the dotless "ı", and the keys drift apart. Identifiers are compared without language rules. Intern does not change the text, ToUpper breaks on the same letter, and Compare with ignoreCase still depends on the culture.

wrong.3: The Compare(a, b, ignoreCase) overload still uses the current culture.

cards.q: id is an int, name is a string. What does C# 12 turn $"{id}: {name}" into?
options: DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler: AppendFormatted(id) without boxing, one result string
string.Format with an object[] and boxing of id
A StringBuilder with three Append calls
string.Concat(id, ": ", name) with boxing of id
cards.explain: Since C# 10 and .NET 6 interpolation goes through a ref struct handler with a buffer from ArrayPool. AppendFormatted<T> is generic, so the int is written straight into the buffer. string.Format was the pre-C# 10 way.

cards.q: Match the construct with what is behind it
pairs: A type check on every store

cards.q: enum Light { Red, Yellow, Green }. A method is a switch expression with arms for the three names and no _. What happens on Act((Light)7)?
options: SwitchExpressionException; the compiler warned with CS8524 in advance
It does not compile: (Light)7 is out of range
The Green arm runs as the last one
cards.explain: An enum is the whole int range; the names are just points in it. The compiler warns about unnamed values, and the generated code throws SwitchExpressionException when no arm matches.

cards.q: A default value without an exception, and parsing with a check that the member is declared
cards.explain: .Value throws InvalidOperationException when there is no value. TryParse also accepts "42", so the IsDefined after it is not redundant.

cards.q: What is true about arrays? Select all.
options: Rows of a jagged array can have different lengths
int[,] is a single heap object
int[] a = []; does not create a new array
cards.explain: Only arrays of reference types are covariant. InlineArray is the safe alternative to a fixed buffer. An empty collection expression for an array is the shared Array.Empty<int>().

cards.q: Which line throws at run time?
cards.explain: Storing a string and null into a string[] is legal. A ReadOnlySpan does not allow writes, so covariance does not hurt it. A Span<object> could write a non-string there — its constructor sees that the array is really a string[] and throws ArrayTypeMismatchException.

cards.q: Public library: enum Level { Low, High }. In v2 they want to add Medium, which logically sits between them. How do you avoid breaking consumers that are already built?
options: Keep Low = 0, High = 1 and add Medium = 2 at the end
Insert Medium in the middle: the names did not change
Turn Level into a class with static fields
cards.explain: Consumers keep numbers in their IL, not names. Inserting in the middle moves High from 1 to 2, and old code starts mixing up levels. New members go only at the end, with explicit values.

units.title: Exceptions and reliability
units.blurb: What finally guarantees and when it does not run, when filters and two-pass handling, throw vs throw ex and ExceptionDispatchInfo, a type broken for good, what crashes the process, the cost of an exception, TryXxx and your own exceptions.

lessons.title: finally and when filters
lessons.sub: What finally promises, two-pass handling and logging without catching

cards.title: What finally promises
cards.body:
A finally block runs no matter how control leaves the try:

  • the code ran to the end;
  • a return, break, continue or goto jumped out;
  • an exception flew out and a catch caught it — right here or several frames up.

using, lock and foreach rely on this: the compiler lowers them into try/finally so that Dispose or Monitor.Exit is called in every case.

cards.q: What does F() return?
cards.explain: return x first copies the value into a temporary, then finally runs, then the method returns the saved copy. Changing x in finally does not touch it. If x were a reference to a list, changes inside the object would be visible — the reference is copied, not the object.

wrong.2: You may change variables in finally. What is forbidden is leaving it: return inside finally is error CS0157.

cards.title: When finally does not run
cards.body:
The finally promise holds only while the process is alive and the stack unwinds normally. It does not run if:

  • the stack overflowed — StackOverflowException ends the process at once (as in the "Memory in .NET" course);
  • Environment.FailFast was called — the process ends immediately, with no finally blocks and no finalizers, writing an entry to the Windows event log;
  • Environment.Exit was called inside try — that thread's finally does not run, though process-exit handlers do;
  • the process was killed from outside: kill -9, "End task", a power cut.

For an unhandled exception the documentation does not promise finally: it depends on how the runtime tears the process down.
cards.deep:
On .NET 9 on Linux, with an unhandled exception in Main, the order is: first the AppDomain.UnhandledException event and the "Unhandled exception" message, and only then finally. The runtime learned there was no handler before unwinding the stack — that is the two-pass scheme, coming up in a couple of screens. Do not rely on that finally: on another OS, version or under a debugger the behaviour may differ.

The takeaway for reliable code: finally is for releasing resources inside a living process. Data that must survive a crash is saved ahead of time (a transaction, a write to disk with fsync), not "at the last moment".

cards.q: In which cases will this try's finally NOT run? Select all.
options: Infinite recursion in the try overflows the stack
The exception from the try is caught three frames up
cards.explain: return and an exception caught higher up are normal exits, so finally runs. FailFast, a stack overflow and SIGKILL end the process without unwinding the stack.

cards.title: An exception from finally wipes out the original
cards.body:
If finally runs because of an exception and throws a new one itself, the original is lost: only the new one travels up the stack. The log shows a cleanup error instead of the real cause.

So code in finally is written not to throw: check for null, and Dispose should not throw per .NET guidelines. The compiler will not let you leave finally with return, break or goto — error CS0157.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: The exception from finally replaced the one in flight. The InvalidOperationException ends up neither in InnerException nor anywhere else — it simply vanished.

wrong.2: AggregateException collects errors from tasks and Parallel. A plain try/finally combines nothing.

cards.title: Two passes: search first, then unwind
cards.body:
The CLR handles an exception in two passes:

First pass — search. The runtime walks up the stack from the throw point looking for a matching catch. when filters are evaluated here. The stack is untouched: every frame, its locals and the throw point are still in place.

Second pass — unwind. Having found a handler, the runtime goes again from the throw point, running every finally along the way and popping frames. Only then does it enter the catch body.

If the first pass finds nobody, the exception is unhandled, and the process learns about it while the stack is still intact. That is why a crash dump shows the exact spot.
cards.deep: The scheme comes from Windows SEH; on Linux and macOS CoreCLR reproduces it on its own. In .NET 9 exception handling in CoreCLR was rewritten in managed code (the implementation came from NativeAOT) — the two passes stayed, and handling got noticeably faster.

cards.q: Log prints a string and returns true. What does the program print?
cards.explain: The outer catch filter is evaluated in the first pass, while the inner finally has not run yet. Then the second pass unwinds the stack — finally — and only then the catch body.

wrong.1: That would happen if the stack were unwound before checking the filter — as with catch and rethrow. The filter sees the stack intact.

cards.title: The when filter and logging without catching
cards.body:
The filter catch (X e) when (condition) arrived in C# 6. If the condition is false, this catch is skipped and the search continues — to the next catch or further up the stack. If the filter itself throws, that exception is swallowed and counts as false.

The key trick is logging through a filter: the method writes the log and returns false. The exception is not caught, the stack is not unwound, yet the entry is written. Compare with catch { Log(e); throw; }: there the stack has already unwound to this frame, and a dump or debugger no longer shows the locals at the throw point.
cards.deep:
In IL a filter is a separate filter block next to the catch; VB.NET had it from the start, C# caught up in version 6 (F# by default checks when after the catch, inside an ordinary catch block). A filter runs while frames below it are not yet unwound, so keep it short and free of side effects other than logging: inner finally blocks have not run, and a lock taken deeper is still held.

Even earlier than filters, the AppDomain.CurrentDomain.FirstChanceException event fires — on every throw, even a caught one. Good for diagnostics, not for logic.

cards.q: Retry on a transient error, and only log the other errors without catching them
cards.explain: The filter keyword is when. Log returns false, so the second catch never enters its body: the exception keeps travelling up the stack, but it has been logged while the stack was intact.

cards.title: Then and now: ThreadAbortException and CER
cards.body:
In .NET Framework an exception could arrive at any point: Thread.Abort injected a ThreadAbortException into another thread — even between creating an object and storing the reference. Once caught, it was automatically rethrown at the end of the catch until someone called Thread.ResetAbort. ASP.NET timeouts and Response.Redirect worked this way.

The defence was the CER (constrained execution region): RuntimeHelpers.PrepareConstrainedRegions and the ReliabilityContract attribute made the runtime compile the finally code ahead of time, so cleanup would not fail on low memory or an abort.

Modern .NET has none of this: Thread.Abort throws PlatformNotSupportedException (since .NET 5 also with warning SYSLIB0006), CERs are not supported (SYSLIB0004). Stopping a thread is cooperative only, through a CancellationToken.
cards.deep:
Dropping asynchronous exceptions made everything simpler: an exception only appears where code calls or checks something. Running out of memory has not gone away, but OS resources have SafeHandle: it closes the handle both in Dispose and in the finalizer if Dispose was forgotten, and it will not close the handle while another thread is using it. And when the process ends, the OS closes its handles itself.

Code unloading, for which Framework aborted a domain's threads, was replaced by collectible AssemblyLoadContexts, and unloading there is cooperative too: while a thread runs code from the context, it does not unload.

pairs: An exception inside a when filter
throw in finally during an exception

lessons.title: Rethrowing and broken types
lessons.sub: throw vs throw ex, ExceptionDispatchInfo and TypeInitializationException

cards.title: What is in StackTrace
cards.body:
An exception's stack trace is collected during unwinding: the runtime records into the exception object the frames it passes — from the throw point to the frame with the catch. Frames above the handler do not get in. For the full stack of the current thread use Environment.StackTrace.

The text is built lazily: until you read e.StackTrace or e.ToString(), the object holds only method addresses. The runtime resolves names and line numbers on read, and line numbers come from the PDB if it is next to the binary.

cards.title: throw; vs throw ex;
cards.body:
Inside a catch there are two ways to pass a caught exception on:

throw; — a rethrow. The same object flies on, and the collected stack is extended: the original throw point is kept.

throw ex; — a new throw of the same object. The runtime takes this line as the origin and starts the stack over. The method where the error really happened disappears from the log.

The .NET analyzer flags this as CA2200. The rule is simple: inside a catch, rethrow only with throw;.

cards.q: The error log has no Parse method in it, even though Parse is what failed. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: throw e throws the exception anew, and the stack starts at the line in Load. You need throw; — then Parse and everything below it stays in the stack.

cards.title: Wrap without losing the cause
cards.body:
Sometimes a low-level exception should become your own: the caller does not care about SqlException, it cares that "the order was not saved". So you throw a new exception and pass the old one to the constructor — it lands in InnerException.

e.ToString() prints the whole chain: the outer one, then ---> and the inner one with its own stack, then the line --- End of inner exception stack trace ---. Log through ToString() or hand the whole exception to the logger — e.Message shows only the top level.

cards.q: The repository layer caught a DbException and wants to report upward with its own error. What is right?
cards.explain: The original exception goes into InnerException whole: type, message, stack. Glued strings lose the type and half the details, and return null turns the error into a silent bug further down.

wrong.2: A stack written as a string into Message is invisible to the debugger and to error-tracking systems. And the original error type is lost too.

cards.title: ExceptionDispatchInfo: rethrow somewhere else
cards.body:
throw; works only inside a catch — outside it is error CS0156. But sometimes an exception is caught in one place and must be thrown later or on another thread: a worker thread saved an error, and the main thread must throw it.

That is what ExceptionDispatchInfo is for (namespace System.Runtime.ExceptionServices). Capture(e) remembers the exception and its stack, Throw() throws the same object, keeping the original stack. In the log the new frames are separated by the line --- End of stack trace from previous location ---.

This is exactly how await throws a failed task's exception: the stack shows both the place inside the task and the place of the await.
cards.deep:
There is also a short static form, ExceptionDispatchInfo.Throw(e). Both methods are marked [DoesNotReturn], so nullable analysis knows code does not continue after them. But C# reachability rules ignore this attribute: in a method with a return value you still need a return or throw after Throw().

.NET 5 added ExceptionDispatchInfo.SetCurrentStackTrace(e) — it writes the current stack into an exception that has never been thrown.

cards.q: Save the exception from the handler and throw it later with the original stack
cards.explain: Capture remembers the exception together with its stack; Throw throws the same object and appends the new frames to the stack after a separator.

cards.q: After which options will e.ToString() in the top-level handler still show the method where the error happened? Select all.
cards.explain: throw; and ExceptionDispatchInfo keep the original stack. A wrapper with ex in the constructor keeps it in InnerException, and ToString prints it. throw ex; starts the stack over, and a wrapper without ex loses the original exception entirely.

cards.title: TypeInitializationException: a type broken for good
cards.body:
A static constructor and static field initializers run once — before the first use of the type. If they throw, the CLR wraps the exception in a TypeInitializationException and puts the original in InnerException.

There is no second attempt. The runtime marks the type as failed to initialize, and any use of it — a static field, a method, new — throws TypeInitializationException again, for the rest of the process's life. Even members that have nothing to do with the error. Only a restart fixes it.
cards.deep:
In CoreCLR a repeated access throws the same object — the TypeInitializationException saved on the first failure, with the stack of that first failure. Handy for diagnostics: the cause is visible even if somebody swallowed the first exception.

Exactly when initialization runs depends on the beforefieldinit flag: without an explicit static constructor the runtime may do it before the first access (details in the "Type members and versioning" unit). So the exception may fly out somewhere you do not expect.

cards.q: The LIMIT variable is not set. A service reads Settings.Path on every request. What happens from the second request on?
options: TypeInitializationException again; initializers are not rerun
ArgumentNullException from int.Parse on every access
Path works: Root was initialized after all
Limit is 0 and everything else works
cards.explain: The initializers of all static fields are part of one static constructor. It failed, the type is marked broken, and Path is unavailable along with everything else until the process restarts.

wrong.1: int.Parse(null) does throw ArgumentNullException, but only once and wrapped. The initializer is not run again.

cards.title: How not to break a type
cards.body:
The rule: static initialization holds only what cannot fail. Reading configuration, files, the network, parsing strings — move them where the error can be handled: an explicit Initialize method, a service constructor at startup, the DI container.

Lazy<T> does not save you automatically: in its default mode it also caches the factory's exception and throws it on every access to Value. Only LazyThreadSafetyMode.PublicationOnly retries the factory after a failure.
cards.code:
static readonly Lazy<Config> _config = new(
    LoadConfig,
    LazyThreadSafetyMode.PublicationOnly);  // failed — try again

public static Config Config => _config.Value;
cards.deep: In .NET Framework a broken type could be "cured" by unloading the AppDomain: in a new domain the type was loaded and initialized afresh. Modern .NET has no domains; only a collectible AssemblyLoadContext gives a similar effect: an assembly loaded into a new context means new types with new statics. For an ordinary application the answer is a restart.
