lessons.title: Unhandled, cost and your own exceptions
lessons.sub: What brings the process down, what throw costs, the TryXxx pattern and designing exceptions

cards.title: Where an exception brings down the whole process
cards.body:
An exception not caught in any frame of its own thread terminates the whole process — whether it is the main thread or not. This has been so since .NET 2.0; in .NET 1.x errors on background threads were silently swallowed.

The process crashes on an unhandled exception:

  • in a new Thread(...) thread;
  • in thread pool work: ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem, a System.Threading.Timer callback;
  • in a finalizer — the finalizer thread is just a thread;
  • in async void — the exception goes to the synchronization context or the pool.

An exception inside Task.Run does not crash the process: the task stores it, as in the "Async/await in depth" course.

cards.q: Which of these unhandled exceptions will terminate the process? Select all.
options: throw in the body of new Thread(...)
throw in Task.Run, nobody awaits the task
throw in a catch that is itself inside an outer try with a catch
cards.explain: A thread, the finalizer thread and a pool work item — the exception has nowhere further to go, so the process crashes. Task.Run puts the exception into the task. An exception from a catch is caught by the outer try — it is handled.

cards.title: AppDomain.UnhandledException — the last word
cards.body:
Before the crash the runtime raises AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException. The stack is not unwound yet, e.ExceptionObject holds the exception, and e.IsTerminating is true.

It is a notification, not a handler: it cannot cancel termination. Its job is to write a log, flush the logger's buffers, send a report. After the handler the process ends anyway.

One more thing: an exception from another thread cannot be caught by a try around Start or Join. Each thread has its own stack, and the handler search walks only that stack. Catch inside the thread.
cards.deep:
ExceptionObject is typed object: in IL you can throw anything, not just an Exception. C# will not let you, and the runtime wraps foreign objects in RuntimeWrappedException (the RuntimeCompatibility(WrapNonExceptionThrows = true) attribute, which the C# compiler puts on the assembly itself).

In ASP.NET Core an unhandled exception in a request does not crash the process: the server catches it and turns it into a 500 response. But background threads and async void crash there just the same. For background work there is BackgroundService; since .NET 6 a failed ExecuteAsync stops the host by default (BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost).

cards.q: What will the user see?
options: The process crashes, caught is not printed
Nothing: the thread's exception silently vanishes
cards.explain: The exception travels up thread t's stack, and there is no handler there. The main thread's try has nothing to do with that stack. Join just waits for the thread to finish; it does not pass errors along.

wrong.3: That was .NET 1.x. Since .NET 2.0 an unhandled exception on any thread terminates the process.

cards.title: What throw costs
cards.body:
A throw is not just a jump. The runtime:

  • creates the exception object on the heap;
  • in the first pass walks the stack and evaluates filters;
  • in the second pass unwinds frames, runs finally blocks and records each frame into the exception's stack.

The orders of magnitude: on .NET 9, throwing and catching a failed int.Parse takes a few microseconds, while int.TryParse on the same string takes a few nanoseconds. About a thousandfold difference, and it grows with stack depth. Exact numbers depend on the machine.

Hence the rule: exceptions are for exceptional situations. If failure is an ordinary outcome (bad input, missing key), return it as a value.
cards.deep: The most expensive part is turning the stack into text (method names, line numbers from the PDB), but it is lazy: you pay only if you read StackTrace or log ToString(). In .NET 9 CoreCLR switched to the managed exception handling from NativeAOT, and throws got several times faster — but the gap with a plain return is still huge.

cards.q: A file with a million lines, every tenth is not a number. Parsing uses int.Parse with catch (FormatException). Roughly how much time goes to the exceptions alone?
options: None: the JIT removes exceptions in Release
cards.explain: A hundred thousand throws at a few microseconds each — hundreds of milliseconds. With TryParse the same work would take a few milliseconds for the whole file. With a deeper stack exceptions cost even more.

wrong.3: The JIT does not turn throw into a returned value: every throw is a real stack walk and unwind.

cards.title: The TryXxx pattern
cards.body:
For operations where failure is a normal outcome, .NET uses the TryXxx pattern: the method returns bool, and the result comes through out. Usually there is a twin without Try that throws: int.Parse and int.TryParse, the dictionary indexer and TryGetValue.

The [NotNullWhen(true)] attribute tells nullable analysis: if it returned true, the out is not null. Without it the caller has to write user!.

A Try method does not swallow everything: it returns false only for the expected failure. Programmer and environment errors — a bad argument, a broken disk — it still throws.
cards.deep: The alternative is "test, then do" (tester-doer): if (dict.ContainsKey(k)) v = dict[k];. That is two lookups instead of one, and a race if another thread changes the collection. A Try method does the check and the action as one operation — which is why almost all of ConcurrentDictionary's API is TryAdd, TryRemove, TryUpdate.

cards.q: Finish the Try method so that after true the caller gets a non-null user with no warnings
cards.explain: NotNullWhen(true) ties the result to the out parameter. When there is no row, the method returns false and puts null into out — an ordinary outcome, not an exception.

cards.title: Your own exception: when and how
cards.body:
First ask whether you need a new type. A standard one often fits: ArgumentException and its descendants — a bad argument, InvalidOperationException — the object is in the wrong state, NotSupportedException, ObjectDisposedException. Your own type is needed when the caller will catch exactly it and react specially.

If you need one:

  • derive from Exception (not ApplicationException — that idea was dropped long ago);
  • end the name with Exception;
  • provide three constructors: empty, with a message, with a message and an inner exception;
  • put data for handling into properties, not just into the text.

Do not write the serialization constructor (SerializationInfo, StreamingContext) anymore: in .NET 8 it was obsoleted along with BinaryFormatter (SYSLIB0051).
cards.deep:
For argument checks there are ready-made helpers: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull (.NET 6), ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty and ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf (.NET 7), ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative and friends (.NET 8). They take the parameter name themselves via [CallerArgumentExpression].

Why throws are moved into a separate method: building the exception and the string bloats the method's code and gets in the way of inlining it. A call to a helper that only throws is recognized by the JIT as a no-return branch and moved to cold code. The [StackTraceHidden] attribute (.NET 6) hides the helper itself from the stack.

cards.q: Which exceptions should library code not throw itself? Select all.
cards.explain: Exception is too general: you cannot catch it separately from the rest. NullReferenceException and IndexOutOfRangeException are thrown by the runtime and signal a bug in the code. For a bad argument use ArgumentNullException and ArgumentOutOfRangeException, for a wrong state InvalidOperationException.

cards.title: Where to catch Exception as a whole
cards.body:
catch (Exception) without a filter catches everything: bugs, cancellation and things you did not think of. Its place is at the boundaries: the top of request or message handling, a thread's entry point, a background job's loop. There the error is logged and a decision is made: skip the item, retry, stop.

Inside the logic catch specific types or add a filter. Above all do not swallow OperationCanceledException: cancellation is not an error, and by swallowing it you keep doing work the user asked to stop.

cards.q: The user pressed Cancel, but the upload went on through the remaining files. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: Upload throws OperationCanceledException, and catch (Exception) catches it too: the cancellation is logged as "file skipped" and the loop goes on. You need the filter when (e is not OperationCanceledException) — then cancellation flies out and stops the loop.

lessons.title: Final: exceptions and reliability
lessons.sub: Two passes, rethrowing, broken types and cost

cards.q: Log prints a string and returns true only for "B". What does the program print?
cards.explain: First pass: filter A is false, the search goes on, filter B is true. Only now does the second pass unwind the stack: the inner finally prints F. The catch body runs last.

wrong.1: The inner try's finally runs in the second pass, which starts only after the first pass has found a handler — filter B.

cards.q: In which cases will finally not run? Select all.
options: The try is left by a break out of a loop
The process is killed with SIGKILL
The exception is caught in the calling method
cards.explain: Environment.Exit inside try does not run that thread's finally, and SIGKILL lets the process run nothing at all. break and an exception caught higher up are normal exits.

cards.q: The LIMIT variable is not set. Accessing Settings.Path throws TypeInitializationException. Which line is the real cause?
cards.explain: int.Parse(null) throws ArgumentNullException, which ends up in InnerException. The initializers of all fields form one static constructor, so the whole type is broken, Path included, until the process restarts.

cards.q: A background thread saved a caught exception in a field. The main thread must throw it with the original stack. How?
options: ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(e) in the thread, Throw() in the main one
throw saved; in the main thread
cards.explain: ExceptionDispatchInfo throws the same object and keeps the original stack, appending the new frames after a separator. await works the same way.

wrong.1: throw saved starts the stack at this line; the place in the background thread is lost.
wrong.2: throw; without an argument outside a catch is compile error CS0156.

cards.q: Match how it was in .NET Framework with how it is now
pairs: Unhandled on any thread crashes the process

cards.q: In a hot loop half the keys are missing from the dictionary. What is wrong with this code?
options: Every miss is a throw with a stack walk and unwind, microseconds instead of nanoseconds; use TryGetValue
Nothing: a try without an exception is free, and an exception costs as much as an if
The dictionary indexer returns default for a missing key, so the catch never fires
KeyNotFoundException must not be caught, it is a runtime exception
cards.explain: The try itself costs almost nothing; the throw is what is expensive. When a missing key is an ordinary outcome, check it with a value: TryGetValue does one lookup and does not throw.

wrong.2: The Dictionary indexer throws KeyNotFoundException. GetValueOrDefault and TryGetValue are the ones that return default.

cards.q: What is true about AppDomain.UnhandledException? Select all.
options: It fires for an unhandled exception on any thread
It lets you cancel process termination
It is the place to write a log and flush buffers
It fires for an exception in a Task nobody awaited
cards.explain: It is a notification before the crash: IsTerminating is true and it cannot be cancelled. Exceptions of unawaited tasks go to TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException and do not crash the process.

cards.q: The boundary of a background job: log any error, but let cancellation through
cards.explain: The when filter excludes OperationCanceledException: cancellation is not caught and stops the work, while the other errors go to the log.

units.title: Attributes and reflection
units.blurb: A custom attribute and where it lives in metadata, AttributeUsage and pseudo-attributes; the cost of reflection: Invoke, delegates, Expression, UnsafeAccessor and Activator; source generators instead of reflection, trimming and Native AOT.

lessons.title: A custom attribute
lessons.sub: The class, AttributeUsage, the metadata blob and pseudo-attributes

cards.title: An attribute is a class
cards.body:
An attribute attaches data to a type, method, field or parameter — data that is not executed but read. The reader can be the compiler ([Obsolete] → a warning at the use site), the runtime ([StructLayout]) or a framework: ASP.NET looks for [Route], a test runner for [Fact].

A custom attribute is an ordinary class derived from System.Attribute. Constructor parameters give positional arguments; public fields and properties with a set give named ones. Inside square brackets you can drop the Attribute suffix.
cards.deep:
Since C# 11 attributes can be generic: class TagAttribute<T> : Attribute and [Tag<int>]. The type argument follows the same rules as typeof: no dynamic, no nullable reference annotations, no tuples with element names.

Put [Conditional("DEBUG")] on the attribute class itself, and the compiler records the attribute in metadata only where the DEBUG symbol is defined. A Release build simply does not have it.

cards.title: Where an attribute lives: bytes, not an object
cards.body:
The compiler does not create an attribute object. It writes one row into the CustomAttribute metadata table: the owner (a type, method, field…), a reference to the attribute constructor and a blob — the arguments serialized to bytes.

Loading the assembly does not create an object either, and the constructor does not run. An instance appears only when someone asks for it through reflection — and every request gets a new one.

The key consequence: an attribute does nothing on its own. A [Route] that nobody looks for is just bytes in a file.
cards.deep:
Here is the blob the compiler writes for [Route("/orders", Order = 2)]:

01 00 — the prolog; 07 2F 6F 72 64 65 72 73 — a length-prefixed UTF-8 string; 01 00 — one named argument; 54 — it is a property (53 would be a field), 08 — type int32, 05 4F 72 64 65 72 — the name "Order"; 02 00 00 00 — the value.

The blob has no references to the constants the value was computed from — only the final values. How metadata tokens and tables work is covered in the ".NET inside out" course.

cards.q: How many times is ctor printed?
cards.explain: new Order() does not touch the attribute: it sits in metadata and is not needed to create an object. Each GetCustomAttribute parses the blob again and calls the constructor — two calls, two objects; x and y are different references.

wrong.2: The runtime does not cache attribute instances: every request creates a new object.
wrong.3: Creating an Order does not create the attribute. The attribute belongs to the type, not to an instance.

cards.title: Arguments: only what fits in the blob
cards.body:
Arguments are written to bytes at compile time, so the compiler must know the value. An argument can be:

  • a constant expression: a literal, a const, nameof, "a" + "b";
  • typeof(…);
  • a single-dimensional array creation.

And the parameter type comes from a short list: bool, char, the integer types and float/double, string, Type, enums, object and single-dimensional arrays of these. decimal, DateTime and Guid are out: the metadata format does not treat them as primitives.
cards.code:
[Timeout(Cfg.Ms * 2)]          // ok: a constant expression
[Tags(new[] { "db", "slow" })] // ok: a single-dimensional array
[Handler(typeof(List<int>))]   // ok: typeof
[Price(9.99m)]                 // CS0181: decimal is not an attribute parameter type
[Retry(Cfg.Retries)]           // CS0182: static readonly is not a constant
cards.deep:
The workaround for decimal and dates is a string parsed on read. That is how [DefaultValue(typeof(decimal), "9.99")] works.

typeof goes into the blob as a string — the full type name, plus the assembly name for a type from another assembly. On read the runtime loads the type by that name, so renaming the type in the other assembly breaks reading an already compiled attribute.

For an object parameter the blob stores a type tag before the value: [Value(5)] and [Value("5")] read back differently.

cards.q: Which line does not compile?
cards.explain: static readonly is a field filled in at run time, not a constant. The compiler has nothing to write into the blob: error CS0182. Cfg.Ms * 2 and nameof are computed at compile time, and typeof is allowed by a separate rule.

cards.title: AttributeUsage: where and how many times
cards.body:
[AttributeUsage] is an attribute on the attribute class. It sets three things:

  • where it may be applied — AttributeTargets flags: Class, Method, Property, Parameter, ReturnValue… The wrong place is error CS0592;
  • AllowMultiple — whether it may repeat on one element. By default it may not: CS0579;
  • Inherited — whether derived types see it when searched with inherit: true. Yes by default.

Without [AttributeUsage] the defaults apply: All, false, true. Placement and repetition are checked by the compiler — the runtime no longer checks them.
cards.deep:
A trap with Inherited: PropertyInfo.GetCustomAttributes(true), and the same on EventInfo, ignores the inherit parameter — an attribute on the overridden base property is not found. To walk the chain, use the static Attribute.GetCustomAttributes(member, true).

Interface attributes are never inherited: a class implementing an interface does not get them, whatever Inherited says. The chain follows base classes only.

The extension GetCustomAttribute<T>(member) searches with inherit: true by default, while Type.GetCustomAttributes(bool) makes you say it explicitly.

cards.q: Allow a route to be applied to a method twice
cards.explain: The attribute class derives from Attribute, and AttributeUsage with AllowMultiple = true allows repetition. Without it the second [Route] is CS0579.

cards.title: Reading: GetCustomAttribute and its cost
cards.body:
GetCustomAttribute<T>() finds the CustomAttribute rows for the element, picks the right type, parses the blob, calls the constructor and assigns named arguments. Every call does it again: parsing plus a fresh allocation. If two matching attributes exist, you get AmbiguousMatchException and need GetCustomAttributes.

Cheaper options:

  • IsDefined — a check only, no object is created;
  • GetCustomAttributesData() — arguments as data, without calling the constructor.

Frameworks read attributes once at startup and cache the result, for example in a static readonly field or a dictionary keyed by Type.

cards.q: What is true about reading attributes? Select all.
options: Two GetCustomAttribute calls return two different objects
IsDefined checks presence without calling the attribute constructor
The attribute object is created when the assembly loads and kept in a CLR cache
CustomAttributeData gives the arguments without calling the constructor
GetCustomAttribute only sees attributes from a Debug build
cards.explain: An instance is built from the blob on every request, so the objects differ and reading in a loop is expensive. IsDefined and CustomAttributeData work with metadata directly. The build configuration does not affect how attributes are recorded — except attributes marked [Conditional].

cards.title: Pseudo-attributes: flags, not rows
cards.body:
The compiler does not write some attributes into the CustomAttribute table. It turns them into bits and dedicated metadata tables that the type loader reads itself:

  • [Serializable] → a bit in the type flags;
  • [StructLayout] → type layout flags and the ClassLayout table (Pack, Size);
  • [FieldOffset] → the FieldLayout table;
  • [DllImport] → a method flag and the ImplMap table;
  • [NonSerialized], [MethodImpl] → field and method flags.

Reflection returns them inconsistently. It rebuilds Serializable and DllImport from the flags, but StructLayout cannot be found through GetCustomAttribute — only through the Type.StructLayoutAttribute property.
cards.code:
[Serializable]
[StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential, Pack = 1)]
struct Header { public byte Kind; public int Size; }

var t = typeof(Header);
var pack = t.StructLayoutAttribute!.Pack;              // 1 — from the ClassLayout table
var sl = t.GetCustomAttribute<StructLayoutAttribute>(); // null
var sr = t.GetCustomAttribute<SerializableAttribute>(); // not null: rebuilt from the flag
cards.deep:
This behaviour was checked on .NET 9. The runtime synthesizes such attributes in the PseudoCustomAttribute class, and which of them GetCustomAttribute returns is an implementation detail. Do not rely on GetCustomAttribute for pseudo-attributes; read the flags and the dedicated properties.

The Serializable flag can also be read through Type.IsSerializable, but since .NET 8 that property is marked obsolete (SYSLIB0050) together with all formatter-based serialization.

cards.q: Match the attribute with where it ends up in metadata
pairs: A bit in the type flags
Layout flags and the ClassLayout table
A row in the CustomAttribute table

cards.q: In version 2 of Shop.dll MaxItems became 100. Shop.dll was replaced, the app was not rebuilt. What maximum does a validator read from the attribute?
options: An exception when reading the attribute
cards.explain: The constant was evaluated when the app was compiled and sits in the attribute blob inside the app. Metadata has no reference to Limits.MaxItems at all, so replacing Shop.dll changes nothing. The new value appears only after a rebuild.

wrong.1: That would be the case with static readonly, but you cannot pass one to an attribute: CS0182.

lessons.title: The cost of reflection
lessons.sub: Invoke, delegates, Expression, UnsafeAccessor and Activator

cards.title: Reflection: a type as data
cards.body:
Reflection is the API that hands you metadata as objects: Type, MethodInfo, PropertyInfo, FieldInfo. Through them you can find a member by name, read and write a value, call a method, create an object.

The cost has two parts. Lookup: GetMethod("WithTax") compares strings and checks BindingFlags. The call: the compiler does not know the types, so the arguments travel in an object[] and the runtime checks them on every call.
cards.deep:
The runtime caches MethodInfo objects inside the type, so a repeated GetMethod is cheaper than the first, but the string lookup and flag checks remain. How these caches and metadata tokens work is covered in the ".NET inside out" course.

typeof(Order) compiles to loading the type token and calling Type.GetTypeFromHandle; the JIT usually folds that into a constant.

cards.q: Shop.Order lives in Shop.dll, which is already loaded. Code in App.dll calls Type.GetType("Shop.Order"). What comes back?
options: It depends on the assembly load order
cards.explain: Without an assembly name, Type.GetType searches only the calling assembly and System.Private.CoreLib. For a type from another assembly you need an assembly-qualified name: "Shop.Order, Shop". You get an exception only if you pass throwOnError: true.

wrong.3: Whether Shop.dll is loaded does not matter: without an assembly name it is simply not searched.

cards.title: Five ways to call a method
cards.body:
Orders of magnitude for calling a small method on a typical x64 machine (exact numbers depend on the hardware and version — measure with BenchmarkDotNet):

  • a direct call — about a nanosecond or less: the JIT can inline the method;
  • UnsafeAccessor (.NET 8) — like a direct call, even to a private member;
  • a delegate from CreateDelegate or a compiled Expression — a few nanoseconds: an indirect call with no inlining;
  • MethodInfo.Invoke — tens of nanoseconds plus allocations on every call;
  • GetMethod + Invoke on every iteration — more still.

The gap is orders of magnitude, not percent. You notice it in a hot loop; for a couple of calls at startup you do not.

cards.q: Order from fastest to slowest. The method is small, everything is prepared in advance, the call is in a hot loop.
items: GetMethod by name and Invoke on every iteration
cards.explain: The JIT can inline a direct call. A delegate is an indirect call. Invoke boxes arguments, allocates an array and checks types. A lookup by name adds string comparison on top.

cards.title: Why Invoke is expensive
cards.body:
On every MethodInfo.Invoke call:

  • an object[] is allocated for the arguments;
  • value-type arguments and the result are boxed;
  • the runtime checks the number and types of the arguments and the method's accessibility;
  • an exception from the method is wrapped in TargetInvocationException, the real one sits in InnerException.

None of this is needed when the signature is known in advance: then you use reflection once — to get a delegate.
cards.deep:
Since .NET 7, after the first calls the runtime generates an IL stub for the method, and Invoke became much faster than in .NET Framework. .NET 8 added MethodInvoker and ConstructorInvoker: arguments are passed without an object[], though value types are still boxed.

The BindingFlags.DoNotWrapExceptions flag turns the wrapping off: the method's exception propagates as is.

cards.q: The Pay method throws InvalidOperationException. What does this code print?
cards.explain: Invoke wraps the called method's exception in TargetInvocationException, so the first catch does not match. The original exception is in e.InnerException. To skip the wrapper, use BindingFlags.DoNotWrapExceptions.

wrong.1: That is what a direct call would do. Invoke puts its own wrapper between you and the method.

cards.title: CreateDelegate: reflection once
cards.body:
If the signature is known at compile time, turn the MethodInfo into a delegate. You pay once, at creation; after that it is an ordinary delegate call: no array, no boxing, no checks.

An open delegate takes the instance as its first parameter: one delegate for all objects. A closed one is bound to a single object: m.CreateDelegate<Func<decimal, decimal>>(order).

A property is a pair of methods: build the delegate from p.GetMethod or p.SetMethod.
cards.deep:
The generic CreateDelegate<T>() arrived in .NET 5; before that you wrote (Func<…>)Delegate.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<…>), m).

The delegate type must match the signature exactly, allowing for variance of reference types. For a struct method, an open delegate takes the instance by reference — you need your own delegate type with a ref parameter.

cards.q: Build a fast getter for the Total property
cards.explain: The getter is the get_Total method; its MethodInfo is in p.GetMethod. It takes an Order (an open delegate) and returns a decimal — that is Func<Order, decimal>. GetValue is the same slow path through object.

cards.title: Expression.Compile: when the types are known only at run time
cards.body:
A serializer or a mapper needs a getter for any property, and the type is known only at run time. Then a Func<object, object?> is built from an expression tree and compiled.

Compile() generates IL through DynamicMethod, and the JIT turns it into machine code. It is expensive: from hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds. But the call afterwards costs as much as a delegate call. So the result must be cached, for example by PropertyInfo.
cards.deep:
Where code cannot be generated at run time — Native AOT, iOS — Compile() does not fail; it returns a delegate over a tree interpreter. It works, but many times slower, and the win over Invoke is gone.

A value-type property is boxed when such a getter returns object — that is the price of the universal signature, not of reflection.

cards.title: UnsafeAccessor: private access without reflection
cards.body:
.NET 8 introduced [UnsafeAccessor]. You declare an extern static method, say which member it accesses, and the runtime generates the body itself. Kinds: Constructor, Method, StaticMethod, Field, StaticField.

The cost is that of a direct call: the JIT can inline it. The member is named statically, so it works with trimming and Native AOT.

Downsides: the name is a string. A typo surfaces on the first call as MissingFieldException or MissingMethodException. And you depend on private details of someone else's type — the next version may rename them.
cards.deep:
For a field the method returns a ref — you can both read and write. The first parameter is the instance (for static members too: its value is ignored, and its type says where to look).

.NET 9 added generics support: declare the method in a generic class with the same type parameters. .NET 10 added [UnsafeAccessorType] for when the type itself is not accessible at compile time.

cards.q: Match the approach with when you pay for it
pairs: Allocations and checks on every call
Expensive compilation, then a delegate-speed call
Almost nothing: access like a direct call
Looking up a member by string

cards.title: Activator and new T()
cards.body:
Activator.CreateInstance(Type) creates an object with the parameterless constructor. For new T() in a generic method with the new() constraint the compiler emits a call to Activator.CreateInstance<T>() — there is no dedicated IL instruction for it.

In modern .NET the runtime caches the constructor it found, and the cost is close to a plain new plus a few nanoseconds. In .NET Framework the gap was much larger — hence the old advice to "cache a factory via Expression".

The expensive variant is CreateInstance(type, args) with arguments: matching a constructor by argument types, plus an array and boxing on every call.

cards.q: What does the compiler turn new T() into in Make<T>() where T : new()?
options: A call to a static method T.New()
cards.explain: newobj needs a concrete constructor, and T has none until run time: for reference types the JIT even shares one body across all of them. So the compiler calls Activator.CreateInstance<T>(), which finds and caches the constructor of the actual type.

lessons.title: Generators, trimming and AOT
lessons.sub: Code at compile time instead of reflection at run time

cards.title: What is wrong with reflection at startup
cards.body:
A reflection-based serializer, DI container or logger does its work on every launch: it walks properties, reads attributes, compiles delegates. That costs startup time and memory. And nobody but the runtime sees that code: not the compiler, not the tool that strips unused code.

A source generator moves that work to compile time. It is a Roslyn component: it runs inside the project build, sees syntax and types, and adds new C# files. It cannot change existing code — so generators work through partial classes and partial methods: you declare, the generator writes the body.
cards.deep:
Generators arrived in .NET 5 (C# 9), and .NET 6 brought incremental ones (IIncrementalGenerator): the IDE reruns only the part whose inputs changed. Generated files show up in Solution Explorer under Dependencies → Analyzers, and with <EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>true</EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles> they are written to disk under obj.

A generator sees attributes as symbols (AttributeData): the arguments from the blob, without creating an object and without running your code.

cards.q: What can a source generator do?
options: Add new C# files to the compilation
Change the body of an existing method
Create an attribute object through GetCustomAttribute
cards.explain: A generator only adds code, and only during compilation. To plug into your type it needs partial: you write the declaration, the generator writes the implementation. It reads attributes as compiler metadata, not as objects.

wrong.1: Existing code is read-only for a generator. That is why every .NET generator requires partial.

cards.title: System.Text.Json: a context instead of analysing the type
cards.body:
Without hints, JsonSerializer walks a type's properties with reflection the first time it meets the type, builds metadata and caches it. The first call is noticeably more expensive than the rest.

With the generator you declare a partial class derived from JsonSerializerContext and list the types with [JsonSerializable] attributes. The generator writes a ready JsonTypeInfo<T> for each: the property list, getters and setters as plain code. Pass it to Serialize — no reflection.
cards.deep:
The System.Text.Json generator arrived in .NET 6. Modes: metadata — generates a description of the type and the serializer works from it; serialization (fast path) — generates direct code writing to Utf8JsonWriter, serialization only. Choose with [JsonSourceGenerationOptions(GenerationMode = …)].

Since .NET 8 there is a project property JsonSerializerIsReflectionEnabledByDefault=false: serialization without a context throws InvalidOperationException with a clear message. That way a forgotten call shows up in normal debugging, not after publishing with AOT.

cards.q: Hook up the System.Text.Json generator for Order
cards.explain: Types are listed with [JsonSerializable], and the class must be partial so the generator can extend it. The ready context instance is the static Default property, with one JsonTypeInfo property per type. [Serializable] is a pseudo-attribute of the old serialization; the generator ignores it.

cards.title: Regex and logging: the same trick
cards.body:
new Regex(p, RegexOptions.Compiled) parses the pattern at run time and generates IL through Reflection.Emit — expensive at startup. [GeneratedRegex] (.NET 7) writes C# matching code at compile time: startup is free, and you can read the generated code and step through it in the debugger.

logger.LogInformation("Order {Id} paid", id) parses the template on every call (with a cache), boxes id into a params object[] and allocates the array — even when the level is disabled. [LoggerMessage] (.NET 6) generates a strongly typed method: an IsEnabled check, no array, no boxing.
cards.deep:
With C# 13 and .NET 9 [GeneratedRegex] can also go on a partial property: public static partial Regex IsoDate { get; }.

Where code cannot be generated at run time, RegexOptions.Compiled is silently ignored and the interpreter runs. [GeneratedRegex] has no such drop.

Other generators from .NET 8: configuration binding (EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator), options validation, the Request Delegate Generator for Minimal APIs.

cards.q: Match the tool with the work it removes from run time
pairs: Walking the type's properties on the first Serialize
params object[] and boxing on every call

cards.title: Trimming and Native AOT
cards.body:
Trimming removes, at publish time, code that static analysis cannot reach. Analysis does not see a call by string: the method may be removed, and at run time you get MissingMethodException or null from GetMethod.

Native AOT compiles the whole program to machine code ahead of time and always trims. There is no JIT at run time — so no Reflection.Emit, and a generic built through MakeGenericType may have no ready machine code. Reflection itself works — for whatever was kept.

The analyzer flags risky spots with warnings: IL2xxx for trimming, IL3xxx for AOT. Turn them on with <IsAotCompatible>true</IsAotCompatible> in a library or PublishAot in an app.
cards.code:
string a = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order);    // IL2026 + IL3050
var t = typeof(List<>).MakeGenericType(type);  // IL3050
Type? u = Type.GetType(Console.ReadLine()!);   // IL2057
cards.deep:
IL2026 is a call to a member with [RequiresUnreferencedCode], IL3050 — with [RequiresDynamicCode]. In .NET 8+ these mark the APIs that cannot work without reflection over unknown types or code generation. Mark your own such method with the same attributes — the warning moves to its callers.

[UnconditionalSuppressMessage] silences a warning for good, including at publish time. Use it only once you have proven the needed members will be kept.

cards.q: What produces an analyzer warning with PublishAot? Select all.
options: Type.GetType(name), where name is read from a file
cards.explain: Serialize without a context is marked RequiresUnreferencedCode and RequiresDynamicCode (IL2026, IL3050), DynamicMethod is RequiresDynamicCode (IL3050), an unknown string in Type.GetType is IL2057. But the analyzer understands typeof plus a constant string: the Calc method will be kept.

cards.title: DynamicallyAccessedMembers: a contract about what to keep
cards.body:
When a method takes a Type and does something with it through reflection, the analyzer does not know which members to keep. A [DynamicallyAccessedMembers] annotation on the parameter says: "this type needs its public constructors" (or methods, properties…).

The requirement flows up the call chain. A caller that passes typeof(Order) — the analyzer keeps what is needed. A caller passing its own Type parameter must annotate it too. And if at the top the type came from a string — that is where the warning lands.

cards.q: On which line does the trimming analyzer warn?
cards.explain: Inside Run everything is clean: the parameter is annotated, so GetMethod is allowed. The analyzer sees typeof(Job) and keeps Job's public methods — through a local variable too. But a type from a typed-in string is unknown: IL2057 on the last line.

cards.title: Then and now
cards.body:
In .NET Framework reflection was the norm: XmlSerializer generated assemblies at run time, BinaryFormatter wrote any object through reflection, DI containers scanned assemblies, and RegexOptions.Compiled generated IL. The JIT was always there; trimming was not.

Today the .NET libraries are annotated for trimming and AOT, and hot paths move to generators. BinaryFormatter was removed in .NET 9: its methods throw PlatformNotSupportedException.

The rule: reflection over known types at startup or in tools is fine. On a hot path — a delegate, UnsafeAccessor or a generator. Under AOT — a generator.

cards.q: At startup a mini-framework finds every class with [Handler] via Assembly.GetTypes() and creates them through Activator. The app must be published with Native AOT. What is best?
options: A generator: build the handler list and their creation code at compile time
Cache the found types in a static field
cards.explain: Trimming removes classes nothing references in code, and GetTypes simply does not return them — silently, with no error. A generator finds [Handler] at compile time and writes new HandlerA(), new HandlerB(): the analyzer sees direct references, and there is no reflection at run time.

wrong.1: The warning goes away, the problem stays: removed classes are not found at run time.
wrong.3: A cache speeds up repeated lookups but does not bring back removed types.

lessons.title: Final: attributes and reflection
lessons.sub: Metadata, call cost and AOT

cards.q: Type t has one [Route] attribute. How many RouteAttribute objects does the loop create?
cards.explain: IsDefined looks at metadata and creates no object. GetCustomAttribute parses the blob and calls the constructor anew every time — 1000 calls, 1000 objects. Read once and cache.

wrong.2: IsDefined does not call the constructor — it only checks that the row exists.

cards.q: Which line does not compile? The attribute constructor parameters match the argument types.
cards.code:
enum Level { Low, High }

[Priority(Level.High)]
[Since("2026-01-01")]
[Owner(nameof(Billing))]
[Limit(1.5m)]
[Types(new[] { typeof(int), typeof(string) })]
class Billing { }
cards.explain: decimal is not on the list of attribute parameter types: CS0181. An enum, a string, nameof and a single-dimensional Type array are all allowed. Pass a fractional value as a double or a string.

cards.q: Which attributes does the compiler turn into flags and dedicated metadata tables rather than a CustomAttribute row? Select all.
cards.explain: Serializable is a bit in the type flags, DllImport is the ImplMap table, StructLayout is layout flags plus ClassLayout. The type loader reads them. Obsolete and Flags are ordinary attributes: the compiler and Enum.ToString read them.

cards.q: Put in order what happens inside t.GetCustomAttribute<RouteAttribute>()
items: Find the CustomAttribute rows owned by t
Keep those whose constructor belongs to RouteAttribute
Call the constructor with the positional arguments
Assign the named properties and fields
cards.explain: The object is built only at the very end and only on request. Until then the attribute is a table row and blob bytes.

cards.q: A hot loop calls a private method of someone else's type millions of times. The project targets .NET 8 and will later be published with Native AOT. What do you pick?
cards.explain: UnsafeAccessor costs as much as a direct call and needs no code generation at run time. Invoke is tens of nanoseconds and allocations on every call. A compiled expression is fast under the JIT but becomes an interpreter in Native AOT. dynamic does not see private methods.

wrong.2: Under the JIT it is a good option, but in Native AOT Compile returns a delegate over an interpreter — slower than Invoke.

cards.q: Match the diagnostic code with its cause
pairs: A Type passed without the required DynamicallyAccessedMembers annotation

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: For properties and events PropertyInfo.GetCustomAttributes ignores the inherit parameter and looks only at the override itself. The static Attribute.GetCustomAttributes walks the chain and finds [Track] on Base.Qty.

cards.q: In version 2 of the library the enum became enum Level { Low, Mid, High }. An app with [Priority(Level.High)], built against version 1 (Low, High), was not rebuilt. What does the attribute read?
options: An exception when reading the attribute
cards.explain: The blob holds the number 1 — the value of High in version 1, not the name. On read that number becomes a Level from the new library, where 1 is Mid. Add new enum members at the end, or better, give values explicitly.

units.title: LINQ and its cost
units.blurb: Deferred execution and Take, ToList and multiple enumeration, the buffering OrderBy, IQueryable and SQL from lambdas.

lessons.title: Lazy LINQ
lessons.sub: A query is a recipe, not a result

cards.title: Describing ≠ running
cards.body: The line var q = numbers.Where(…).Select(…) computes nothing. It only builds a chain. The work starts when something enumerates the result: foreach, ToList, Count, First…

cards.task: Step through the query. Watch the order in which Where and Select are called and where the query stops.

cards.q: Why were only four of the six numbers read?
options: Take(2) got two elements and stopped asking for more
cards.explain: The chain pulls elements one at a time. Once it has enough, it stops pulling.

cards.q: In what order do the calls happen?
options: Each element goes through the whole chain before the next is taken: Where(1), Where(5), Select(5)…
Where for all of them first, then Select for all
cards.explain: This is what streaming means.

cards.title: Trap: the data changed
cards.body: Since the query runs when it is enumerated, it sees the data as of enumeration, not as of when you wrote it.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: 2, 3 and 10 — the query ran after the Add.

cards.q: What triggers the query to run? Select all.
cards.explain: Where and Select only add links to the chain.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: ToList and multiple enumeration
lessons.sub: When to store the result, and when not to

cards.title: Every enumeration starts over
cards.body: A query does not remember its result. Enumerate it twice and the whole chain runs twice: reading again, Where again, Select again. If the source is a database or a file, that is two trips to it.

cards.task: The query is enumerated twice: Count() and foreach. Make the source read at most 6 times in total.

cards.q: With ToList, why is the source read only once even though it is still enumerated twice?
options: ToList ran the chain once and stored a list; Count() and foreach work on that list
cards.explain: Once materialized, you enumerate the list, not the query.

cards.task: Here ToList is unnecessary: because of it, Where runs for all six numbers. Get Where down to at most 4 calls.

cards.q: With ToList before Take, why did Where run 6 times?
options: ToList needs every element, so Take can no longer stop the reading
cards.explain: ToList is a wall: everything before it runs to completion.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Materialize (ToList, ToArray) if the result is enumerated several times or the source is expensive.
Don't materialize if you enumerate once or a Take/First comes later — laziness saves work.

The IDE warns you: "Possible multiple enumeration".

cards.q: Where does the database query run a second time?
cards.explain: Any() ran the query, and foreach runs it again. If you need all the users, call ToList() right away.

cards.q: When should you call ToList()? Select all.
options: The result is enumerated several times
The source is a slow database or file, and you need the result later
You need to freeze the data before the source changes
cards.explain: Before First(), ToList only forces reading everything.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: The cost of LINQ, and IQueryable
lessons.sub: Buffering, allocations and SQL from lambdas

cards.title: Not every operator streams
cards.body: To hand out the first element, OrderBy has to see them all — the smallest one might be last. Operators like this buffer: OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse, Distinct (partly).

cards.task: Add OrderBy before Where and step to the end. How many numbers have to be read?

cards.q: Take(2) comes after OrderBy. Does Take save you from reading every element?
options: No: OrderBy reads and sorts everything before handing out the first one
Only if there is little data
cards.explain: Sorting is a buffering operation.

cards.title: Where LINQ costs you
cards.body:
Every capturing lambda is an object; every operator has its own enumerator. In everyday code this does not matter. In a hot loop that spins millions of times a second (a game, a server under load), a plain for loop can be several times faster.

LINQ gets faster with every .NET release — profile first, rewrite second.

cards.q: What is faster for checking "is there at least one element"?
options: Any() — stops at the first one
cards.explain: For a list Count is cheap, but for a query or a database Any() does not scan everything.

cards.title: IQueryable: a lambda becomes SQL
cards.body: In Entity Framework, queries are IQueryable. A lambda there is not compiled into a method; it becomes an expression tree that EF translates into SQL.
cards.code:
db.Users.Where(u => u.Age > 18).Select(u => u.Name)
// SELECT Name FROM Users WHERE Age > 18

cards.q: Inside an EF Where you call your own C# method IsVip(u), which SQL knows nothing about. What happens in EF Core?
options: An exception: the expression cannot be translated to SQL
EF quietly loads the whole table
The method runs on the database server
cards.explain: Since EF Core 3.0, untranslatable expressions are no longer run quietly in memory — EF fails loudly.

cards.q: After which line does filtering happen in memory instead of in the database?
cards.code:
var names = db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
    .AsEnumerable()
    .Where(o => IsVip(o.Customer))
    .Select(o => o.Id);
cards.explain: AsEnumerable switches to LINQ to Objects: from there on everything runs in C#, and the database sends every order over 100.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The lambda is a regular method
The lambda is an expression tree

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: EF Core translates Where lambdas into SQL
AsEnumerable moves the rest of the work into memory
LINQ is always 100 times slower than for
cards.explain: There is a difference, but it is usually small and matters only on hot paths.

lessons.title: Final: LINQ
lessons.sub: Laziness, materialization and SQL

cards.task: The query is enumerated twice, and an extra OrderBy gets in the way. Make the source read at most 6 times and Where run at most 6 times.

cards.q: How many times does the query run?
cards.explain: Count, First and ToList each run the chain from scratch.

cards.q: What does OrderBy do when Take(1) follows it?
options: Reads and sorts everything, then hands out one
cards.explain: For the minimum, Min() or MinBy() is better — one pass, no sorting.

cards.q: Which line pulls extra data from the database?
cards.code:
var vip = db.Customers
    .ToList()
    .Where(c => c.Total > 1000)
    .Take(10);
cards.explain: ToList loaded every customer into memory, so the filter and Take ran in C#.

cards.q: Which of these run the query? Select all.
cards.explain: OrderBy and Where only describe steps.

cards.q: Match the symptom to the cause
Check for a match without scanning everything
cards.code: if (orders.___(o => o.IsLate)) Warn();
cards.explain: Any with a condition stops at the first match.

cards.q: When is it worth rewriting LINQ as a loop?
options: When the profiler shows a hot path with LINQ and its allocations
cards.explain: Measure first, optimize second.

units.title: Performance
units.blurb: Span<T> and copy-free slices, the rules of ref struct and Memory<T>, readonly struct, in and defensive copies.

lessons.title: Span<T>
lessons.sub: A window into memory, no copying

cards.title: A window, not a copy
cards.body: Span<T> is a "window" into a chunk of memory: a start and a length. The memory can be an array, a string, the stack or a native buffer. A slice span[2..5] copies nothing — it is a new window onto the same bytes.

cards.q: What is in arr[1] after middle[0] = 20?
options: 20 — the Span looks at the same array
cards.explain: A Span does not own memory; it just looks at it.

cards.task: Parsing the string "12,34,56" creates garbage right now. Pick a way that puts not a single object on the heap.

cards.q: Why does Split create 4 objects for the string "12,34,56"?
options: An array for the parts plus three new strings
cards.explain: Strings are immutable, so every part is a new string.

cards.title: ReadOnlySpan<char> and the stack
cards.body:
You can view a string as a ReadOnlySpan<char>: slices without copies, and int.Parse can read straight from a slice.

A small temporary buffer can live on the stack — no heap at all:
cards.code:
Span<byte> buf = stackalloc byte[256];
int written = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("hello", buf);

cards.q: Slice a string without copying
cards.code:
ReadOnlySpan<char> s = line.___();
var head = s[..___];
cards.explain: Substring would create a new string.

cards.q: Match them up
What can a Span look at? Select all.
cards.explain: Native memory too. A file has to be read into a buffer first.

cards.q: Why bother, if the GC cleans up garbage anyway?
options: Less garbage means fewer collections and pauses; in hot code the difference is huge
The GC cannot clean up strings
cards.explain: The fastest object is the one you never created.

lessons.title: ref struct: the rules of Span
lessons.sub: Why a Span can't be a field or cross an await

cards.title: A Span lives only on the stack
cards.body: A Span can point into stack memory. If a Span ended up on the heap, it would outlive its method — and point into a stack that now belongs to someone else. That is why Span is a ref struct: the compiler won't let it reach the heap.

cards.title: What you can't do
cards.body:
You can't store a Span in a class field, box it (into object or an interface), capture it in a lambda, or hold it across await or yield.

Since C# 13 you can declare a Span in an async method — but only between awaits, not across them.

cards.q: Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: A class field lives on the heap, and a Span is not allowed there.

cards.q: Where is the error?
cards.explain: head is used after the await — so it would have to survive the suspension and move to the heap. Not allowed.

cards.title: Memory<T> — for the heap and async
cards.body: Need a window you can store in a field or pass across an await? Use Memory<T>: a regular struct that can live anywhere, and .Span gives you a Span for work right here, right now.

cards.q: You need to keep a slice of a buffer in a class field. What do you choose?
cards.explain: Memory<T> is a regular struct with none of the ref struct restrictions.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Fine in a field and across await
Get a Span from a Memory

cards.q: What can't you do with a Span<T>? Select all.
options: Store it in a class field
Pass it as a parameter to a regular method
cards.explain: Passing it as a parameter is fine — that is still the stack.

lessons.title: readonly struct and in
lessons.sub: Defensive copies you can't see in the code

cards.title: A struct is copied whole
cards.body:
Pass a struct to a method and it gets copied. For a small one (int, Point) that is cheap. A 4×4 matrix is already 64 bytes on every call.

ref and in pass a reference instead of a copy. in also promises that the method won't change the struct.

cards.task: Get rid of the matrix copies, but make sure the method can't mess up the caller's matrix.

cards.q: Why did copies remain with in but without readonly struct?
options: The compiler doesn't know whether Det() and Trace() change the struct, so it calls them on a copy to keep the in promise
cards.explain: That is a defensive copy: invisible, but real.

cards.task: This one already uses in, yet there are two copies per call. Remove them without changing how the matrix is passed.

cards.title: readonly struct
cards.body:
readonly struct promises that no method changes the fields. The compiler checks this and can then call methods directly on the original — even through in.

In a regular struct you can mark individual methods readonly.

cards.q: What is the danger of ref instead of in?
options: The method can change the caller's struct
cards.explain: ref is for when you actually want the change.

cards.q: Match the passing mode to its behavior
No copies and no changes
cards.code:
public ___ struct Vec4 { … }
float Len(___ Vec4 v) => …;
cards.explain: The pair that in was invented for.

cards.q: A Point struct holds two ints. Is it worth passing it with in?
options: Usually not: copying 8 bytes costs no more than passing a reference
cards.explain: in pays off for large structs — 16–32 bytes and up.

lessons.title: Final: performance
lessons.sub: Span, ref struct, copies

cards.task: Start with Substring and find a way with no allocations.
The method takes the matrix by ref. Make it safe and copy-free.

cards.q: What will not compile?
cards.explain: A ref struct cannot be boxed: an object lives on the heap.

cards.q: You need to pass a buffer to an async method that writes to a stream. What do you pass?
cards.explain: A Span cannot be held across an await.

cards.q: What reduces pressure on the GC? Select all.
cards.explain: ToList creates a new list — that is extra garbage.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A window for the heap and async

cards.q: Why can't a Span be a field of a class?
options: It may point into the stack, and a class object outlives the method — the window would point at garbage
cards.explain: ref struct is how the compiler guarantees safety without run-time checks.

cards.q: in + a regular (non-readonly) struct with two method calls inside. How many defensive copies?
options: Two — one before each method call
cards.explain: Each method call on an in parameter is made on a copy.

units.title: Modern C#
units.blurb: Pattern matching, records, nullable references, required and what is new in C# 12, 13 and 14. The course final.

lessons.title: Pattern matching
lessons.sub: is, switch expressions and arm order

cards.title: Check and extract in one go
cards.body: is checks the type and declares a variable at the same time. Property patterns look inside the object.
cards.code:
if (shape is Circle { R: > 10 } big)
    Console.WriteLine($"big circle {big.R}");

cards.title: The switch expression
cards.body: Arms are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. _ means "everything else", null included. The compiler complains (CS8510) if an arm can never be reached because everything is already caught above it.

cards.task: The arms are mixed up: a point becomes a circle, a square becomes a rectangle, and null becomes "something else". Put them in order with the ▲ buttons.

cards.q: Why did null end up in "something else"?
options: _ catches everything, null included, and the null arm was below it
You can't check for null in a switch
cards.explain: Specific cases go higher, general ones lower.

cards.title: More patterns
cards.body:
Relational: < 0, >= 18.
Logical: and, or, not.
List (C# 11): [1, .., var last].

cards.q: What does Grade(95) return?
cards.explain: 95 is neither below 0 nor above 100, but it is ≥ 90 — the first matching arm.

cards.q: Not null and not an empty string
cards.code: if (name is ___ null ___ "") Greet(name);
cards.explain: name is not null and not "" — it reads almost like plain English.

cards.q: Match the pattern to its meaning
The arm Rect r sits above Rect { W: var w, H: var h } when w == h. What does the compiler say?
options: CS8510: the second arm is unreachable — every Rect is already caught
It picks the more specific arm by itself
cards.explain: The compiler doesn't reorder arms — the first one wins.

lessons.title: Records
lessons.sub: Value equality and with

cards.title: A value type in one line
cards.body: A record (C# 9) is a class for which the compiler writes the constructor, properties, content-based equality, ToString and deconstruction for you.

cards.q: a and b are two different record Point(1, 2) objects. What does a == b return?
cards.explain: A regular class would give False — it would compare references.

cards.title: with: a copy with changes
cards.body: The properties of a positional record are init: they don't change after creation. Need a modified version? Make a copy.
cards.code: var moved = a with { X = 10 };   // Point { X = 10, Y = 2 }, a is unchanged

cards.q: Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: Age is an init property. You change it with with.

cards.title: record struct
cards.body: Since C# 10 there is record struct — a value type with the same conveniences. Its properties are mutable by default; readonly record struct makes them init.

cards.q: What does a record generate for you? Select all.
options: A ToString that shows the contents
cards.explain: Saving is the ORM's job, not the language's.

cards.q: Where do records shine?
options: DTOs, messages, dictionary keys, immutable values
EF entities with mutable state and identity
cards.explain: An entity with an Id is usually compared by Id, not by every field.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Value type with the same conveniences
Can only be set at creation

lessons.title: Nullable references
lessons.sub: string and string? are different promises

cards.title: The billion-dollar mistake
cards.body:
NullReferenceException is the most common error in .NET. Since C# 8 you can turn on the nullable context: then string means "never null here", and string? means "may be null". The compiler keeps track and warns you.

New projects have it on by default: <Nullable>enable</Nullable>.

cards.q: On which line does the compiler warn about a possible null?
cards.explain: CS8602: name may be null. Check it, or use name?.Length.

cards.title: Keeping the compiler happy, honestly
cards.body:
Check: if (name is not null) — after that the compiler knows it is not null.
A default value: name ?? "guest".
Last resort: name! — "trust me, it's not null". If you're wrong, you get that very exception.

cards.q: What does the ! operator do in name!.Length?
options: It only silences the warning; nothing is checked at run time
It checks for null and throws a clear exception
It turns null into an empty string
cards.explain: It exists only for the compiler.

cards.title: required
cards.body: A property can't be null, but it is set by an initializer rather than the constructor? required (C# 11) forces you to set it at creation.

cards.q: The name, or "guest" if it is null
cards.code: var shown = name ___ "guest";
cards.explain: The null-coalescing operator.

cards.q: Match them up
Which are true about nullable references? Select all.
options: It is a compiler check, not a runtime one
They are on by default in new projects
After if (x is not null) the compiler treats x as not null
cards.explain: Nullable<T> is only for value types. string? is just an annotation for the compiler.

lessons.title: C# 12, 13 and 14
lessons.sub: What the latest versions added

cards.title: C# 12: primary constructors
cards.body: Constructor parameters go right in the class header. Key point: these are not properties but parameters available throughout the class body.

cards.q: Given class Service(IRepo repo), can outside code write service.repo?
options: No: repo is a parameter, not a public property
cards.explain: In a record, positional parameters become properties; in a regular class they don't.

cards.title: C# 12: collection expressions
cards.body: Square brackets create an array, a list, a Span — whatever the target type needs. .. spreads another collection in.

cards.q: A list of zero, the elements of a, and five
cards.code: List<int> all = [0, ___a, 5];
cards.explain: The spread is two dots.

cards.title: C# 13
cards.body:
params collections: params ReadOnlySpan<int> instead of an array — no allocation.
A new lock type, System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9): lock on it is faster than on an object.
ref struct in async methods — between awaits.
cards.code:
private readonly Lock _gate = new();

lock (_gate) { _count++; }

cards.title: C# 14 (.NET 10)
cards.body:
field — the hidden backing field of an auto-property.
extension blocks — extension properties, not just methods.
?.= — assign only if the left side is not null.
Implicit Span conversions: an array turns into a Span by itself wherever one is expected.
cards.code:
public string Title { get; set => field = value.Trim(); }

order?.Status = Status.Paid;

cards.q: Match the feature to the version
What does order?.Status = Status.Paid do if order == null?
cards.explain: Null-conditional assignment, new in C# 14.

cards.q: What arrived in C# 12–14? Select all.
cards.explain: async is from C# 5, LINQ from C# 3.

lessons.title: Course final
lessons.sub: Everything together

cards.task: Fix the switch: every shape should land in its own arm.
The method puts T into a stack buffer and sorts it. It must accept int.
Make it print 0 1 2 while keeping the for loop.

cards.q: How many times does the query run?
cards.code:
var q = users.Where(u => u.IsActive);
if (q.Any()) Console.WriteLine(q.Count());
cards.explain: Any and Count are two separate enumerations.

cards.q: Where is the compile error?
cards.explain: The properties of a positional record are init-only.

cards.q: Match the task to the tool
pairs: Parse a string with no garbage
A big struct with no copies
A sum for any number type

cards.q: What does the compiler check, rather than the runtime? Select all.
options: Going out of a Span's bounds
cards.explain: Span bounds are checked at run time — IndexOutOfRangeException.

cards.q: Why can't a List<string> be assigned to a List<object>, while an IEnumerable<string> can go into an IEnumerable<object>?
options: IEnumerable only hands out elements (out T), but you could put a foreign type into a List
cards.explain: Variance is about type safety.

cards.code: public string Name { get; set => ___ = value.Trim(); }
cards.explain: this.Name would recurse forever.
